articles.title_orig: Dow rises, Nasdaq slides as investors continue to rotate out of AI stocks: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow rises, Nasdaq slides as investors continue to rotate out of AI stocks: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stocks were mixed on Friday as traders headed for a mostly losing week amid a rotation out of tech and artificial intelligence-related names.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 129 points, or 0.3%, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 1.1%. The S&P 500 traded down 0.4%.
Chipmakers were lower again. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) lost 1%, led by declines in Micron Technology , Advanced Micro Devices and Sandisk . Semiconductors have struggled this week amid jitters about competition from China . The SMH is down 8% week to date.
Those declines, coupled with drops in other stocks linked to AI, put the S&P 500 on pace for a losing week. The benchmark index is down almost 1% this week, while the Nasdaq has shed about 3%. The Dow, on the other hand, has moved higher by more than 1% on the week.
Investors have also grown concerned that tech companies are borrowing too much for the AI buildout . Shares of neoclouds like CoreWeave , which has seen its total debt rise to more than $51 billion , were down around 9%, putting the stock's week-to-date losses at more than 22%.
"The question is: Is this a systemic issue?" said Michael Rosen, Angeles' chief investment officer. "Obviously, increased debt issuance is something to observe and continue to watch and be concerned about if it continues to get to levels of excessiveness. But we're not remotely close to that right now."
Other areas of the market such as financials saw gains. JPMorgan advanced around 2%. Additionally, shares of sporting goods retailer Nike and drugmaker Merck each climbed around 1%, adding to the Dow's rise.
Simultaneously, investors have been grappling with hotter-than-expected inflation data, which has been exacerbated by elevated energy prices in the wake of the U.S.-Iran war. Wholesale inflation this week saw its biggest gain since 2022 , while consumer inflation remained well above the Federal Reserve's target of 2%.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke at an IMF event in Bangkok overnight. And while he didn't comment on whether the Fed would raise rates before year-end, traders took that as a sign that the central bank will hold policy steady later this month. The CME Group's FedWatch tool points to an 85% chance the Fed keeps its overnight rate unchanged at its Oct. 27-28 meeting.
Early in the "SaaSpocalypse" that roiled software companies this year, Manish Gupta, a portfolio manager at First Eagle Investments, added to Workday as he parsed through the wreckage for some bargains.
In recent months, that bet has paid off for the value investor. After falling about 40% in the first quarter of 2026, during which the enterprise software stock at various points was trading at not even three times revenue, the stock went on to surge more than 55% in the third. It's also outperforming this week, rising more than 2% amid a broader tech sell-off as investors exit for safer assets.
Gupta, who attended the company's analyst day this week, remains confident in Workday, which he said is trading at a discount to similar businesses in the private markets. Workday is a top 10 holding in the First Eagle Global Fund (SGENX) , which he co-manages and which had nearly $75 billion in total net assets as of Sept. 30.
"The price has moved up, but the business has also become better," Gupta said. "The 'SaaSpocalypse' has also turned around, but the stock's still attractive."
CNBC Pro subscribers can read more here .
The near-term case against stocks is growing, according to Bank of America.
Strategist Michael Hartnett laid out four reasons why the bank is taking a "risk-off" approach for the next month:
CNBC Pro subscribers can read more here .
The spread is widening between AI leaders OpenAI and Anthropic as a sell-off in CoreWeave leads neocloud stocks lower.
OpenAI's valuation is down more than 4% the past 24 hours after briefly slipping under $1.5 trillion, according to perpetual futures pricing on decentralized exchange Hyperliquid. Meanwhile, Anthropic perps are up 2.4% over the same time period, recovering an overnight dip and indicating a valuation of just over $2 trillion.
Read the full story here .
The S&P 500 kicked off Friday's session in positive territory.
The broad market average moved up 0.1% just after 9:30 a.m. ET, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 0.2%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 188 points, or 0.4%.
Wells Fargo Investment Institute isn't buying longer-term bonds yet, despite the move lower in Treasury yields.
The firm doesn't believe investors are still adequately compensated for the risks associated with extending duration, which is a measure of interest rate sensitivity.
"Financial conditions are tightening, long-term borrowing costs face upward pressure, and investors are increasingly demanding additional compensation to hold longer-maturity bonds," said Darrell Cronk, president of Wells Fargo Investment Institute and  chief investment officer of Wealth & Investment Management.
"Currently, we do not believe we have reached the peak in interest rates for this cycle, so caution is warranted."
Greg Abel, the new leader of Berkshire Hathaway "pushes into new territory" with the firm's latest investment in Bending Spoons, an Italian-based private equity firm, Morningstar wrote Wednesday.
Abel, who took over as CEO in January, led a $330 million investment in Bending Spoons, following Berkshire's $600 million investment from July, when the Italy-based serial acquirer went public on the Nasdaq.
"It is a sign that the firm is finally moving out of its comfort zone to find places to put capital to work," Morningstar analyst Greggory Warren wrote.
The investments is already bearing fruit. As of Oct. 15, Berkshire is sitting on a nearly 80% gain on its investment in Bending Spoon, Morningstar noted, after shares rose in the days following the announcement of Berkshire's additional stake.
Tesla shares climbed nearly 5% premarket after the EV maker unveiled its long-awaited second-generation Roadster on Thursday. The vehicle features SpaceX-developed rocket-style thrusters, giving investors another reason to focus on the overlap between Elon Musk's companies.
SpaceX also rose after Evercore ISI raised its price target on the stock to $275 from $230, while reiterating an outperform rating, citing stronger AI and Starship catalysts. Tesla describes it as the world's first flying car and expects production to begin in 2028.
The aluminum producer, Alcoa rose more than 2% after stronger quarterly results, while CoreWeave fell 4% premarket after the stock came under pressure this week as investors braces for higher interest rates that might impact the highly indebted company.
Read more here on companies making the biggest moves premarket.
Travelers shares were down 4% even after the company reported third-quarter results that beat analyst expectations. The insurance giant posted core third-quarter earnings of $9.18 per share on revenue of $12.48 billion. Analysts polled by LSEG expected a profit of $7.42 per share on revenue of $11.38 billion.
CoreWeave shares were 4% lower in premarket at 4:40 a.m ET on Friday, following a rollercoaster session in which it tumbled on fears over its debt pile before ending higher.
Tesla shares were up 4.4% after the electric vehicle maker unveiled its next-generation Roadster , which can accelerate from zero to 60 miles per hour in less than a second.
U.S. Treasury yields declined on Friday as investors weighed hotter-than-expected inflation data and Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh's latest comments on interest rates.
Shares of renewable energy firm Nordex jumped nearly 14% in early deals after the company raised its earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) margin guidance for full-year 2026 to 11.5% to 12.5% from 8% to 11%.

articles.title_orig: Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs moved to a new prison after reports of a luxury lifestyle behind bars
articles.title_zh: Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs moved to a new prison after reports of a luxury lifestyle behind bars
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK -- Sean "Diddy" Combs has been moved to a federal prison in Pennsylvania after reports that the hip-hop mogul was living the high life and was injured in a fight at his New Jersey lockup, a person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press on Friday.
The federal Bureau of Prisons is transferring Combs, 56, from FCI Fort Dix to FCI Allenwood Low, a low-security facility south of Williamsport and about 155 miles (250 kilometers) west of New York City, the person said. The person was not authorized to speak publicly and did so on condition of anonymity.
The Bureau of Prisons confirmed the move but provided no further details. The agency said it does not discuss conditions of confinement for anyone in its custody, including reasons for transfer, for privacy, safety, and security reasons.
"Decisions about inmate placement are made by the BOP, and we are not in a position to speak to the circumstances surrounding this transfer," said Combs' spokesperson, Juda Engelmayer. "Sean remains focused on moving forward, and we hope that his time at the new facility will be productive and without unnecessary disruption."
Combs is serving a four-year, two-month sentence for his conviction last year on prostitution-related charges for transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters. The case featured harrowing testimony about violence and sex parties he called "freak-offs." It was a forceful reckoning for one of music and entertainment's most influential figures.
Last month, NBC News reported that Combs was continuing to enjoy aspects of his millionaire lifestyle at FCI Fort Dix, smuggling in Hennessy, having fellow inmates cook, clean, make his bed and give him massages, and using a contraband cellphone to view social media and an ex-girlfriend's nude selfies.
On Wednesday, TMZ reported that Combs was injured in a fight with another inmate at Fort Dix and had to be taken out of the prison for treatment. In a rare rebuttal, the Bureau of Prisons refuted TMZ's report, telling the AP: "The story you are referring to is false and did not happen."
In the wake of the NBC report, Combs was placed in the prison's special housing unit, a heavily secured part of the facility away from the general population, for inmates with disciplinary issues or security concerns. He has also been docked 41 days of good-conduct credit, pushing his release date back to March 2, 2028, according to the person familiar with the matter.
In April, the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals heard arguments in Combs' bid to overturn his conviction and sentence, which his lawyers argued was too harsh. The court has yet to rule.

The statement noted that, facilitated by the China-EU Trade Consultation Mechanism (TIC), both sides recently reached multiple agreements on bilateral economic and trade issues — including the automotive sector — on the basis of equality and mutual benefit.
The principles affirmed in this consultation respect facts and ensure fairness, aligning with WTO rules while balancing the legitimate rights of all parties and addressing reasonable concerns. This lays a solid foundation for long-term, stable cooperation between enterprises on both sides. It also helps prevent trade frictions from escalating, keeps the automotive supply chain stable and flowing, and creates a more predictable environment for trade and investment among automakers.
Moving from "Made in China" to "Globally Trusted," GAC Group has consistently relied on strategic resolve, deep technological expertise, and extensive local layouts to drive high-quality global expansion for Chinese industries — delivering the value of better mobility to users worldwide.
GAC Group pledged to continue operating in strict compliance with the law. Using the consensus from this China-EU hybrid vehicle trade consultation as a springboard, the automaker plans to deepen its presence in Europe and strengthen mutually beneficial ties with European partners. By delivering high-quality products and services, GAC aims to foster shared growth in the China-EU auto industry and ensure bilateral economic cooperation remains steady and enduring.

articles.title_orig: First images released of Pope Leo celebrating Mass at hospital after cancer surgery
articles.title_zh: First images released of Pope Leo celebrating Mass at hospital after cancer surgery
articles.content_orig:
The first images of Pope Leo since his lung cancer surgery have been released, showing him standing up and celebrating mass in a makeshift hospital chapel.
Leo led mass at midday on Friday with off-duty medical and nursing staff from the Gemelli Hospital present as the Vatican said he showed “steady improvement” after having part of his lung removed earlier in the week.
The pope thanked staff for their work caring for himself and others who are sick during his homily, the Vatican said.
The Mass took place in a room on the 10th floor of the hospital where a suite of rooms is set aside for any time a pope is admitted for medical treatment.
The Vatican also said that Pope Leo will recite the traditional Angelus prayers on Sunday in what will be his first public appearance since his treatment.
In the latest update from the Vatican, the press office said Leo underwent blood tests and a chest X-ray on Friday morning.
The pontiff is continuing his respiratory physiotherapy sessions, doctors involved in his treatment said, adding that his  recovery allows him to carry out normal daily activities independently.
The 71-year-old is completely autonomous now in movement and breathing, the Vatican added.
Post-operative test results to confirm whether the pope is completely cancer free and what, if any, treatment is needed have not been released yet.
The news of the pope’s diagnosis has been received with shock inside the Vatican, with Leo known as someone as physically active and seen to be in good health.
The pope’s engagements have been cancelled until 20 October and it is not clear whether his planned trip to Latin America from 6-17 November will take place.
The Vatican, however, are continuing with preparations for the visit and on Friday posted the list of journalists traveling with the pope to report on the trip.
This story has been updated.

articles.title_orig: Warsh Boosts Market Expectations of Fed Rate Hold in October
articles.title_zh: Warsh Boosts Market Expectations of Fed Rate Hold in October
articles.content_orig:
BANGKOK — Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh refrained from signaling whether there will be another interest rate hike again this month, while acknowledging a "synchronous tightening" by central banks around the world.
"I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year," Warsh said, reiterating his opposition to the use of forward guidance for markets that should rely on interpreting data.
He also acknowledged that stance may disappoint anyone who had hoped for a steer ahead of the central bank meeting later this month. "It's a new chapter at the Fed [and] we're not in that business anymore," he said.
Warsh spoke at a fireside chat with the International Monetary Fund's managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, as part of the weeklong IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday.
"Alongside other recent comments from FOMC participants, Warsh's comments indicate that the FOMC is set to pause in October," Goldman Sachs economists led by Jan Hatzius wrote in a note. "We continue to expect a second and final hike in December."
S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures edged higher following the speech, while stock market indexes in Asia and Treasury yields were largely stable.
Warsh described the global shift toward tighter monetary policy as a common fight on prices. Central banks made their own choices under their own mandates, he said, but the result was "a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world," which means "there's no free riders."
Surging energy costs stemming from the Iran war and artificial intelligence investment boom are stoking inflation and pushing up borrowing costs around the world, just as global public debt is on pace to exceed 100% of the world's GDP, a level last breached in the aftermath of World War II.
The U.S. government has insisted that strong growth would be the best way to grow out of its rising debt pile, dismissing IMF's warning that the plans of relying solely on growth won't work as something that needs to be taken "with a grain of salt."
Warsh also expressed optimism about how AI will make economies that use it well more productive and wealthier, while warning the road there may be "very bumpy," and its near-term effect on employment is still uncertain.
"I want you to hear from me optimism, but optimism leavened by the seriousness of purpose," Warsh said.
A decade from now, he said, people will look back on the developments and "say this was hugely consequential."
The Fed raised rates to a range of 3.75% to 4% last month, its first hike since 2023 . Traders see a 72.3% chance for the Fed to keep the interest rate unchanged at the Oct. 27-28 meeting, according to CME FedWatch, while the majority expect a 25 basis point hike at the December meeting.

articles.title_orig: “Against Tech Oligarchy”: Inside the Worker Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry - Democracy Now!
articles.title_zh: “Against Tech Oligarchy”: Inside the Worker Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry - Democracy Now!
articles.content_orig:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.
Longtime tech worker organizers Clarissa Redwine and JS Tan’s new book, Against Tech Oligarchy: Worker Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry , draws on the authors’ experiences at major tech companies to chronicle the rise and fall of the tech worker movement, its early victories, and the repression and slide to corporate control that followed.
“Over the course of the 2010s, what we saw was that the tech industry wasn’t quite the industry that it had promised to its workers and to the public. Rather than making the world more open, more democratic, we saw it really be the culprit of misinformation,” says Tan, who was pushed out of Microsoft after raising objections to the company’s ties to fossil fuel companies.
Silicon Valley’s slide to the right was influenced by corporate backlash to labor’s demands, explains Redwine, who was fired from Kickstarter for union organizing. She says she hopes to inspire a new generation of tech workers to organize “within these tech oligarchs’ own empires, to stand up and push back.”

articles.title_orig: 'We're not moving fast enough': World falling short of promised 30% land and water goals ahead of UN biodiversity summit
articles.title_zh: 'We're not moving fast enough': World falling short of promised 30% land and water goals ahead of UN biodiversity summit
articles.content_orig:
Efforts to raise hundreds of billions of dollars to preserve the world’s oceans, forests, rivers, lakes and other parts of the natural world have fallen short ahead of a key U.N. summit on biodiversity.
The yawning gap between the stated ambition of nations to protect biodiversity and what money has been raised will be a central topic in Yerevan, Armenia, when the biodiversity conference, known as COP17, gets started on Monday. The nearly two-week event, scheduled to end Oct. 30, is a chance for nearly 200 countries that are part of the treaty to take stock of their progress on 23 global targets after agreeing to a historic deal crafted in Montreal in 2022. The United States is not a party to the treaty.
Countries in Montreal committed to protect 30% of land and water considered important for biodiversity by 2030, a goal known as 30×30.
They also promised to raise $200 billion a year by 2030 for biodiversity and begin phasing out or reforming subsidies that could provide another $500 billion for nature. There were also commitments to increase to $20 billion annually by 2025 money that went to poor countries. That number would increase to $30 billion each year by 2030.
“We’re not moving fast enough,” convention executive secretary Astrid Schomaker told The Associated Press, before a U.N. progress report released Thursday found fewer than half of parties’ biodiversity targets are on track and that current commitments would only protect 26% of land and only 12% of sea by 2030.
Data from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development showed countries were raising between $75 billion and $92 billion each year from 2023 to 2025 — less than half the 2030 goal. Commitments to reduce $500 billion in harmful subsidies — government support and funding for sectors like fisheries and agriculture — have gained little traction, with few countries identifying which subsidies they would cut.
Countries were on track to provide the $20 billion to poor countries by 2025. The latest data showed $19 billion had been raised in 2024. But a drop in foreign aid raises questions over whether the upward trend will continue.
“Do we have enough money actually to finance the commitments that countries have made? And how do we get more finance to flow toward biodiversity positive outcomes?” Schomaker said. “That is the crucial question for the COP.”
The campaign to protect biodiversity, which first garnered global attention with the Rio Earth Summit in 1992, has often seemed like a losing battle.
In a bid to grow their economies and support increasing populations, countries have converted forests into farm land, overfished their waters and reduced habitats of many plants and animals through unchecked development. Climate change , at the same time, has created the conditions for widespread wildfires and prolonged droughts that have decimated ecosystems.
As a result, three-quarters of the world’s land has been “severely altered” by humans and a million of the world’s plants and animals are threatened with extinction, according to a 2019 U.N. report . Wildlife populations have also plummeted, according to the WWF’s 2026 Living Planet Report released this month. They have declined on average by 73% between 1970 and 2022.
“We are losing everything that matters for us as humans on this planet,” Schomaker said.
Meanwhile, there are some signs that countries are protecting more biodiversity. Countries have announced over 5,000 initiatives tied to the treaty.
A report from the Campaign for Nature, a global initiative which has spearheaded the 30×30 effort, found that countries in Latin America have already committed to protecting 29% of their land while those in Oceania have promised to preserve 41% of their seas. Last year, the Philippines created a marine protected area where catching rays and sharks is prohibited, according to the Wildlife Conservation Society. In 2023, Cambodia set aside almost 100,00 acres (40,000 hectares) of flooded grassland habitat for protection while Argentina created a national park in 2024.
Brian O’Donnell, director of the Campaign for Nature, said where and what we need to protect is clear, as are the methods to do so.
“What is now needed is an upswing in political ambition and determination,” said O’Donnell.
O’Donnell said an international agreement reached last year to protect marine diversity on the high seas — the High Seas Treaty — would help but more was needed.
Many expected conference attendees are hoping countries, the private sector and philanthropies use the meeting next week to announce major biodiversity funding initiatives.
Susan Lieberman, the vice president for international policy for WCS, said that protecting important biodiversity required money and expertise.
“You can’t just say, OK, there’s a line on the map. You need to do the science,” she said. “You need to know if it’s in the right place. If you’re going to establish a park, you better have management of the park, governance, infrastructure.”
That is especially true in poorer countries, according to Dorothy Maseke, head of the African Natural Capital Alliance Secretariat, an African-led initiative to integrate nature into financial decision-making. Many developing countries with significant biodiversity are not able to finance protecting and conserving it, as governments are trying to also pay to finance healthcare, education, infrastructure and public services.
Daniel Mukubi, the biodiversity negotiator for Congo, agreed it was “not possible to scale up protected and conserved areas” without sufficient financial help. He lamented that overseas development assistance, including from the United States, has dropped significantly. That has resulted in “weakened law enforcement and eco-guards patrolling critical habitat” including at several of the country’s UNESCO World Heritage sites.
“If these valuable ecosystems collapse because international funding fails to secure them, the resulting economic damages will cost the global market tens of trillions of dollars,” Mukubi said. “So, investing in the Congo basin is not an expenditure. It is the most cost-effective insurance policy the West can buy.”
Another topic expected to be big is how to get governments to reduce an estimated $7.3 trillion in subsidies and redirect that money into nature. That is about 30 times more than what was invested in nature-based solutions in 2023, according to the Campaign for Nature.
“Every year, trillions of dollars go into subsidies that harm nature, even as funding to protect it falls far short of what’s needed,” Patricia Zurita, Conservation International’s executive director, said in a statement. “We can’t reverse biodiversity loss while continuing to finance the activities that drive deforestation, overfishing, pollution and more.”
Associated Press reporter Sibi Arasu in Bengaluru, India, contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: The incredible flying Tesla Roadster is just for show
articles.title_zh: The incredible flying Tesla Roadster is just for show
articles.content_orig:
It’s OK to marvel at the stunt — it’s pure spectacle.
It’s OK to marvel at the stunt — it’s pure spectacle.
Last night, Elon Musk gave the people what they want: a car driving vertically up a multi-story ramp, launching off the edge, executing a mid-air “kickflip” over a lineup of Teslas, and landing via cold-gas thrusters.
That’s what the people want, right? “We were promised flying cars,” sure, but isn’t the operative word in that statement “we”? Because as far as I can tell, everything we saw last night — while extremely cool and incredibly impressive — won’t result in a real, production-ready car you can park, or, I guess, land in your driveway.
Tesla’s late-night demonstration in Waco, Texas, certainly gave some corners of the internet what it wants. And the gushing praise and wide-eyed reactions on X, a platform already predisposed to absolving Musk of all his sins , were hard to avoid.
Taken purely as a stunt, the demo was jaw-dropping. Equipping an electric supercar with 600 liters of compressed air, 10 directional cold-gas thruster nozzles, and a 2G suction-fan system directly inspired by SpaceX is undeniably rad. Seeing a 0-to-60 mph launch in under a second pushes the absolute outer limits of physics — even if it could lead to a detached retina or two.
Yet, calling this a “car reveal” or even viewing the flying Roadster as a real product, in the sense that it can be purchased by an unaffiliated third-party for private ownership, stretches the definition beyond recognition. Tesla says the “Rocket” configuration of the Roadster, the one we saw doing all the cool shit, will be “invite only.” But even that strains credulity. That version of the Roadster removes the passenger seat to make room for the ultra-high-pressure gas tanks, and trades road practicality for short bursts of thruster-powered levitation. But where you can take your flying Tesla remains a mystery, because the company admits it won’t be approved for “public road use.”
Taken purely as a stunt, the demo was jaw-dropping.
Even for the wealthy supercar shoppers, the event offered almost nothing of substance. Tesla skipped basic commercial details like pricing or battery range specs. The Roadster’s range estimate was downgraded from 600 miles to 300 miles. And Musk casually pushed the production window out to 2028 — more than a decade after early adopters handed over $50,000 deposits.
Musk himself has acknowledged the Roadster is a “small potato” project that won’t move the needle financially compared to mass-market models like the Model Y. He also called it “the last best driver’s car,” in a nod to his belief that autonomous driving will define Tesla’s future.
Some analysts are already theorizing that the Roadster’s re-release is an attempt to set the stage for a rumored Tesla-SpaceX merger . Musk’s fans on X are practically begging for it — even though it would likely result in the dilution of their own equity. But that’s just table stakes in Musk’s quest to consolidate control of his companies.
In some sense, the car had to fly in order to make the preceding decade of missed deadlines feel worth it. Tesla has already been lapped several times in the electric hypercar market. Even some of the Roadster’s most impressive tricks have already been done. There are cars that can drive upside down , cars that can jump in the air , and cars that can accelerate very, very fast.
BYD’s Yangwang U9 Extreme uses four electric motors (one more than the Roadster) to produce an insane 3,000 horsepower for a top speed of 308mph in testing — beating Rimac’s Nevera 268mph record. And the McMurtry Spéirling single-seater holds the record for quickest acceleration from 0 to 60 mph in 1.35 seconds. The Roadster could best it, but we’ll need to wait for independent testing to confirm.
But no one puts on a show quite like Elon Musk. So if the goal is to score a PR victory, dominate social media feeds, and cement Tesla’s brand as a frontier tech pioneer, than I would say the Roadster demo was a success. Competitors like Rimac, Porsche, and BYD will continue shipping real, track-ready hypercars while Tesla spends another few years refining its rocket-boosted prototype.
It’s completely useless as a viable product. But as a 30-minute flex of engineering muscle, it was truly a sight to behold.

articles.title_orig: Bystander 'heroically intervened' after three children and teacher killed in US school shooting in Bend, Oregon
articles.title_zh: Bystander 'heroically intervened' after three children and teacher killed in US school shooting in Bend, Oregon
articles.content_orig:
Oregon Governor Tina Kotek has praised a bystander who "heroically intervened" to stop a shooting at a primary school
Kotek added that lives have been "forever changed" after four people - including a teacher and children aged five, eight and 11- were killed in a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend on Thursday
Police responded after receiving a call that an armed person had fired at a car before he was seen going into the school with a long gun
The attacker, a 16-year-old boy, was shot dead by a community member who "pursued him into the school" , Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz says
Two additional victims, a seven-year-old and a 54-year-old teacher, were taken to hospital in a critical condition
Schools in the district will remain closed today "due to the tragedy", officials say
Edited by Oliver O'Connell and Jenny Matthews
US Education Secretary Linda McMahon said she was "heartbroken" by the shooting
As well as local politicians, tributes and sympathies have been pouring in from across the country after a primary school shooting left four people dead and two in a critical condition.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who is a member of the Democratic Party, said he was "absolutely devastated" by the shooting. "Gun violence is a stain on our nation. We must come together to stop it," he added.
Education Secretary Linda McMahon, a Republican, said she was "heartbroken" by the attack. She added: "We are grateful to the brave first responders who rushed to protect students and staff and the Good Samaritan whose heroic actions helped prevent further tragedy."
Arizona Senator Mark Kelly, from the Democratic Party, said in a statement which he filmed with former Rep Gabby Giffords that "these mass shootings, and shooting in elementary schools, are just like the worst thing that happens in our country".
In a statement through the Oregon House Republicans Caucas account on X, Rep Breese Iverson said "the senseless violence against our children today is heartbreaking", adding that she is grateful to "every first responder who stepped in with urgency to protect our community".
Oregon Governor Tina Kotek spoke at a candlelight vigil at Drake Park for victims of the shooting last night
Four people have died, including three children, after a school shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in the US state of Oregon yesterday. Here is a reminder of how some politicians have responded:
Bend Mayor Melanie Kebler said it was an "awful day" for the community which had a "profound impact on so many people, especially the children, families, educators and school staff whose lives have been forever changed".
"I'm struggling to make sense of a loss that feels unimaginable," she told a press conference yesterday evening, and added, addressing those impacted: "We grieve alongside you and we will get through this together."
Governor Tina Kotek told the same press conference that her heart is "absolutely broken" and the Oregon state is ready to support those in the community "in whatever you need".
She also thanked the "quick thinking and courage" of school staff, parents and first responders at the scene, and extended her thoughts to the community member who "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life":
"Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well."
Oregon Senator Jeff Merkley asked people to "hold the students, teachers, families, and entire Silver Rail Elementary School community in your hearts" as details emerge about the victims.
In a post on X, he said he was grateful to first responders and emergency personnel who responded to the "horrific shooting".
12:59 on Thursday: Local police receive a 911 call from a person in a vehicle saying they have been shot at multiple times by a person with a long gun
Several more phone calls were made to police in the ensuing few minutes, reporting a shooter had entered Silver Rail Elementary School
13:00: Police dispatch alerts local law enforcement
13:01: Officers responding to the scene directed the school to go into lockdown
13:02: The first officers arrive on the scene, where they find the suspected gunman dead. They then clear the school and administer emergency aid to the victims
Four other people, including three children aged five, eight and 11 and a teacher, are also found dead, while a seven-year-old and a 54-year-old teacher are transported to hospital with critical injuries
17:30: During a press briefing, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz confirms the suspect is a 16-year-old Bend resident. He also says the suspect was shot dead by a bystander after pursuing him into the school
19:00: A candlelit vigil is held at Drake Park, in Bend, to honour the victims of the attack
People affected by yesterday's shooting will be able to receive free support at walk-in events today.
Deschutes County Health Services announced a partnership with Bend-La Pine Schools and St Charles Health Services to provide "immediate support, connection and crisis stabilization tools" to the community.
The sessions will take place from 10:00 to 15:00 local time at  Deschutes Public Library and from 16:00 to 19:00 local time at Larkspur Community Center.
Oregon has passed a broad range of gun safety laws in recent years, placing it 12th out of 50 states in terms of their strictness, according to gun control advocacy group Everytown for Gun Safety.
The Oregon State Police conducts background checks on all people attempting to purchase firearms. Around 96% of background checks are approved within minutes, it says.
Reasons for a person being denied include having been convicted of a felony or found to be mentally ill and subject to an order prohibiting them possessing a firearm.
A person under the age of 18 cannot buy a firearm in Oregon. The state does allow juveniles to possess one with the permission of their parents but only for certain uses like hunting.
A police vehicle in a cordoned-off area outside Silver Rail Elementary School, captured this morning
Bend Education Association, the local teachers' union in the city, has said in a statement that "every student and every person who works in our schools deserves to be safe", following the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School.
In a statement posted on Facebook, the union said the shooting, which killed four people, including three children, "reaches deeply into our entire community", adding: "Our hearts are with everyone affected."
"When violence happens in one of our schools, it reaches far beyond that building," the statement continued.
"It affects our families, our colleagues, and communities across our country."
In their update on Thursday evening, police said a member of the public stepped in to stop the shooting.
A bystander who saw the incident begin to unfold pursued the attacker into Silver Rail Elementary School and shot him dead, the force explained.
The identity of the bystander hasn't been made public but audio recordings of Emergency Medical Services dispatch suggested he could be the parent of a pupil.
Oregon Governor Tina Kotek praised the community member who "heroically intervened" to stop further loss of life.
She added: "Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well."
Fifth-grade teacher Kathy Sheil Smith was in her class with students when she spotted the suspected shooter approaching Silver Rail Elementary.
She told CNN-affiliate KPTV she immediately alerted the main office before instructing her students to move into a corner.
"They were so afraid," Sheil Smith said. "The looks on their faces was really hard to see."
"I'm sure that every teacher at the school thought, 'today is the day that I'm going to die'."
She also paid tribute to the member of the public who intervened to stop the 16-year-old suspect: "They did something, and that took its own courage."

articles.title_orig: Katie Zacharia’s first week has been so rough that even Fox News has questions
articles.title_zh: Katie Zacharia’s first week has been so rough that even Fox News has questions
articles.content_orig:
New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia’s first week has been all about Katie Zacharia, when the role should be about the president and his agenda.
Zacharia has been on the defensive, including in interviews with President Donald Trump’s allies, most starkly on Thursday night when the president’s longtime friend Sean Hannity repeatedly challenged her on Fox.
The scrutiny from Fox, which continued Friday on the president’s favorite morning show, reflects serious skepticism about her ability to represent the president going forward.
Hannity called Zacharia’s all-too-brief debut press briefing “widely panned.” She defended herself by admitting she had “very little prep time” since Trump offered her the job during their first in-person meeting about it.
Hannity sounded like he was belatedly vetting Zacharia for the job — unintentionally highlighting Trump’s lack of vetting.
The president’s Truth Social post appointing Zacharia called her “an attorney,” but she failed the bar exam, a fact she acknowledged to Hannity on Thursday night.
CNN’s Andrew Kaczynski has shown how Zacharia repeatedly amplified stories and posts identifying her as an attorney in recent years. The issue ultimately comes down to credibility, an essential attribute for any press secretary.
The new White House press secretary failed the bar exam. She shared posts calling her an attorney anyway
“Between her lying about being an attorney and that humiliating debut, I have to imagine her West Wing colleagues are absolutely livid. And I suspect the knives are already out for her,” said Sarah Matthews, who served as deputy press secretary in the Trump White House until resigning the night of the January 6, 2021 attack.
White House communications director Steven Cheung has publicly defended Zacharia as “uniquely qualified and whip smart.” On Wednesday, he wrote, “At the end of this second term, she’ll be remembered as one of the all-time greats.”
But some White House officials have anonymously questioned how long Zacharia will remain in the role. And many Trump detractors have drawn parallels to Anthony Scaramucci’s infamous 11-day stint as White House communications director in 2017.
“The clock is running,” Scaramucci quipped after Tuesday’s mini-briefing. But for the record, he predicted Zacharia will last longer than he did.
“She clearly can’t handle the podium, but she doesn’t seem like a bad person,” Scaramucci told CNN on Thursday night.
Scaramucci’s theory is that Trump is focused on “bigger things and bigger personnel problems.” Amid widespread expectations of Democratic gains in the midterm elections, he thinks the president is “likely” to remove chief of staff Susie Wiles and defense secretary Pete Hegseth “right after the midterms.”
As for Zacharia, he said, “She probably won’t see the podium anytime soon because she’s not ready for that.”
Conservative commentators are not holding back their criticism. Podcaster Meghan McCain said Friday morning that Zacharia shouldn’t be anywhere near a briefing room.
“One of the biggest problems with the administration right now is every issue facing Americans is serious and all they do is keep hiring deeply unserious people to represent them,” McCain wrote on X . “It gives the impression the administration just simply doesn’t care what Americans think and that their problems aren’t worth hiring capable people with real experience.”
Zacharia’s predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, held one press briefing a week on average. Leavitt stepped down in August, shortly after returning from maternity leave. Fox News recently hired her as an on-air contributor.
Zacharia was announced as Leavitt’s successor last Friday, hours after she flew to Washington to meet with Trump about the position.
The president cited her “unblemished record of support” for his presidency and her regular TV appearances.
Zacharia’s cable news credentials are well-established. She was a popular MAGA defender on cable, including on CNN, while living in California with her family.
However, representing the US from the White House podium requires a different skill set. In Thursday interviews, Zacharia rather candidly said she might not have been ready for her briefing room debut.
Talking with Jack Posobiec, the “Pizzagate” conspiracy theorist who now hosts on the pro-Trump streaming channel Real America’s Voice, Zacharia said she “never had a full briefing beforehand.”
It was a whirlwind hiring process, Zacharia said, starting with an unexpected call from the president on Wednesday, October 7: “Wednesday phone call; Thursday flight; Friday meeting; Saturday flight; Sunday flight; Monday, Columbus Day, federal holiday. Start work, wants a brief Tuesday morning.”
While Zacharia didn’t say so, the implication was that Trump wanted her out there and on camera as soon as possible.
Zacharia read pro-Trump talking points, then called on three reporters — one asked about Kimberly Guilfoyle, then the embattled US ambassador to Greece, which led Zacharia to announce that the president had asked Guilfoyle to resign.
Speaking with Hannity, Zacharia touted that moment: “I delivered some breaking news. I think I’m one of the first press secretaries to deliver staff changes for the administration, and I was honored that President Trump trusted me delivering that information.”
Hannity, a close confidant of the president, sounded unimpressed with her press briefing performance and her answers on Thursday night.
As the TV segment’s outro music began to play, indicating Zacharia was out of time, she tried to reassure Hannity: “I will be very prepared, Sean, and I will step up to the duty President Trump has asked me to as press secretary.”
Later in the evening, Trump indicated he had watched the broadcast because he posted on Truth Social praising one of Hannity’s other guests.
On Friday morning, “Fox & Friends” co-host (and Hannity’s fiancée) Ainsley Earhardt referenced the previous interview and expressed sympathy for Zacharia. “You were just thrown into this role,” she remarked.
“Fox & Friends” interviews with Trump administration officials are often genial, but Earhardt’s fellow co-hosts appeared skeptical. “It’s been a tough week for you,” Lawrence Jones said to her.
Jones asked whether she wished she had told the president she never passed the bar exam — a fact that emerged amid days of press scrutiny of her background.
“Those questions weren’t asked,” she said. “I’m being hired as White House press secretary, not White House counsel.”
Even as the Fox hosts — known for their Trump boosterism — scrutinized her credentials and credibility, Zacharia pivoted to blaming the “legacy media,” arguing that unnamed other outlets want to “put the focus and attention on me” because they “want to be distracted from the major wins that President Trump is making for America.”
When Earhardt asked when the next press briefing would be, Zacharia didn’t say. Then Jones asked: “Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?”
“I’m standing here,” Zacharia responded, referring to the fact that she was live from the White House North Lawn.
When the interview ended, Zacharia said hello to a crowd of reporters gathered outside, but declined to answer any questions.
“I’m not taking any questions, but I wanted to let you know I’m looking forward to working with all of you so much,” she said. “Please get my number, reach out to me, call me, text me, email me.”
Matthews told CNN that Zacharia should have waited to hold her first briefing “until she felt adequately prepared.”
“Karoline Leavitt was doing that job while pregnant and was ruthlessly efficient at it,” Matthews said. “Now, much of that involved lying and gaslighting the American public, but she knew how to command a briefing room. And if Zacharia can’t even handle a Hannity interview? She is in for a rough ride.”
Molly English and Kit Maher contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: YORK | ‘Digger’: Making Art in a Hopeless World
articles.title_zh: YORK | ‘Digger’: Making Art in a Hopeless World
articles.content_orig:
Digger is not what I expected. The latest from Alejandro González Iñárritu, whose recent films (notably Birdman and The Revenant ) have been Oscar players, advertised itself accordingly. When the marketing campaign kicked off with a teaser that felt more like an ode to its lead actor’s filmography, it seemed obvious that this film was a Tom Cruise vehicle meant to earn him his first competitive Academy Award. I expected another film like 2021’s Don’t Look Up , which did well at the Oscars, but fell a little short for me. This false advertising was intentional: What Digger is doing is much more interesting and part of what makes the film work is its subversion of expectations. All of this makes it feel nearly impossible to review Digger , which is better experienced with no background knowledge at all, but it feels equally important to write about what might just be the most important film of the year.
Digger follows Tom Cruise’s Digger Rockwell, the cartoonishly evil owner of an oil company whose rig explodes, creating an environmental disaster. As an ice shelf dislodged by the explosion hurtles towards Europe, threatening to flood Norway, Digger must work with environmental expert Dr. Nirav Ganesh (Riz Ahmed) and U.S. President Compson (John Goodman) to decide what comes next. The film isn’t really about an environmental crisis, though climate change is clearly on Iñárritu’s mind. What Digger gets at is the power of storytelling and the different ways it can be utilized. After hearing of the explosion, Digger is fairly uninterested in stopping the ice shelf from colliding. He has no control over nature, as Dr. Ganesh constantly reminds him. What he can control, however, is the narrative, and in the age of modern technology, Digger finds it easy to shape the story that the public begins to tell.
Some might scoff at Iñárritu’s hyper-contemporary setting: Like Ari Aster’s controversial Eddington from last year, Digger directly addresses the effects of social media, short form content and even AI chatbots on our culture. I find this extremely effective — when Digger and Compson discuss deploying a firewall to track and prevent any mention of the incoming ice shelf on social media, rather than warning Norway ahead of time, the audience becomes aware of how our own internet activity can easily be monitored and censored. Even more strikingly, when Iñárritu abruptly cuts from a 10-minute long take to an insert shot of someone’s Instagram live footage, he pulls the audience out of the massive aspect ratio to the vertical smartphone screen. This juxtaposition takes viewers out of the flow of the film, making it suddenly seem much more personal. Digger constantly reminds you that this is not something to watch from a distance, it is a story that must be taken seriously and acted upon: or else the same thing will happen in our own world.
Digger is not just criticizing the rich and powerful, but forces all of us to look within ourselves. In this moment, when Iñárritu switches from VistaVision camera to phone, he also exposes how the audience uses their technology as a shield. In the scene, Digger is monologuing to an audience of politicians and representatives, turning their attacks back onto them. As they blame him for environmental collapse, Digger reminds his audience that the very phones they use to film him require the oil he digs up for energy. Still, his audience watches him only through their screens. Throughout the film, Iñárritu constantly turns his critique back onto the audience, and even onto himself. No one is guiltless in the collapse of our planet and to watch a film like Digger , or any of its predecessors mentioned above, laugh at the antics of the out-of-touch elite, and return to our normal lives without another thought is not a neutral act.
Some have said that Digger seems to hate its own existence, but I see something much more hopeful in its message. There’s a power in storytelling that can be harnessed by all, whether its by the rich and powerful, who use it to censor and control us, by satirists, who find no other choice in times such as these but to laugh, or by audiences, who find comfort in worlds far from our own that make us forget our own problems. Digger questions what it means to create art when it feels like the world is falling apart, probing at the ethics of accepting funding from corrupt corporations, the interplay between artmaking and activism and, ultimately, the communal experiences that art makes possible. Ultimately, while Digger doesn’t pretend to have any answers to the questions it presents, it makes it impossible to watch idly without thinking deeply about the film’s narrative. While some audiences may not connect with the film, I still think it’s worth seeing Digger in the theatre and letting yourself sit in the discomfort.
‘Projections’ is a column focused on reviewing recent film releases.
Nicholas York is a member of the Class of 2027 in the College of Arts and Sciences. He is a columnist for the Arts & Culture department and can be reached at nyork@cornellsun.com.

articles.title_orig: Palestinians, US journalist attacked in West Bank pogrom: What we know
articles.title_zh: Palestinians, US journalist attacked in West Bank pogrom: What we know
articles.content_orig:
Israeli settlers brutally attacked Palestinian olive pickers and a photojournalist working for The Washington Post in the occupied West Bank on Friday, beating villagers and setting olive groves ablaze.
The attack was among several targeting Palestinians trying to gather their olive harvest, with further assaults and arson reported in nearby communities as well.
These incidents are just the latest in weeks of intensifying pogroms on local communities in the West Bank by Israelis from illegal settlements who are largely protected – or at least unrestricted – by Israeli forces.
Veteran journalist Heidi Levine, 64, was taken to hospital after the assault on Friday in Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah. A Palestinian man was also shot in the thigh by Israeli soldiers, according to a witness who spoke to Al Jazeera and the Palestinian news agency Wafa.
Dozens of masked settlers attacked Palestinian farmers harvesting olives, throwing stones, using slingshots and setting trees on fire.
Levine, an American freelance photojournalist who works for The Washington Post, fell to the ground during the attack before she was set upon, witnesses said. “We looked and saw that there was a journalist … on the ground with people surrounding her, beating her, clubbing her, robbing her, pulling her up, beating her again and kicking her,” Jasper Nathaniel, an independent journalist who witnessed the attack, told Al Jazeera.
Levine later told reporters that her attackers “just kept kicking me and kicking me, like probably 50 times”.
Levine was wearing a protective vest marked “PRESS” on the front and back. Her cameras and phone were taken from her during the assault, the Washington Post reported.
Nathaniel said he and others managed to reach her when the settlers briefly backed away, but she struggled to stand. “She was in very, very bad shape. She couldn’t really get up off the ground,” he said.
As they helped her towards paramedics, settlers charged again, throwing more stones, he added. Levine was eventually taken to hospital in Ramallah.
Nathaniel said Israeli soldiers arrived after the settler assault and opened fire and used tear gas against Palestinians, shooting a man in the leg. “They do nothing to stop the settlers, and they speed into town and start firing their guns and tear-gassing, and they shoot a Palestinian man in the leg,” he said.
“They’re pointing their guns at the paramedics who are helping him, shoving journalists, including myself,” Nathaniel said, adding that the man was eventually taken away in an ambulance.
“We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities,” Matt Murray, executive editor of The Washington Post, said in a statement.
Wafa also reported that Israeli forces fired live ammunition and tear gas at Palestinians during the attack. After the soldiers left, Palestinians returned to harvesting their olives, Nathaniel added.
There was violence in other parts of the occupied West Bank on Friday, as well. In Burqa, east of Ramallah, four Palestinians were reported to have been injured in a settler attack on olive pickers. In nearby Turmus Aya, settlers assaulted farmers and burned vehicles and olive trees. A civil defence volunteer was also injured, according to Wafa.
The attacks follow the killing of Ali Hassan Yasser al-Bazzari, 44, during an assault on Palestinians gathering olives near Burqa, northwest of Nablus, on October 7. Witnesses reported that settlers and Israeli soldiers attacked the harvesters.
Journalists documenting the violence have also been targeted. On October 6, armed settlers beat Palestinian AFP photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh, 58, with rifle butts near Aqraba, south of Nablus. He was taken to hospital with injuries to his head and torso, according to witnesses, relatives and colleagues.
The Israeli settler pogroms have been going on for many weeks, and have stepped up as the seasonal Palestinian olive harvest gets under way.
The Israeli rights group Yesh Din has recorded at least 170 pogroms since September 27, around the start of the annual olive harvest, Reuters reported.
The violence threatens Palestinian livelihoods and access to their land. Farmers endure assaults, the destruction of trees and the theft of crops, while settlers have also begun stealing olives from Palestinian-owned groves themselves.
Al Jazeera correspondent Tareq Abu Azzoum reported that the intimidation extends beyond agricultural land to Palestinian homes and vehicles, creating pressure on communities to leave.
“People there are still living under threat of attack, not just on their agricultural lands, but also on their properties,” he said.
“Vehicles and houses have been repeatedly hit by settler attacks, which have been used by the Israeli military, apparently, to create a deterrent environment with Palestinians expected to leave these areas so they can later turn them into Israeli settlements.”

articles.title_orig: National newspaper supplements mark World Mental Health Day 2026 in Bangladesh
articles.title_zh: National newspaper supplements mark World Mental Health Day 2026 in Bangladesh
articles.content_orig:
To mark World Mental Health Day 2026, special
newspaper supplements were published across nine national newspapers in
Bangladesh, helping bring mental health messages to readers across the country.
The supplements appeared in seven
Bangla-language and two English-language newspapers: Bangladesh Pratidin,
Bhorer Akash, Jaijaidin, Jugantor, Kalbela, Dainik Amader Shomoy, Prothom Alo,
New Age and The Daily Star .
Published on 10 October, the supplements
highlighted Bangladesh’s ongoing efforts to strengthen mental health services,
promote mental well-being and raise awareness of the importance of mental
health. By reaching audiences through some of the country’s major national
newspapers, the initiative helped bring mental health into wider public
discussion and reinforce its importance as a national health and social
priority.
The supplements featured messages from national
leaders, senior government officials and health-sector representatives,
reflecting broad engagement with the mental health agenda. Contributors
included the President and Prime Minister of the People’s Republic of
Bangladesh; the Vice President of the Ziaur Rahman Foundation (ZRF) ; the
Ministers responsible for Health and Family Welfare, Social Welfare, and Women
and Children Affairs; the Special Assistant on Health Affairs to the Prime
Minister; the State Minister for Health and Family Welfare; and the Secretary
of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
Messages were also contributed by the WHO
Representative to Bangladesh, the Director General of the Directorate General
of Health Services, and the Director of the National Institute of Mental
Health.
Together, the supplements underscored the
importance of sustained attention to mental health, strengthening accessible
and responsive services, and continuing efforts to reduce stigma and increase
public understanding of mental health conditions.
World Mental Health Day provides an opportunity
each year to raise awareness, strengthen commitment and encourage action to
ensure that mental health is recognized as an essential part of health and
well-being. The nationwide publication of the supplements provided an
opportunity to extend these messages beyond the health sector and reach people
in communities across Bangladesh.

articles.title_orig: No one better connects Boston to the world: Delta announces new route to Iceland
articles.title_zh: No one better connects Boston to the world: Delta announces new route to Iceland
articles.content_orig:
New nonstop service from Boston to Reykjavík joins Boston-Venice, Detroit-Athens and Austin-Paris as new additions to Delta’s 2027 transatlantic season.
Editor's note: This story, originally published on Sept. 25, 2026, has been edited to include information about Delta's new service from Boston to Reykjavík.
Exploration awaits, and Delta is adding more ways to discover all of the natural beauty and adventure that Iceland has to offer.
Delta’s new daily nonstop service between Boston and Reykjavík (KEF) begins April 12, 2027, with flights operating through Oct. 30.
Reykjavík will become Delta’s 14th unique long-haul destination from Boston during the peak summer season and its 16 th international destination.
As Boston’s No. 1 carrier, Delta continues to expand the city’s role as a gateway to Europe. Boston is Delta’s closest U.S. hub to Europe, making it ideally positioned to connect customers across the United States with destinations across the Atlantic.
Delta’s history in Iceland dates back to June 2011, when the airline launched nonstop service between New York-JFK and Reykjavík (KEF), marking the first time a U.S. carrier offered scheduled nonstop flights to Iceland. Delta’s new Boston service builds on that legacy, expanding access to one of the North Atlantic’s most sought-after destinations while offering New England travelers a convenient new gateway to Iceland.
The route will be operated aboard a Boeing 757-200 featuring Delta Premium Select, Delta Comfort and Delta Main.
New nonstop service from Detroit to Athens and Boston to Venice will join Delta’s previously announced route from Austin to Paris. The airline is also extending its transatlantic season, with several popular routes starting earlier in the spring or continuing deeper into the fall and winter.
"Customers continue to seek more flexibility, convenience and choice when traveling to Europe, whether they are planning a spring escape, a summer vacation or a fall getaway,” said Jeff Arinder, Delta’s Vice President of International Network Planning. “By adding new European destinations from Detroit and Boston, establishing Austin as a new gateway to Europe and extending service on several popular routes, we're giving customers more choice, greater flexibility and more opportunities to travel when and how they want.”
In addition to Delta's nonstop destinations, partnerships with Air France, KLM, Virgin Atlantic and other airline partners give customers access to hundreds of destinations across Europe through a seamless travel experience.
Delta will also add four-times-weekly nonstop service between Boston and Venice beginning May 7, 2027, with flights operating through Oct. 29.
“Italy continues to be an incredibly popular destination for New England travelers, and we are excited to add Venice to our growing list of international destinations,” said Sharon Williams, Massport’s Executive Director of Aviation. “This new service provides our passengers with another opportunity to experience Italy’s incredible culture, history and tourism while strengthening the ties between our two regions. We’re grateful to Delta for continuing to invest in Boston and expand choices for our passengers.”
Venice will become Delta’s 13th unique long-haul destination from Boston during the peak summer season and its 12th destination in continental Europe. Boston will also become Delta’s third U.S. gateway to Venice, offering connections to nearly 20 destinations across the United States. In addition, service from Boston to Milan will increase to daily in 2027.
The new route further strengthens Delta’s leading service to Italy, with up to 17 peak-day departures from the U.S. and more than 30,000 nonstop seats to Italy each week.
The route will be operated aboard an Airbus A330-300 featuring Delta One, Delta Premium Select, Delta Comfort and Delta Main.
Beginning June 8, 2027, Delta will launch three-times-weekly nonstop service between Detroit and Athens , operating through Oct. 28.
“For the first time at DTW, travelers in Southeast Michigan will have nonstop access to Athens, one of the world’s most iconic destinations,” said Wayne County Airport Authority CEO Chad Newton. “We appreciate Delta Air Lines’ continued investment in Detroit and are excited about the new opportunities this service will create for tourism, business and cultural connections.”
Athens will become Delta’s 12th unique long-haul destination from Detroit during the peak summer season, as well as its seventh destination in continental Europe. The new flight will also make Detroit Delta’s fourth U.S. gateway to the Greek capital.
With connections available to more than 40 U.S. destinations through Detroit, the route will open a convenient new path to Greece for customers across Delta’s network.
Flights will operate aboard an Airbus A330-200 featuring Delta One, Delta Premium Select, Delta Comfort and Delta Main experiences.
The two new routes join Delta’s previously announced daily service from Austin to Paris, launching March 27, 2027. It will be Austin’s first-ever nonstop service to Paris and will give customers one-stop access to nearly 70 destinations across Europe, India and Africa through Delta’s partnership with Air France-KLM.
Daily summer-season service will operate between Austin (AUS) and Paris-Charles de Gaulle (CDG) starting March 27, 2027, on Delta's Airbus A330-900.
The daily flight will operate aboard an Airbus A330-900neo featuring Delta One, Delta Premium Select, Delta Comfort and Delta Main.
Delta is also extending the European travel season in 2027, giving customers more opportunities to visit popular destinations and more flexibility to travel during the spring and fall months.
Seasonal service from Minneapolis-St. Paul and Detroit to Rome will begin in early March, followed by Seattle-Rome in April. Flights from New York-JFK to Catania , Porto , Prague and Copenhagen will also return earlier, as will service connecting Boston and Seattle with Barcelona and Atlanta with Edinburgh.
Several routes will feature increased or extended service as well. Detroit-Rome and New York-JFK-Copenhagen will operate daily when they resume, while Cincinnati-Paris service will continue three times weekly from January through March.
With new routes and an extended transatlantic season, Delta is giving customers more options, greater flexibility and easier access to destinations across Europe.

articles.title_orig: Donna Vivino Will Be Dorothy Kilgallen in World Premiere of Kilgallen Musical Off-Broadway
articles.title_zh: Donna Vivino Will Be Dorothy Kilgallen in World Premiere of Kilgallen Musical Off-Broadway
articles.content_orig:
Terry Berliner will direct for the York Theatre.
October 16, 2026 By Andrew Gans
Wicked 's Donna Vivino will star as Dorothy Kilgallen —the most powerful female journalist of the 1950s who died under suspicious circumstances in 1965—in The York Theatre's upcoming world premiere of the new musical Kilgallen .
With a book and music by Tony nominee Chuck Strand , lyrics by Strand and Emily Drossell, and additional music by George Petersen, the production will play the Theatre at St. Jean's November 28-December 27. Opening night is scheduled for December 3.
Terry Berliner will direct with choreography by Jennifer Copaken and music direction by Eric Svejcar. Additional casting and creative team members will be announced at a later date.
Vivino, who made her Broadway as the original Young Cosette in Les Misérables , played Elphaba in Wicked, and was recently seen in Hell's Kitchen , says in a statement, " I get to tell the story of a woman who lived, and died, in pursuit of the truth. Dorothy was a trailblazer. I hope audiences walk out knowing who she really was, and how determined and brave she had to be."
Kilgallen is described in press notes as a "musical mystery about Dorothy Kilgallen." When President Kennedy was assassinated, she became convinced that the truth was being buried, and set out to prove it. Even as she realized her life was in danger, she forged ahead. Kilgallen died November 8, 1965, of an accidental overdose of alcohol and barbiturates.

articles.title_orig: Ancient shipwreck found off Turkey may be the world’s oldest
articles.title_zh: Ancient shipwreck found off Turkey may be the world’s oldest
articles.content_orig:
An underwater archaeologist approaches one of the clay containers, which were found lying on a slope
Photo: Hakan Öniz/Akdeniz University
Archaeologists in Turkey have discovered what they believe may be the remains of the world’s oldest known shipwreck. About 30 ceramic storage jars, or amphorae, were found near the small island of Kekova off Turkey’s south-west coast, said Hakan Öniz, a professor of archaeology at Akdeniz University who lead the excavation by the Mediterranean Archaeology Association. They are believed to belong to a vessel that sank some 4,500 years ago, when Bronze Age communities were building far-reaching trade networks across the eastern Mediterranean.
Some of the clay containers, lying on a slope in clear waters at depths of between 25 and 40 metres, still contain the residue of the goods they carried. The jars’ distinctive shape and clay are characteristic of pottery produced in the Jordan Valley during the Early Bronze Age, providing new clues as to the movement of goods between the Levant, Egypt and the Aegean Sea, Öniz told The Art Newspaper . The wooden ship, which may have been 10 metres long, that carried the amphorae has long since disappeared, likely eaten away by Teredo navalis , a wood-boring mollusc common in the Mediterranean.
“This wreck has become the first scientific evidence in the world that maritime routes existed and were used during that period,” he said. While historical sources indicated seaborne commerce occured in the eastern Mediterranean at the time, the Kekova wreck provides rare physical proof, he said.
The site was first identified in 2022 during a survey of the Kekova area, where strong currents can run against the wind through a narrow passage, creating turbulent conditions for ships.
Öniz’s team initially thought the flat-bottomed jars featuring two side handles, which resemble traditional Turkish water jugs, were from the Ottoman period. “To us, it was just another wreck, one of 434,” he says, referring to the number of shipwrecks documented along the coast. The breakthrough came when Öniz encountered similar, far older pottery in a publication on Egyptian archaeology. “I thought, ‘By God.’”
An artefact being removed from the seabed
Photo: Hakan Öniz/Akdeniz University
Öniz consulted with Karin Sowada, an Egyptologist at Macquarie University in Australia, who examined the finds and confirmed their resemblance to imported Levantine amphorae, he said. Similar examples have been found in Egypt and at sites associated with Troy and Minoan Crete.
Preliminary finds, published in the Journal of Maritime Archaeology in July, date the finds to around 2700-2400 BCE. This would make the Kekova wreck older than the current holder of the title for the oldest shipwreck ever discovered: a vessel believed to be 4,200 years old that was found in 1975 off the Greek island of Dokos in the Aegean.
The amphorae “shed light on the deep-rooted history of trade along the Anatolian coast,” Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, Turkey’s culture minister, said in a social media post. “These containers, believed to have been used to transport olive oil or wine, bear important traces of trade and cultural interaction in the eastern Mediterranean.”
Tree resin, dried meat or dried fish are other possibilities for the cargo. Researchers are using X-ray fluorescence and X-ray diffraction to analyse the pottery’s material and contents, Öniz said.
One perforated ceramic vessel, bearing nine symbols that may represent spiritual beliefs, may have been used by the sailors as a churn. Öniz said the ship may have carried a handful of goats to make butter or cheese during the long voyage before they were consumed for meat.
Such glimpses of life aboard an ancient trading vessel remind Öniz of the people who never returned home. “You wonder what the captain was feeling as the ship went down, what the sailors went through trying to reach the shore [and] their families waiting for them in port,” he said.

articles.title_orig: President Oaks welcomes world religious leaders to G20 Interfaith Forum
articles.title_zh: President Oaks welcomes world religious leaders to G20 Interfaith Forum
articles.content_orig:
President Dallin H. Oaks welcomed religious and civic leaders, scholars and others to the Tabernacle on Temple Square on Thursday, Oct. 15, at the 2026 G20 Interfaith Forum.
The President of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints thanked the forum’s attendees for their work to bring people from different backgrounds and beliefs together to form stronger communities.
“People of goodwill, compassion and a desire to understand and help one another — without demanding a compromise of distinctive commitments — are at the core of peacemaking,” President Oaks said. “I commend you for your efforts to be peacemakers in today’s world.”
The forum’s theme this year is “Resilient Hope, Shared Future.” Speaking in the opening ceremony of the three-day forum, President Oaks said the gathering is the “most prominent constellation” of religious leaders to convene in Salt Lake City’s history.
“We are profoundly grateful for your demonstration that faith-inspired insights and initiatives can contribute to meaningful and scalable worldwide solutions,” he said.
President Oaks said the efforts of participants in the G20 Interfaith Forum demonstrate how individuals and groups can come together outside of political motivations and regardless of shared or dissimilar beliefs.
“Your record demonstrates that faith-informed perspectives have a meaningful place in global policymaking,” he said. “But the key to this whole effort is to bring us all together to address common problems.”
At the Church’s April 2026 general conference , President Oaks reiterated the Savior’s teaching to love everyone — including those who do not have the same beliefs as Latter-day Saints.
“Today we might say that we are commanded to love our adversaries,” he said . “All mortals are beloved children of God.”
President Oaks was preceded at the gathering by Sheikh Mohammad bin Abdulkarim Al-Issa, the secretary-general of the Muslim World League, and Archbishop Gabriele Caccia, the apostolic nuncio — or ambassador — of the Holy See to the United States. The Holy See serves as the central governing body of the Catholic Church and is led by Pope Leo XIV.
Al-Issa described his definitions of optimism and hope, saying that hope is not just a feeling but a “faith-based endeavor.”
“Optimism waits for things to improve on their own. Hope, however, is a decision of people with a living conscience,” he said.
Caccia shared a message from Pope Leo XIV.
“His Holiness prays that your fraternal gathering may be a shining example of the solidarity of the human family and promote the dedication of the human family to religious freedom and the common good,” he read.
Other speakers at the event included the interfaith forum’s president and vice president, W. Cole Durham and Katherine Marshall, respectively.
Imam Allahshukur Pashazadeh, chief imam of the Caucasus Region, came from Azerbaijan and expressed urgency for the work of the forum.
“Joint efforts of religious and secular groups matter more than ever,” he said.
Elder Metropolitan Emmanuel of Chalcedon from the Ecumenical Patriarchate in Türkiye also spoke.
Emmanuel said the root Greek word for “share” is also the root for the words “community” and “communion.” He explained that shared beliefs and spaces do not mean individuals are the same.
He pointed to the Tabernacle Choir seated in the choir seats behind him as an example. He said that sopranos and basses are part of the same choir singing the same song, but they don’t sing the same notes. They instead sing in harmony with one another.
Pujya Sadhvi Bhagawati Saraswati, the secretary-general of the Global Interfaith WASH Alliance of India; Rabbi Mark Dratch, executive vice president emeritus of the Rabbinical Council of America; and Dr. Francis Kuria Kagema, the secretary-general of Religions for Peace, also spoke in the event.
The opening ceremony was conducted by President Michael O. Leavitt , president of The Tabernacle Choir and Orchestra at Temple Square. President Leavitt drew on his combined experience as former governor of Utah and former secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services in sharing an anecdote regarding the intertwined nature of governments and religions.
“A government can use taxes to build a clinic,” he said. “But it often takes the voice of a trusted faith leader to walk through the door.”
Policy recommendations established at the interfaith forum are shared with G20 heads of state ahead of their leaders summit in Miami, Florida, on Dec. 14-15. The Salt Lake City event was sponsored by Georgetown University’s Berkley Center for Religion, Peace and World Affairs and Brigham Young University’s International Center for Law and Religion Studies.

articles.title_orig: John Patrick Shanley's Mountain Girl Will Make World Premiere at 154 Theatre
articles.title_zh: John Patrick Shanley's Mountain Girl Will Make World Premiere at 154 Theatre
articles.content_orig:
The Pulitzer- and Tony-winning playwright's newest is being staged by Nylon Fusion Theatre Company with Axial Theatre.
October 16, 2026 By Meg Masseron
John Patrick Shanley's Mountain Girl will make its world premiere Off-Broadway at 154 Theatre next month. The Pulitzer- and Tony–winning playwright's newest work is being staged by Nylon Fusion Theatre Company in association with Axial Theatre. Performances will begin November 4 ahead of a November 6 opening night for an engagement continuing through November 22.
Ivette Dumeng will direct the comedy following Connie, an aspiring writer whose failing marriage and increasingly chaotic life sends her back to Colorado to confront her mother, who she has a complicated relationship with. Their reunion reopens old wounds, including Connie’s abandoned literary ambitions and a childhood spent in the shadow of her parents’ troubled marriage.
The cast will include Tonya Cornelisse, Sophia DeMornay-O’Neal, and Joey Welsh.
The production will feature set design by Elizabeth Chaney, sound design by Andy Evan Cohen, lighting design by Lucky Pearto, costume design by Janet Mervin, and stage management by Karli Fisher.
Two work-in-progress presentations of the play were held in Los Angeles in 2022. The play was then developed during a five-day workshop in Paris in the spring of 2025, concluding with an informal presentation for invited guests.
For tickets and more information, visit EventBrite .
