articles.title_orig: IMF-World Bank meetings focus on global risks and potential benefits of AI
articles.title_zh: IMF-World Bank meetings focus on global risks and potential benefits of AI
articles.content_orig:
BANGKOK (AP) — Guardrails are urgently needed to contain potential risks from the boom in artificial intelligence, the head of the International Monetary Fund said Friday, likening the technology to a Formula 1 race car that might go off the track and run people over.
“We are racing, and the question is how do we put barriers? So if a car was to fly out it doesn’t kill people,” IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said.
“I have high respect for the industry. I think what you’re doing is incredibly important for humanity. You may give us the biggest gift, but if the car runs over people, that gift may not be so worthwhile,” she said while speaking on a panel on the impact of AI on the world economy along with experts including Anthropic co-founder and head of policy Jack Clark.
Clark is among technology industry leaders pushing for faster action on regulating AI. In a blog post last month, the rival to OpenAI proposed that the world’s top artificial intelligence companies come up with a coordinated way to pause development of advanced AI systems, warning the technology is improving so quickly there’s a risk humans would lose control.
“I think it’s worse than you describe. I think it’s Formula 1 at night without maybe brakes in the cars,” Clark said. “And it’s remarkable to me that the toys I buy for my children are regulated more than the literal superintelligence I work on at my day job.”
He added that the effort to build policy frameworks to regulate AI is underway.
“The world is now taking this seriously, and I think if we take it seriously, we are going to be able to get our arms around it,” Clark said. “But it cannot only be companies making these decisions. And if we’re negligent about this, we’re going to get some form of chaos.”
The impact of AI on jobs is yet to be fully understood, but an IMF study found three main trends. About 10% of jobs might be transformed or newly created, while work involving repetitive tasks will be gone, Georgieva said.
The third category will be service sector jobs generated by people who benefit from the investment boom.
“The net impact is positive," she said, though she added that “services don’t pay a lot.”
“So you get young people who normally would have gone into professional routine jobs now serving coffee in Starbucks. And that is not what I think young people in the world aspire for,” she said.
Tiff Macklem, the governor of the Bank of Canada, compared that to the effects on employment from more open trade, which has generated great global wealth and raised millions out of poverty. But many millions also lost their livelihoods as manufacturers moved jobs to China and other developing countries.
He said “in aggregate there is an overall benefit,” but acknowledged that in both trade and technology “there will be winners and losers.”
“You have to find a way to help the losers," Macklem said. “Without a system to help them cope with the loss you get a backlash.”
Dozens of people marched in Bangkok on Thursday and Friday in peaceful protests, seeking to draw attention to growing inequality and other frustrations.
Georgieva noted that to ensure that the benefits of AI can reach the maximum number of people, they have to have electricity and access to digital networks. Cybersecurity also is essential.
During the wide ranging session, the speakers were also asked about how they used AI in their own lives. Georgieva said she'd used it to track calories and lose weight.
The IMF chief, who has described her personal AI assistant as bossy, joked that she'd like AI agents to be more polite.
“I mean, the agents we get, they can be really annoying,” she said. “So can we work on, like, their manners?”
“We have this dial between sycophantic and rude,” he said. “So we'll spin it around the other way.”
AP journalists Haruka Nuga, Tian MacLeod Ji and Sakchai Lalit contributed.

articles.title_orig: Teen shooter kills 3 children, teacher in Oregon elementary school before being shot by bystander
articles.title_zh: Teen shooter kills 3 children, teacher in Oregon elementary school before being shot by bystander
articles.content_orig:
Police tape is placed outside Silver Rail Elementary school in Bend, Ore., on Oct. 15, 2026.
A 16-year-old opened fire at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday, killing three children and a teacher before being shot dead by a community member, police said.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said in a press conference that the children killed at Silver Rail Elementary School were aged 5, 8, and 11. Also, a 7-year-old and a 54-year-old teacher were transported to St. Charles Bend hospital with critical injuries.
Krantz said the suspect, a male city resident who has not yet been publicly identified, was spotted entering the school by a community member, who eventually pursued him into the school and shot him. The chief said the suspect forced his way into the school by firing at locked doors.
Police did not speculate on the shooter’s motive and said they did not know whether the suspect knew anybody in the school or if he had attended.
FBI Director Kash Patel posted on social media that the agency’s Portland field office is assisting in the investigation. “We will make every resource they need available,” he added.
A vigil was held Thursday evening in the wake of the shooting.
Community members grieve during a candlelight vigil at Drake Park in Bend, Ore., on Oct. 15, 2026. Mathieu Lewis-Rolland—Getty Images
“A school should be a safe place where children can learn and feel secure,” Bend Mayor Melanie Kebler said at the same press conference the police chief spoke at. “What happened today should never happen.”
Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek said at the same conference that her heart was “absolutely broken” over the incident: “No parent should have to have this kind of day, and no community should have to live through this kind of day.” She also thanked the community member who pursued the shooter.
CNN’s analysis of incidents reported by the Gun Violence Archive, Education Week and Everytown for Gun Safety shows that the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary marks the 36th one on K-12 school grounds this year. It is the 52nd school shooting in the country this year.
Krantz said that at 12:59 p.m., police received a 911 call from a person in a vehicle who reported being shot at multiple times by someone “with a long gun.”
Multiple calls followed, reporting that a shooter had entered Silver Rail Elementary School, which is about 120 mi. southeast of Portland. The school enrolls more than 400 students from kindergarten to 5th grade.
Krantz said police directed the school to go into lockdown at 1:01 p.m. and first responding officers arrived a minute later. Upon entering the school building, Krantz said, officers confirmed that the suspect was dead and found the four other people who died from their injuries, and their families have been notified.
Krantz did not speak on the weapon used in the shooting. But an unidentified law enforcement official briefed on the shooting told the Associated Press that it was a pump-action shotgun purchased by the suspect’s mother.
Oregon’s Republican candidate for governor, state senator Christine Drazan, posted on social media that her heart was with the affected families, students, and teaching staff. “We have to commit to protecting our kids,” she added. “We have to put a complete stop to shootings at our schools. This has to end.”
Rep. Janelle Bynum, a Democrat who represents the district that includes Bend, said in a statement : “Our babies are supposed to do arts and crafts at school, not use their desks as cover from gunfire. They’re supposed to make friends, not mourn them.”
U.S. Senator Ron Wyden (D, Ore.) lamented in a statement that the victims in Silver Rail Elementary School and their loved ones faced the “awful consequences” of another school shooting in the country. He added that the “best way to honor” them is to “at long last pass common-sense gun laws that reduce the risks of more children, parents, teachers and staff forced to live in fear of similar nightmares for their schools.”

articles.title_orig: Googlebook review: Android on a laptop is still Android
articles.title_zh: Googlebook review: Android on a laptop is still Android
articles.content_orig:
Android was designed for phones, but that hasn’t stopped Google from trying to adapt the OS and its apps to larger machines over the years. Googlebooks are just the latest attempt after tablets, Chromebooks, and foldables induced little change in how people interact with Android software. These new Android-powered laptops are designed to pick up where the web-focused ChromeOS left off, offering premium hardware and native support for Android apps.
Google sees Googlebooks as an alternative to Windows and macOS, but these platforms are entrenched with decades of software and UI conventions that keep users locked in. Googlebooks have to offer something very special to steal users away from either of the dominant operating systems.
For devoted Android phone users, there are some cool things in Googlebook OS, but the Android roots of these machines are impossible to miss. Sometimes it feels like using a Chromebook, and sometimes it feels like using a giant phone. It almost never feels like using a premium laptop, and that’s the problem.
While there were a few premium Chromebooks, the platform was really only successful in the budget segment. With Googlebooks, the company is almost conspicuously ignoring lower-cost options. And as most of the lineup clocks in at well over a thousand dollars, Googlebooks are not just a new take on budget-oriented Chromebooks.
All of the launch Googlebooks have excellent touchscreen displays, aluminum and magnesium bodies, biometric unlock (fingerprint or face), and big trackpads. There’s also the Glowbar, which doesn’t do very much right now. It lights up in Google colors when Gemini is activated with the wake word and during boot-up. It also shows the battery level when you plug in a Googlebook. The latter is modestly useful, but it’s not really a selling point.
There’s something in the lineup for most premium laptop buyers. If you want a convertible, there’s the Acer machine. Sleek and spendy? Asus and HP have you covered. Want something a little bigger? Lenovo has a 15.3-inch model with an HDMI port and USB-A.
The least-spendy model, the Acer Googlebook 14, starts at $899, and that’s a limited-time deal. Even this one gets a lot of the hardware right. It has a vibrant OLED screen, a metal chassis, and three USB-C ports (all of which can charge the laptop). However, you won’t get a haptic trackpad, just the old-fashioned kind that physically clicks. The supposedly DTS-tuned speakers also don’t sound great. Still, the hardware is at least as nice as any $900 Windows laptop. Acer hasn’t decided when the price will change or what it will be, but it’s at $899 for the rest of the year at least.
The next step up from that is the Dell XPS Googlebook at $999, but this model has an LCD instead of OLED. If you want the most capable Google laptops with OLED and haptic trackpads, you’re looking at spending at least $1,100 for the Lenovo version. This machine is solid, and the larger footprint allows for vents in the hinge instead of on the bottom. But I don’t love the slightly wobbly feel of the keys or the flex in the middle of the keyboard. The HP Googlebook 14 has a much nicer keyboard, a better overall look, and a Snapdragon X Elite chip inside. However, it’s also $1,300.
I appreciate that Google is pushing for things like haptic trackpads and high-resolution OLED screens, but the more expensive Googlebooks suffer from the same issue as premium Windows laptops—they don’t exist in a vacuum. If you’re spending $1,300 on a laptop, the entry-level MacBook Air is probably a better overall option for most people.
All of the launch Googlebooks have the same keyboard layout, which is a bit different from what you get on other laptops. There’s a G button that works similarly to the Windows button, and the top F-row has been revamped. You get the usual Windows staples like brightness and volume control, but there are also Android navigation buttons and a voice input key that activates the AI-powered Rambler.
Probably the best change to the Googlebook keyboard is ‘quick insert’ in place of ‘caps lock’ (you can still get caps lock with the Fn toggle). Just press this key to add emoji, recent screenshots, clipboard contents, recently visited URLs, and more. Admittedly, I don’t mind using function layers on a keyboard, so the extra step to access caps isn’t a concern. You may feel differently, and that’s okay.
Googlebooks come in both Intel and Snapdragon variants. I’ve been using both, and general performance feels about the same. There have been some reports of app issues with Intel-powered Googlebooks, but I haven’t run into any apps that will only run on Snapdragon.
The Snapdragon model (HP) seems to have a higher performance ceiling, if you can find a way to reach it. Gaming performance also appears better on Snapdragon, but even the heaviest Android games seem fine on the Intel models (Lenovo and Acer). It can be hard to push these machines when you’re relying on software that was originally designed to run on phones. Unsurprisingly, software proves to be the biggest hurdle for Googlebooks.
Google has flirted with Android on larger screens on a few occasions, mostly with tablets and tablets that impersonate laptops. This is the first time it has totally revamped the OS for a laptop, but it’s still Android under the hood. Sometimes that’s good, and other times not so much.
Setting up a Googlebook is a snap for Android users. Just like configuring a new phone, you can scan a QR code with your current phone to copy your accounts, data, and apps over automatically. You can be up and running in minutes, and your phone will integrate deeply with the OS. Well, provided it runs Android 17. That’s going to be a sticking point, since most phones don’t have that update yet.
With Google’s “Better Together” services, a Googlebook can access files on your Android 17 phone, sync notifications, remember where you left off in apps, and even mirror apps from your phone. This all sounds great, and when it works, the experience can be good. However, there are various limitations and bugs that get in the way.
To remain in contact, the phone and Googlebook need to be on the same Wi-Fi network, and switching to other networks can break the connection in annoying ways. Even when the devices appear to have a solid connection, I have rarely seen any hint of Google’s Continue On feature, which is supposed to let you pick up where you left off in a phone app. Mirroring phone apps on your laptop can also be handy, but the performance is varying degrees of bad, and apps with system-level security features won’t work at all. You are also limited to one app at a time, and they won’t stay open in the background.
Accessing the files on your phone from the laptop is a good idea, but the transfer speed is often sluggish. More annoyingly, the connection only goes one way—the Files app on the Googlebook can see your phone, but the Google Files app on a phone can’t see the Googlebook. Speaking of the Files app, this is emblematic of how far behind Google is with desktop software. The app lacks basic things like tabs and support for network shares. It’s nice that it can access my phone, but it feels very restrictive if you’re used to Finder or Windows Explorer.
Google has at least done a good job of making Android look like a desktop OS. There’s a proper desktop that you can fill with app shortcuts, folders, widgets, and files. There’s a folder in the storage tree where you can manage that content, or you can simply drag things onto it from a file manager. You also get ChromeOS-style split-screen support and multiple desktops. These features work, but they’re not as intuitive or capable as what you get on either macOS or Windows.
AI is a big part of the Googlebook experience. Google talks a lot about Magic Pointer, which you can activate by wiggling the cursor. This allows you to hand any content on your screen over to Gemini, but calling it magic is a little silly. You can

articles.title_orig: GOP senators press Pentagon over Ukraine’s loss of Starshield data
articles.title_zh: GOP senators press Pentagon over Ukraine’s loss of Starshield data
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine is bracing for a difficult winter as restrictions on military applications of Starlink have emboldened Russia to intensify attacks on civilian and energy targets, a senior Ukrainian official told CNBC on Friday.
Serhiy Derkach, Ukraine's first deputy minister for recovery, infrastructure and transport, said Russian forces had stepped up strikes on bridges in Kyiv, threatening to isolate nearly 2 million residents on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, while also targeting railway networks and border crossings in an effort to disrupt transport and sow panic among civilians.
"With U.S. limiting the use of Starlinks on the battlefield, Russia feels that this is their moment to try and inflict even more pain and suffering on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure," Derkach said.
"We are definitely moving towards very harsh weeks and months and need our partners' support now more than ever," he said, adding that Ukrainians already experience blackouts lasting 4-12 hours per day.
His warning came as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday called for support from European leaders in Brussels to help Ukraine prepare a winter support package, including energy assistance, air defenses and funding.
Zelenskyy praised Europe's "real leaders" for standing by Kyiv on Friday, as his strained relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump clouds a summit focused on securing further support for Ukraine.
"I'm so thankful that we have such huge support from EU Council Commission and leaders – real leaders," Zelenskyy said, emphasizing Europe's backing since the beginning of the war.
His remarks come as tensions between the U.S. and Ukraine have flared up after SpaceX's Starlink service was restricted in Ukraine earlier this week, slowing down the connectivity Ukraine relies on to defend against Russian attacks.
Zelenskyy is also reportedly facing increasing pressure to tone down public criticism of Trump.
Three officials familiar with the EU summit preparations told the Financial Times that they plan to privately urge Zelenskyy to tone down his rhetoric when they meet him in Brussels on Friday.
According to Politico , some EU leaders are also concerned about Zelenskyy's handling of his strained relationship with Trump, with one EU diplomat saying Zelenskyy's public criticism of the president was "not helpful."
"We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don't see now signals from Russia side that they are ready for this to end this war," Zelenskyy told reporters in Brussels on Friday after he on Wednesday lamented that Russia didn't respect the "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump.
Trump last week surprised both Russian and Ukrainian officials by announcing the countries had agreed to stop attacking each other's power infrastructure, in an apparent attempt to ease prices of oil and diesel ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November.
Zelenskyy later welcomed the proposal and said Ukraine had held off strikes on Russian energy targets for three days to abide by Washington's wishes, but he described the deal with Russia to supply diesel to global markets as "weak."
Russia hasn't confirmed it agreed to an energy ceasefire, saying only that talks are "ongoing." Russian authorities didn't respond to multiple CNBC requests for comment.
— CNBC's George Bextor contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: China tells Israel to stop settlement expansion in occupied West Bank
articles.title_zh: China tells Israel to stop settlement expansion in occupied West Bank
articles.content_orig:
China has been positioning itself as a mediator for conflicts in the Middle East
Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi has told Israel to stop its "forced establishment" of settlements in the West Bank and reverse its actions, his office said.
The "Palestinian question" is "the greatest historical injustice of this century", Wang told Israeli President Isaac Herzog in a face-to-face meeting on the sidelines of a conference in Azerbaijan on Thursday.
Beijing has been a longstanding supporter of the Palestinian cause and has maintained that a "two-state solution" is the "correct direction".
It has also been positioning itself as a mediator for conflicts in the Middle East.
In 2023 Beijing brokered a deal to restore diplomatic ties between Iran and Saudi Arabia after years of hostility. Earlier this year, it was part of efforts, along with Pakistan, to propose a ceasefire in the US-Israel war against Iran .
Beijing's efforts to tackle the war in Gaza have focused on Palestinian unity.
In 2024 Beijing got rival Palestinian factions to agree to form an interim "national reconciliation government" for the occupied West Bank and Gaza after the war with Israel, although it was never implemented.
Now, Wang says the "immediate priority" is to fully open access to Gaza and stop the continued spread of a "humanitarian catastrophe".
China is willing to work with the international community to get the parties to return to dialogue and "seek a political solution to the conflict", Wang said.
In a post on X, Herzog said he was "pleased" to meet Wang and their talk "focused on the relations between our countries and the situation in the Middle East".
"I emphasised Israel's desire for peace in the region, alongside the strategic threats to our security, first and foremost from Iran and its terror proxies," he wrote.
China maintains close ties with Iran and is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which had previously come under US sanctions because of Tehran's nuclear programme.
One year into the ceasefire, people in Gaza continue to live under the regular threat of Israeli strikes, displacement and food security challenges.
Although large-scale bombardment has stopped, Israel has continued strikes in Gaza almost every day . More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli strikes there in the year since the ceasefire started in October 2025.
The US-brokered ceasefire was the first phase of a deal to end the war in Gaza, which had been triggered by a deadly Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.
But progress into the deal's next phase has been stalled, with both Israel and Hamas accusing each other of violating the terms of their agreement.

articles.title_orig: 'Well, it worked': Elon Musk unveils new Tesla Roadster that can fly
articles.title_zh: 'Well, it worked': Elon Musk unveils new Tesla Roadster that can fly
articles.content_orig:
Houston — Tesla CEO Elon Musk unveiled what he described as a "flying" car, equipped with thrusters, during a livestreamed event at his SpaceX rocket company's facility on Thursday.
Technical and regulatory challenges have so far prevented the much-hyped flying car sector from getting off the ground.
Musk revealed Tesla 's new Roadster sports car during a launch event at a SpaceX test facility in Texas.
During the demo, which was livestreamed on Tesla's X account, the car launched from a ramp that curled over so the vehicle was upside down, appearing to defy gravity by clinging to the surface before flying off the end, and then rolled over 180 degrees midair to land on its wheels.
"Flying cars are real," Musk said during the event, adding that the vehicle's "success is not guaranteed" but "it will probably work."
Musk said the car was equipped with "ultra high-pressure air tanks" to propel itself into the air.
The tech billionaire described the development as "what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company," referring to Tesla and SpaceX.
The vehicle would go into production in 2028, he said.
American aviation pioneer Glenn Curtiss debuted the first flying car prototype in 1917.
But successful designs have become more seriously contemplated only in recent years as electric motors and high-performance batteries have advanced.
Musk, who has appeared to have a close but sometimes tumultuous relationship with President Trump, has thrust his companies to the forefront of several major industries, and he continues pushing into new ones.
SpaceX announced a week ago that it had agreed to buy licenses for radio airwaves that will enable its Starlink Mobile satellite business to provide cellular service inside buildings, a move the company said would allow it to "become a major mobile carrier in the U.S."
"This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America," Musk said in an Oct. 8 social media post .

articles.title_orig: 'Everything got worse': Gen Z express frustration, regret after Trump vote
articles.title_zh: 'Everything got worse': Gen Z express frustration, regret after Trump vote
articles.content_orig:
President Trump speaks at a campaign rally in San Antonio on Oct. 7. Trump made big inroads with young voters in 2024, but some of that support appears to be waning. Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
📲 Follow the midterms & more in the NPR App .
Gen Z Americans were a key part of President Trump's winning coalition in 2024. Nearly two years later — and with early voting underway in multiple states for the midterms — some of that youth support has faded.
That sentiment was on display in a focus group, conducted last week, of eight Generation Z Trump voters, who reported varying degrees of unhappiness and disappointment over the state of politics, with some going as far as to say they regret supporting Trump in 2024.
The conversation was conducted virtually by Navigator Research , a left-leaning polling group. Participants ranged in age from 20 to 29 and spanned five states: Florida, Mississippi, Ohio, Texas and South Carolina — places Trump won by double digits in the last election. Two of those states, Texas and Ohio , are home to competitive races that could be key to control of the Senate .
For participants who now regret their vote for Trump, much of their frustration centers on what they see as a string of failed promises. When asked to give the president's job performance a letter grade, a majority of participants, 6 out of 8, assigned him a grade of either D or F, while two selected C.
"I just feel like nothing went correctly. I just feel like everything got worse," said John, a 29-year-old Black man from Florida. (Participants agreed to be part of the focus group on the condition that they be identified by only their first names.)
John, who identifies as a Republican and has voted for Trump since 2016, gave the president an F and said he now plans to support Democratic candidates this fall, in large part because of the strain he has felt from rising costs.
"I'm willing to give the other side a chance," he added. "I don't think they're going to make a total change. But things are just horrible right now for me. So I feel like even if they make one or two small changes, it will probably benefit me."
Though the focus group is not a nationally representative survey, the frustrations shared by participants echoed Navigator polling released in August, which found that nearly a third of Gen Zers — those under age 30 — regret voting for Trump, higher than older generations do.
Trump's rising unpopularity among young voters isn't in a vacuum. He has also lost ground with other key groups that shifted right in 2024, notably independents and Latino voters — and in a year when the Republican Party is facing political headwinds, it's unclear whether that expanded coalition from two years ago can show up at the same strength now.
While some voters, like John in Florida, do feel compelled to vote blue this cycle in response to Trump, 4 of the 8 who took part in the focus group said they still planned to back Republicans this year. Three said they'd vote for Democrats; one participant said she was still deciding.
Matthew, a 25-year-old Black man living in Texas, said he doesn't regret his support for the president and gave him a C grade.
"I feel like he's done a really good job closing the border," he said. "I also do appreciate his efforts in trying to end some of the conflicts that began under the last administration, besides the fact that the Iran conflict hasn't really worked the best, from my perspective."
He plans to vote in the midterm elections and argued that Trump will be able to carry out more of his agenda if Republicans can secure a larger majority in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, although national polls indicate that the GOP is more likely to lose seats.
But enthusiasm is a different question.
Courtney, a 20-year-old white woman based in South Carolina, said she doesn't regret her vote for Trump in 2024 and overall aligns with Republicans, but she did admit she has grown more distrustful of both major political parties, particularly on foreign policy.
"I just really do feel like we would be in this situation either way. … Education, the economy, everything else would be so much better if we weren't pumping money out into other countries that aren't ours," she said, referring to U.S. aid for Israel and the decision to go to war with Iran.
"I don't think it matters what side you vote on — that's why I voted red, because I agree with those policies more — but at the end of the day, what we do in the Middle East is going to be not at all up to [the] party [in power]," she said during the focus group.
That sense of political disaffection may underscore a growing challenge for both Republicans and Democrats moving forward as both try to repair ties with this generation.
"As we see people regret their vote for Trump, sour on the Republican Party and Republican policies, that doesn't necessarily mean that they're swinging right over to Democrats," said Melissa Toufanian, the managing director at Navigator.
Toufanian points to Navigator's own polling , which has found that even as the GOP has lost trust on economic issues, "it's not a one-for-one with Democrats gaining that trust."
"A lot of people are moving to this middle, this category that 'I don't trust either party,'" she said. "We are seeing people who are becoming increasingly pessimistic about our political parties and our political system, and they're not feeling strongly that either party can really deliver for them."

articles.title_orig: Net FDI hits highest H1 in four years
articles.title_zh: Net FDI hits highest H1 in four years
articles.content_orig:
Inflow’s strong results reflect growing confidence among foreign investors
Net foreign direct investment inflows into China reached the highest first-half level in four years, reflecting growing foreign investor confidence as the Chinese economy shifts toward more resilient growth driven by innovation and domestic demand, according to an official, experts and executives.
China recorded net FDI inflows of $60.9 billion in the first half of 2026, up 81 percent year-on-year, according to the latest balance of payments data released by the State Administration of Foreign Exchange.
An administration official confirmed that the figure was the highest for the corresponding period in four years.
“In the first half of 2026, foreign direct equity investment totaled $63.8 billion, up 55 percent year-on-year, indicating that FDI inflows into China are stabilizing and gaining momentum,” the administration official said.
Within foreign direct equity investment, inflows of new capital, which reflect long-term investment intentions, rose 10 percent to $43.1 billion in the first half, the official said.
Furthermore, reinvestment of earnings by foreign-invested enterprises in China increased 31 percent, indicating that they were using more of their earnings to expand investment with a stable willingness to invest and operate here, the official said, adding that “China’s steady expansion of institutional opening-up and improvements to its foreign investment services have helped create a favorable development environment for foreign investors to invest and operate in China”.
“Combined with its vast market, comprehensive industrial system and strong supporting capabilities, these advantages have enabled foreign-invested enterprises to earn relatively high returns, consistently ranking among the highest across major economies,” the official said.
According to the first-half balance of payments data released by the administration, FDI returns in China came in at $179.8 billion in the first half of 2026, remaining stable compared with the same period last year.
Amid persistent global economic and geopolitical uncertainties, executives said that China’s relatively stable growth and pursuit of high-quality development have provided foreign companies with sources of confidence and opportunity, citing the nation’s role as an innovation hub and the growth opportunities offered by its vast domestic market.
Australian wine company Treasury Wine Estates said it will continue to deepen its focus on the Chinese market as its flagship Penfolds brand gains momentum in China.
“The Chinese mainland is one of the world’s most dynamic luxury beverage markets,” said Wu Mingfeng, managing director for China at Treasury Wine Estates.
Iris Cui, vice-president of Asia procurement and operations at Apple, said that more than 80 percent of Apple’s 200 major suppliers worldwide operate manufacturing facilities in China, while work on its newest product — the iPhone Duo — was carried out exclusively in China, from early-stage product development to final assembly.
New capital contributions by foreign direct investors into high-tech services and high-tech manufacturing saw a 61 percent year-on-year increase in the first half, the State Administration of Foreign Exchange said in the latest balance of payments report, indicating that foreign investors are shifting from seeking the cost and scale advantages of “Made in China” to participating in “Created in China”.
Pan Yuanyuan, a researcher at the National Institute for Global Strategy at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, underscored the need for drawing on China’s institutional strengths to further provide a predictable business environment for foreign investors.
The administration official said that further measures are planned to facilitate cross-border investment and financing by multinational companies, providing more convenient and efficient services for them.
Contact the writers at zhoulanxv@chinadaily.com.cn

articles.title_orig: Warsh Vows Price Stability as A.I. Delivers ‘Shock’ to Economy
articles.title_zh: Warsh Vows Price Stability as A.I. Delivers ‘Shock’ to Economy
articles.content_orig:
BANGKOK — Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh refrained from signaling whether there will be another interest rate hike again this month, while acknowledging a "synchronous tightening" by central banks around the world and there's "no free riders."
"I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year," Warsh said, reiterating his opposition to the use of forward guidance for markets that should rely on interpreting data.
He also acknowledged that stance may disappoint anyone who had hoped for a steer ahead of the central bank meeting later this month. "It's a new chapter at the Fed [and] we're not in that business anymore. But we can go in any direction you'd like," he said.
Warsh spoke at a fireside chat with the International Monetary Fund's managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, as part of the weeklong IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday.
"Alongside other recent comments from FOMC participants, Warsh's comments indicate that the FOMC is set to pause in October," Goldman Sachs economists led by Jan Hatzius wrote in a note. "We continue to expect a second and final hike in December."
S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures edged higher following the speech, while stock market indexes in Asia and Treasury yields were largely stable.
Warsh described the global shift toward tighter monetary policy as a common fight on prices. Central banks made their own choices under their own mandates, he said, but the result was "a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world," which means "there's no free riders."
Surging energy costs stemming from the Iran war and artificial intelligence investment boom are stoking inflation and pushing up borrowing costs around the world, just as global public debt is on pace to exceed 100% of the world's GDP, a level last breached in the aftermath of World War II.
The U.S. government has insisted that strong growth would be the best way to grow out of its rising debt pile, dismissing IMF's warning that the plans of relying solely on growth won't work as something that needs to be taken "with a grain of salt."
Warsh also expressed optimism about how AI will make economies that use it well more productive and wealthier, while warning the road there may be "very bumpy," and its near-term effect on employment is still uncertain.
"I want you to hear from me optimism, but optimism leavened by the seriousness of purpose," Warsh said.
A decade from now, he said, people will look back on the developments and "say this was hugely consequential."
The Fed raised rates to a range of 3.75% to 4% last month, its first hike since 2023 . Traders see a 72.3% chance for the Fed to keep the interest rate unchanged at the Oct. 27-28 meeting, according to CME FedWatch, while the majority expect a 25 basis point hike at the December meeting.

articles.title_orig: World Food Day 2026: Sudan’s Hunger Crisis Requires Political Action
articles.title_zh: World Food Day 2026: Sudan’s Hunger Crisis Requires Political Action
articles.content_orig:
Today, the world marks World Food Day, renewing the global commitment to ending hunger and building resilient food systems. Yet in 2026, Sudan stands at the centre of one of the world’s most devastating food crises. A country with vast arable land, water resources and the potential to be a major agricultural producer is instead facing widespread hunger and famine.
Today, the world marks World Food Day, renewing the global commitment to ending hunger and building resilient food systems. Yet in 2026, Sudan stands at the centre of one of the world’s most devastating food crises. A country with vast arable land, water resources and the potential to be a major agricultural producer is instead facing widespread hunger and famine.
The war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which began in April 2023, has devastated Sudan’s food systems. Millions have been displaced from their homes and farms, agricultural production and trade have been disrupted, and food prices have surged as the currency has collapsed and supply chains have fractured. Conflict, displacement, economic collapse, disrupted agricultural seasons and climate shocks are pushing millions towards acute food insecurity.
This is not simply a crisis of food availability. It is a crisis of access, production and livelihoods. Farmers cannot safely cultivate their land; livestock owners have lost assets and grazing routes; markets and trade routes have been disrupted; and families have seen their purchasing power disappear. At the same time, humanitarian operations face severe funding shortfalls and access constraints, and in some cases are being deliberately targeted. The recent attack on a World Food Programme convoy in Dilling, South Kordofan, is a stark reminder that even life-saving aid is under threat.
Also, Experts are warning against a food crisis driven by the volatile convergence of climate change and armed conflict, heightening fears of an entirely failed rainy season. This year, Sudan has experienced severe delays and unprecedented deficits in seasonal rainfall, compounded by a critical drop in water levels across the Nile River and primary irrigation canals. As a result, vast expanses of fertile land have dried up, causing emerging crops to wither during their crucial early germination stages.  This means strategic staple crops like sorghum and sesame are suffering extensive damage, with outright crop failure reported in essential production hubs, including the Nertiti region and the critical agricultural projects of Gedaref state.
In my consultations with Sudanese business leaders, it has become clear that hyperinflation has caused the prices of food and basic commodities to skyrocket. An increasing number of Sudanese families can no longer afford even the most basic meal. Vital community lifelines, such as local community kitchens and remittances from relatives abroad, are rapidly drying up.  Compounding the crisis, severe funding shortfalls, coupled with delayed and poor rainfall, have undermined the current agricultural season.
The Russian war of aggression against Ukraine and regional maritime trade disruptions in the Red Sea have severely delayed and reduced imports, driving up the cost of essential fuel, food, and fertilizers. This cascade of economic shocks has made farming increasingly unaffordable for Sudan’s farmers, threatening the nation's long-term food security.
Preventing starvation requires the protection of civilians, humanitarian workers, agricultural assets, markets and supply routes, as well as safe and sustained humanitarian access. Food must never be used as a weapon of war.  The international community must press all parties to the conflict to respect international humanitarian law and work towards an immediate cessation of hostilities. A humanitarian truce should allow food and other life-saving assistance to reach communities in need.
But humanitarian assistance alone cannot solve Sudan’s food crisis. Sudan needs a political solution, one  that creates the conditions for people to produce their own food, earn a living  and begin rebuilding their economy.
The European Union is working on both fronts: advocating politically for the conditions that make recovery possible while investing directly in food security and resilience. These efforts are aimed not only at responding to hunger today, but also at protecting livelihoods, strengthening local food production, and building resilience against future shocks.
Through our humanitarian response, we are funding projects worth €30 million in Gedaref, Kassala, Red Sea and Northern State, providing critical assistance to people facing hunger and displacement.
At the same time, we are investing €165 million in food-security projects in Sudan, supporting sustainable livelihoods, local food production, agriculture and livestock value chains, climate-resilient farming, inclusive markets, and home-grown school feeding across Darfur, Blue Nile, White Nile, Sennar, Gedaref, Kassala, Red Sea, River Nile, Northern State, and North, South and West Kordofan. These projects aim not only to respond to hunger today, but to protect livelihoods, strengthen local food production and build resilience against future shocks.
The EU is also supporting the population through three complementary programmes worth 40 million, targeting 12 states across Sudan and addressing education,
Our political engagement complements these efforts towards recovery. We advocate for humanitarian access, protection of civilians and food systems, an end to the use of starvation as a weapon, and a political pathway towards peace and civilian governance. We work with Sudanese, European and international partners to keep food security at the centre of the response to the crisis.
Long term recovery will require investment in rural infrastructure, irrigation and water systems, modern agricultural technologies, quality seeds, livestock, storage and markets, alongside accessible finance for smallholder farmers. It will require the private sector to return, financial institutions to support productive investment, and Sudanese farmers, businesses and communities to lead recovery. The European Union stands ready to support all these efforts, standing hand-in-hand with the Sudanese people.
Sudan has the land, people and resources to feed itself and to become a major agricultural producer in the region. What it lacks is the peace and enabling environment to turn that potential into food on people's tables.
On World Food Day, let us be united in our message: Peace is not separate from food security. In Sudan, it is its prerequisite.

articles.title_orig: Race Across the World's Kush Burman hopes to help others affected by suicide
articles.title_zh: Race Across the World's Kush Burman hopes to help others affected by suicide
articles.content_orig:
When Kush Burman won BBC's Race Across the World, he wanted to use his new-found platform to help those who had supported him and his family after his dad took his own life.
Burman opened up about his struggles on the popular BBC show following Matt's suicide during the coronavirus lockdown in 2020.
"I had no clue what was going on when I was 14... I had zero indication," said the 20-year-old from Liverpool.
"So it was such a surprise, but I think going through life now I've always got at the back of my mind, just be nice, because you will never know.... you can't know unless someone directly comes to you."
Burman is now an ambassador for Alfie's Squad - a Liverpool-based charity providing support to children and young people just like him.
Race for a Reason - which is in its second year - aims to raise money and awareness of Alfie's Squad as the teams race to different checkpoints across the UK over the next three days.
Kush said he was honoured to be an ambassador of the charity that provided so much help to him, his mum and brothers.
"It's amazing and so to say that I'm an ambassador it does mean a lot," he said.
Kush said his birth father passed away when he was one to lymphoma so he was raised by his stepdad Matt.
"He took his own life in 2020, I was just 14," he said.
"It was the most difficult thing to have to go through in my entire life."
Alfie's Squad was set up by 17-year-old Alfie and his mum after he lost his dad to suicide when he was just eight.
Support groups take place in Liverpool every week.
Kush said Alfie's Squad was "like a family...it's a whole community".
"I think the most valuable aspect I found is that it's not all about the grief, it's about fun and life".
Alfie is doing the race with the former Liverpool goalkeeper and charity patron Chris Kirkland, who said he struggled in the past with his mental health and "not wanting to be here".
"It makes you realise now, when you see these kids and you see the parents that have lost their partner, that could have been my wife and that could have been my daughter - seeing the impact it has.. the devastation... it's why I wanted to get involved," he said.
Thirty teams will travel 650 miles and finish back in Liverpool on Sunday.
None of the teams know anything about the route or the tasks they will have to complete along it.
Kush said he hoped Race for a Reason would allow Alfie's Squad to support more families like his.
"I guess that's my advice for everyone is just be patient with each other and take into consideration what someone might be going through, even if you can't see it," he said.
If you or someone you know are having feelings of despair or are emotionally distressed, the BBC Action Line has advice and support.

articles.title_orig: The World Will Still Be There
articles.title_zh: The World Will Still Be There
articles.content_orig:
t’s 1 a.m., and I am wide awake in my third-floor single in Leverett’s G-Tower. For the third night in a row, I am up late, scrolling on Instagram, the bright fluorescent light of my screen reflecting against my glasses as I rest my head on my pillow. Every once in a while, I swipe down to check my phone’s lockscreen. I see dozens of texts from different group chats, from different people. I ignore them all and keep scrolling mindlessly.
I often joke to my friends that I am chronically online, though I can never seem to answer a text. Yet there’s a pit in my stomach, because I know that it’s not really a joke. Lying in bed, I wonder: How did I get here?
I can’t seem to look away.
I used to be good at disconnecting. As an Orthodox Jew, this tendency comes naturally; every Friday at sundown, my phone and devices go dark for 25 hours.
Growing up, I relished the act of slowing down. My mother, sister, and I would begin Shabbat by singing the blessing over the candles together. We would sit on the couches of our living room, singing and praying as the delicious smell of my mom’s fresh chicken soup wafted in from the kitchen. At dinner, my dad would lead us in the traditional blessing over the wine (or for me: grape juice in a tiny silver cup).
Breakfast the morning after would be Entenmann’s donuts, eaten over the New York Times’ weekly news quiz, before we went to synagogue for Saturday morning services. Afternoons were filled with reading books and playing games at the kitchen table. In the evening, we’d always know that Shabbat was over when my grandmother called our landline to ask: “How’s all?”
Shabbat was my oasis. It was the one day a week where work couldn’t keep my parents from family dinner; the one day that my brother would play CATAN with me instead of me watching him play “The Legend of Zelda”; the one day my older sisters, six and eight years my senior, were forced out of their rooms to spend time with little old me.
For 25 hours, it was almost as if time stopped entirely. Nothing was allowed to be more urgent than the people sitting across the table. No one could be reached, and so no one was expected to be. The world kept turning without me, and I learned that it could.
Throughout high school, no matter how busy my weeks became, Shabbat was always a day for myself. Whatever there was to worry about was Sunday’s problem — until I found I could no longer be the person who could unplug easily.
While I was studying in a religious seminary during my gap year in Israel, the unthinkable happened . On Oct. 7, 2023, slowing down and disconnecting — what had always felt like peace — suddenly felt dangerous.
In the weeks that followed, I felt like I constantly needed to be tapped in. If there was a rocket siren, I needed the app on my phone to warn me; if I was traveling, I needed to be able to refresh the news to make sure there were no new terrorist attacks. I listened to the radio like a broken record: what of the hostages? What of the soldiers and reservists?
In September 2023, the students at my seminary began every morning by tucking our phones away in big, hanging pocket holders by the door to the building. By the end of October, there wasn’t a single person in the Beit Midrash who didn’t have her phone close by at all times.
After my year in seminary, I chose to stay for another year in Israel. This time, I completed national service (Sherut Leumi) where I worked at Israel’s press office, mainly managing its English-language social media account.
As part of my job, I was constantly online. When I wasn’t working on a specific task, I was reading the news — understanding how foreign media outlets reported on Israel and looking for any media bias. The news cycle surrounding Israel in 2024 was relentless, and much of what I read was painful.
The effects on my mental health were tangible; I spent many days on the phone with my parents, crying that I had made the wrong choice, that I had taken on the wrong job, that I had realized just how bad of a place the world could be.
I started down the path of ignoring my texts and calls if they didn’t have to do with work. Since then, I’ve ignored messages from friends and fallen out of contact with those with whom I wish I could still talk. I haven’t cleared out all my WhatsApp notifications since August 2024. I did this not because I was busy, but because the thought of being always available to everyone became unbearable.
And yet, throughout my two years in Israel, I kept observing Shabbat.
In the immediate wake of Oct. 7, it was harder to do so; the attack, after all, had happened on a Shabbat. The following Saturday, I stayed with my great-aunt and her family in the coastal city of Herzliya. I remember feeling grateful that she and her family were less religious, because it meant that I could overhear the radio and updates.
But I quickly realized how important these Shabbats were in maintaining my sanity and sense of normalcy. Over the week, I lived inside the news, but on Shabbat — this one day — it couldn’t reach me. The war was still on my mind, but the singing, the walks, and the long, quiet afternoons reminded me that life was still happening alongside the war, and that I was still allowed to be part of it.
It was also an act of trust, and a hard one. Letting go of my phone meant accepting that I might not know something the moment it happened. And it also meant remembering that my knowing wouldn’t change the outcome anyway. Every Saturday night when I turned my phone back on, the world was still there, and so was I.
Last fall, I arrived on campus for freshman orientation almost directly from Israel. The first few days, I felt glued to the world I had left behind. After the long orientation day and nightly entryway meeting, I would trudge back to my room and focus my energy into the world on my screen, instead of the world out in the yard.
Then came the first Shabbat of the semester. From the wide windows of Harvard Hillel’s Smith Hall, I watched the sun slowly dip behind Quincy House to the soundtrack of 15 new friends singing together with me. At dinner that night, I talked to total strangers as if we had known each other forever, while we sipped our bowls of HUDS chicken soup. I returned to my room at 4 a.m., bleary-eyed and content with my newfound community.
Since then, Shabbat at Hillel has been my mainstay. It is a reminder that I can be present somewhere without being present everywhere; I can let the world reach me when it reaches me, rather than constantly reaching for it myself.
Back in my G-Tower single, I lose track of time. It is Thursday night — no, now it is already Friday morning, somehow. A few days ago was the third anniversary of Oct. 7, and I lie tapping through countless memorial posts on Instagram, again glued to my screen.
And yet, tomorrow night when Shabbat begins, I know I will put down the phone for a day, as I always manage to do. When my screen goes dark, I will trust that the world will still be waiting for me.
For a brief 25 hours, I’ll let myself look away.

articles.title_zh: Press secretary Katie Zacharia confirms she didn’t pass the California bar exam
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
The new White House Press Secretary says that the results of her bar exam are “inconsequential” when it comes to referring to herself as a lawyer.
​Katie Zacharia, who replaced Karoline Leavitt , became the subject of controversy shortly after assuming her new role as it became clear that she had been describing herself as a lawyer despite failing the bar exam .
​Addressing the rumors on Thursday’s episode of the Real America’s Voice show Human Events Daily with Jack Posobiec , Zacharia explained that she was preparing to move to Beijing , where her now-husband worked, when she took the bar exam.
​“The results are somewhat inconsequential, because I knew I wouldn’t need the bar in China, and we left shortly thereafter,” she claimed. “And after moving to China, I think, I didn’t really think much of the bar results or consider that something that I needed to focus on, and I was offered a job at an international practice division of a Chinese law firm.”
​Zacharia added, “There’s no Chinese bar. I had enough credentials, which was my law degree, to be able to do this practice.”
​The bar exam is a major qualification needed for U.S.-based aspiring lawyers to receive a license to practice law.
In China, non citizens cannot become lawyers or sit for the bar exam. Foreign lawyers must practice law for at least two years in their country of origin before being able to practice as a foreign representative attorney in China.
​Zacharia, though, has repeatedly been described as a “lawyer”.
​According to an analysis by Popular Information journalist Judd Legum, she has been referred to as such during 18 appearances on Fox News since March 2025. President Trump has described her as an “attorney” on Truth Social .
​During her appearance on Real America’s Voice on Thursday, Zacharia addressed concerns over being described as a lawyer.
​“And I consulted for a very long time many people in the field: ‘Is it okay and acceptable if I label myself lawyer, not attorney-at-law, not Katie Zacharia, esquire, but lawyer, and provide legal analysis, not legal advice?’” she said.
Zacharia continued, “And they said: ‘Absolutely, absolutely across the board you can call yourself a lawyer, you have a J.D. and to buffer that, you have international legal experience and transactional law, which gives you the ability to analyze it, not necessarily give advice.’”
​Amid the controversy, the White House has rallied to Zacharia’s defense with Communications Director Steven Cheung telling The Independent : “She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary.”
During her appearance on Jack Posobiec’s show, Zacharia described the pressure she had been under when she failed the bar exam and detailed why she chose not to retake it upon returning from China - given that passing the exam would have given her a license to practice law.​
“And I was obviously incredibly, I know, distracted and overwhelmed and excited for finally being married to someone who had been long-distance for at least a year, a year-and-a-half, when you include the engagement,” she said, explaining why she failed.
​The White House press secretary went on to tell Posobiec that she did not retake the bar exam since she became pregnant upon returning to the U.S.
​“We got pregnant, and we decided, all right, well, we’re going to stay in the United States, and we are not going to move back abroad, because that was still an option we were considering,” she said.

articles.title_orig: ‘You got to be the most optimistic human in the world:’ Colorado apple farmers hit hard by devastating April freeze
articles.title_zh: ‘You got to be the most optimistic human in the world:’ Colorado apple farmers hit hard by devastating April freeze
articles.content_orig:
COLORADO SPRINGS, Colo. (KKTV) - Colorado apple farmers are facing devastating losses after an April freeze wiped out crops across the state, and for one Penrose orchard owner, 2026 marks the second straight year of being hit hard.
I spoke with Tony Ferrara, owner of Happy Apple Farm in Penrose, who says he lost his entire apple orchard due to the cold temperatures in spring. He says this is the worst the farm has been impacted since it opened in 1984.
“We lost our crop April 18th. It hit about 22 degrees, and that’s when all the blossoms were on the tree, and uh, it was a total loss.” Ferrara said.
Making matters worse, Ferrara says back-to-back losses are virtually unheard of for the farm.
“2 years in a row and that’s unheard of. The farm has been in the family for 42 years, and I’ve never had back-to-back losses, so it’s not a happy apple farm; it’s a crappy apple farm.” Ferrara said.
The pain extends far beyond one operation. According to Dawn Thilmany, a professor of agriculture and resource economics at Colorado State University, farmers across Colorado have suffered complete or nearly complete losses.
“I would say 90 to 95% of the commercial production is in those handful of counties on the Western slope. Um, there’s about 1400 acres in total, and that is equivalent to about $300 million in production.” Thilmany said.
Despite the losses, Thilmany is urging consumers to support what remains of Colorado’s apple industry.
“We still have a pretty vibrant industry here in Colorado, and we want it to stay, um, so where you do see them, still buy them and support them,”Thilmany said.
For Ferrara, pumpkins are helping keep Happy Apple Farm afloat while he waits for a new crop.
“Luckily we have pumpkins. We do the pumpkins, and we will survive, but it’ll, it’ll be tight until next August, uh, when the new crop will come in, hopefully. There’s no way we can lose them three years in a row, but it’s, it, yeah, financially it’s, it’s a disaster.” Ferrara said.
Ferrara says he is remaining optimistic despite the massive loss and hopes this fall will still be a successful one for the farm. Thilmany says new methods are also being tested to keep crops from freezing in the future, including using solar panels to heat the soil.

articles.title_orig: Megadonors are powering Republicans’ spending advantage
articles.title_zh: Megadonors are powering Republicans’ spending advantage
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk has spent $158m in a month to back Republicans in midterm races – with his efforts mostly focused on Texas
Tens of millions of dollars are pouring into Texas as Democrats stage an audacious bid to win a US Senate seat in the Republican stronghold.
Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, is among those wading into the closely watched race as November’s midterm elections approach.
In September alone, Musk gave $158m to the Senate Leadership Fund , the primary super political action committee (Pac) backing Republican Senate candidates, Axios first reported. The donation accounted for more than half of the Senate Leadership Fund’s fundraising in the third quarter.
Separately, Musk donated $10m to Lone Star Liberty Pac, the committee dedicated to supporting Ken Paxton , the Republican candidate in Texas, after Alex Latcham, the president of the Senate Leadership Fund, requested the funding.
A source familiar with the matter confirmed Axios’s reporting to the Guardian. The Guardian has also asked representatives for America Pac, the political operation founded by Musk, for comment.
The donations came as Republicans were struggling to keep up with spending by Paxton’s Democratic opponent , James Talarico. Over the summer, Talarico released an ad painting Paxton negatively as a politician with a history of corruption.
Talarico, a young, progressive candidate known for his faith-based messaging, made strides with liberal voters in Texas when he defeated an established Democrat for the Senate nomination earlier this year. Talarico raised $64m – the largest third-quarter fundraising of a Senate candidate in history, just this summer, Politico reported.
“He’s fighting this battle basically alone while Elon Musk and the full weight of the GOP fundraising apparatus outspends him 2:1. This is still an uphill battle,” an unnamed Democratic strategist working in Texas told Politico.
Polls have shown the two candidates are essentially tied, though some have Talarico polling narrowly ahead of Paxton.
The Texas Senate race is one of the most competitive races in the country and was expected to cost millions of dollars because it’s an expensive state to run a campaign.
The Senate Leadership Fund warned, months earlier, that supporting Paxton would cost anywhere from $150m to $200m. But Donald Trump chose Paxton himself to run against Talarico.
When Musk’s team and the Senate Leadership Fund analyzed polling, they found Paxton’s chances of winning dwindling, leading Musk to step in, Axios reported.
after newsletter promotion
In the 2025-2026 election cycle, Musk has donated approximately $366m to federal committees, the New York Times reported earlier this week. That is significantly more than he did during the 2024 election cycle, when he gave about $290m to help Trump.
The increase in spending contradicts a statement Musk made in May 2025 when he predicted : “I think, in terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future.”
Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for America Pac, told the New York Times: “These robust investments have allowed the GOP apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history.
“If Democrats take control of Washington and win key gubernatorial and attorney general races this November, then America risks becoming a socialist, woke and borderless country,” Romeo added.

articles.title_orig: Fed's Warsh withholds rate signal, praises recent global tightening with 'no free riders'
articles.title_zh: Fed's Warsh withholds rate signal, praises recent global tightening with 'no free riders'
articles.content_orig:
BANGKOK — Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh refrained from signaling whether there will be another interest rate hike again this month, while acknowledging a "synchronous tightening" by central banks around the world and there's "no free riders."
"I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year," Warsh said, reiterating his opposition to the use of forward guidance for markets that should rely on interpreting data.
He also acknowledged that stance may disappoint anyone who had hoped for a steer ahead of the central bank meeting later this month. "It's a new chapter at the Fed [and] we're not in that business anymore. But we can go in any direction you'd like," he said.
Warsh spoke at a fireside chat with the International Monetary Fund's managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, as part of the weeklong IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday.
"Alongside other recent comments from FOMC participants, Warsh's comments indicate that the FOMC is set to pause in October," Goldman Sachs economists led by Jan Hatzius wrote in a note. "We continue to expect a second and final hike in December."
S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures edged higher following the speech, while stock market indexes in Asia and Treasury yields were largely stable.
Warsh described the global shift toward tighter monetary policy as a common fight on prices. Central banks made their own choices under their own mandates, he said, but the result was "a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world," which means "there's no free riders."
Surging energy costs stemming from the Iran war and artificial intelligence investment boom are stoking inflation and pushing up borrowing costs around the world, just as global public debt is on pace to exceed 100% of the world's GDP, a level last breached in the aftermath of World War II.
The U.S. government has insisted that strong growth would be the best way to grow out of its rising debt pile, dismissing IMF's warning that the plans of relying solely on growth won't work as something that needs to be taken "with a grain of salt."
Warsh also expressed optimism about how AI will make economies that use it well more productive and wealthier, while warning the road there may be "very bumpy," and its near-term effect on employment is still uncertain.
"I want you to hear from me optimism, but optimism leavened by the seriousness of purpose," Warsh said.
A decade from now, he said, people will look back on the developments and "say this was hugely consequential."
The Fed raised rates to a range of 3.75% to 4% last month, its first hike since 2023 . Traders see a 72.3% chance for the Fed to keep the interest rate unchanged at the Oct. 27-28 meeting, according to CME FedWatch, while the majority expect a 25 basis point hike at the December meeting.

articles.title_orig: Woodbury resident's 'Bob's World' celebrates found family
articles.title_zh: Woodbury resident's 'Bob's World' celebrates found family
articles.content_orig:
Woodbury resident Wisdom Nunn hopes to bring more diverse voices into animation through his YouTube series "Bob's World." As the drummer for the band Nunnabove with his siblings, Nunn already works in a family setting. He brings that same connection into "Bob's World," which follows a pair of teenage bunnies looking for their lost parents and the family of friends they find along the way. FOX 9’s Maury Glover has the story.
WOODBURY, Minn. (FOX 9) - Woodbury resident Wisdom Nunn hopes to bring more diverse voices into animation through his YouTube series "Bob's World."
As the drummer for the band Nunnabove with his siblings, Nunn already works in a family setting. He brings that same connection into "Bob's World," which follows a pair of teenage bunnies looking for their lost parents and the family of friends they find along the way. Nunn said creating the series still feels surreal. "It really is a dream, and I don't think I kind of talk about it enough," said Nunn. He said the show's focus on community and family reflects a big part of his life. "Family is your friends. Family is people that you confide in, people that can talk to, and I think family isn't just blood," said Nunn.
Nunn said the series was inspired by two stuffed animals he and his brother made when they were little. After he taught himself animation, he decided to turn their imaginary adventures into a show. "It's such a wild culmination of things to come together. It warms my heart. I think it's great," said Nunn.
Nunn has completed four episodes of "Bob's World," and each one can take anywhere from eight months to two years to finish. His brother and sisters also help write, voice and score the series, making the project a family effort offstage too. Nunn hopes to complete six more episodes of "Bob's World," but he said that pace will probably take a few years. The show is also up for a regional Emmy. He said getting to illustrate the importance of found family already feels like a win. "I love that the show is about community and family. That's a big theme in my life that I hold very dearly, and I can't wait to see what comes next with it."

articles.title_orig: Live updates: 3 children among dead in Bend school shooting, OPB sources say - Oregon Public Broadcasting
articles.title_zh: Live updates: 3 children among dead in Bend school shooting, OPB sources say - Oregon Public Broadcasting
articles.content_orig:
Three children and a teacher were killed, and two others critically wounded, in a shooting on Thursday at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, authorities said.
The suspect, a 16-year-old male, was shot and killed by a bystander, Bend police said.
Along with the teacher, the three children killed were ages 5, 8 and 11, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said in a news conference Thursday night. Two others, a 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher, were taken to St. Charles Medical Center   with critical injuries. No names were immediately released.
Krantz said that officers were called to the school just before 1 p.m. on a 911 call from a person who said they had been shot at several times while in their vehicle by a suspect with a long gun. Emergency dispatchers then received dozens of 911 calls that the suspect had entered the school.
The shooter forced his way into the school by "shooting at locked doors," Krantz said.
When officers arrived at the school within three minutes of the first 911 call, they discovered that the suspect had been killed by a bystander, Krantz said.
"An officer reported that the suspect had been shot by a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him," Krantz told reporters.
After officers entered the building, Krantz said, they found the four deceased victims.
Officials would not say exactly what type of weapon was used in the attack or how many rounds were fired. Multiple law enforcement sources told CBS News the suspect used a shotgun.
There was no word on a motive. Police could also not say if the suspect had a connection to the school. No details were provided on the bystander who shot and killed the suspect.
Authorities evacuated the school and transported all students and staff to a nearby church where they could be reunited with their families, Krantz said.
"Today an unthinkable tragedy happened at Silver Rail Elementary School," Bend-La Pine Superintendent Steven Cook said in the news conference. "No community should have to do what we are doing right now. I don't have any words for what this community is feeling right now."
FBI Director Kash Patel said the agency's local office was on scene and assisting local law enforcement. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives was also on scene to assist local authorities, including the Oregon State Police, a law enforcement source said.
Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek praised the bystander who "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life," saying the person's actions carry "a heavy emotional burden."
"All Oregonians mourn this loss today," Kotek said in the news briefing. "This is a horrible day. No parent should have to have this kind of day. And no community should have to live through this kind of day."
Bend-La Pine Schools said that all schools in the district would be canceling classes and athletic events on Friday due to the shooting.
Bend is located in central Oregon, about 150 miles southeast of Portland.
Last year there were 235 shooting incidents at K-12 schools in the U.S., according to data from the K-12 School Shooting Database . So far this year, there have been at least 149, including the one in Bend, Oregon. While still higher than pre-pandemic levels, school shooting incidents appear to be decreasing from a peak in 2023.
Grace  Manthey contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: At least 30 children killed in Pakistan school roof collapse
articles.title_zh: At least 30 children killed in Pakistan school roof collapse
articles.content_orig:
The families of children killed in a roof collapse at a school in northwest Pakistan called for "justice" on Friday, a day after more than 30 pupils and a teacher were crushed to death.
A woman teacher and 34 students, mostly younger than 14, died in the building collapse in the city of Peshawar on Thursday morning.
"The parents of all these children must receive justice," tailor Muhammad Wahab, who lost his 11-year-old nephew Hammad in the accident, told the AFP news agency on Friday.
"I appeal to our rulers," he said, adding that Hammad had been "doing well in school" before the tragedy.
Dozens of people gathered outside the school on Friday to mourn the children who were killed in the collapse, which officials blamed on dilapidated infrastructure.
One grief-stricken father showed AFP a picture on his mobile phone of his young daughter, dressed in red and gold, who lost her life.
A rescue worker collects books and school bags of victim children at the site of a roof collapse at a private school in Peshawar, 15 October, 2026 - AP Photo
Another parent, Asadullah, said he lost a son, nephew and three other close relatives in the tragedy.
"The children were good students and often achieved top positions in their classes," he told AFP. "They happily went to school every day."
Residents and rescuers described chaotic scenes in the aftermath of Thursday's collapse, as people scrambled to pull children out from under the rubble.
A man named Sohail told AFP that "everyone began screaming in panic" when his niece, who had escaped the building, arrived home to tell them it had collapsed.
"When I arrived at the scene, I saw around 10 to 15 children trapped beneath the rubble, with debris piled up to their necks. We quickly pulled them out," he said.
School roof collapse kills teacher and at least 32 children in northwest Pakistan
Pakistan: Classrooms reduced to rubble in deadly school disaster, at leat 32 pupils killed
Images released by emergency services showed rescue workers in high-visibility vests scrambling to move debris, rubble and dirt.
A senior official in Peshawar told AFP that initial reports suggested the roof collapse was due to "weak infrastructure".
"The school owner has been detained," the official said on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to talk to media.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed "deep sorrow and grief over the loss of precious lives" in an X post.
President Asif Ali Zardari described the roof collapse as a "heartbreaking tragedy".
Building collapses are common in Pakistan, largely due to poor safety standards and substandard construction materials in the South Asian nation of more than 240 million people.
In June, more than a dozen children were killed when a roof collapsed at a tutoring centre in the eastern city of Lahore.
In 2025, 27 people were killed and 10 injured when a five-storey building collapsed in the impoverished Lyari area of the southern city of Karachi.
