articles.title_orig: Trump says Fort Hood shooter's execution will not be livestreamed
articles.title_zh: Trump says Fort Hood shooter's execution will not be livestreamed
articles.content_orig:
Fox News chief national security correspondent Jennifer Griffin looks at the history of the firing squad being used in the United States and debates over the plan to stream Nidal Hasan’s execution on ‘Special Report.’
President Donald Trump announced that the planned firing squad execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will not be livestreamed, reversing an earlier Pentagon announcement that the public would be able to watch the convicted mass killer's final moments.
Trump said in a Truth Social post that broadcasting the execution could serve as a powerful deterrent to terrorism but acknowledged that many Americans would rather not witness Hasan's death.
"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump wrote.
AMERICANS DRAW THE LINE AT LIVESTREAMING ‘SPECTACLE’ OF FORT HOOD SHOOTER'S EXECUTION: ‘IT’S AN ABOMINATION'
This April 9, 2010, file photo released by the Bell County Sheriff's Department shows Maj. Nidal Hasan at the Bell County Jail in Belton, Texas. (AP)
Hasan’s execution is scheduled for Dec. 3. Trump said immediate family members of the 13 people killed in Hasan's 2009 rampage will be permitted to attend in person if they choose.
"They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" Trump wrote.
The president's announcement comes after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday that the execution would be made public, telling Real America's Voice that Americans would be able to watch Hasan's death.
"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said at the time.
Major Nidal Malik Hasan, the U.S. Army doctor identified by authorities as the mass shooter at the U.S. Army post in Fort Hood, Texas, is seen in this undated handout photo from a pdf file of the U.S. Government Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences downloaded on November 6, 2009. (REUTERS/Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences/Handout)
Pentagon officials subsequently confirmed Thursday that the execution would be livestreamed, though additional details had not yet been released.
Trump suggested in his Truth Social post that broadcasting the execution could have sent a message to would-be terrorists.
"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump wrote.
This undated photo provided by the Bell County Sheriff's Department shows former Army psychiatrist Maj. Nidal Hasan. (HANDOUT/Reuters)
The president added that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device."
Hasan, a former Army major and psychiatrist, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others during a shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, on Nov. 5, 2009.
FORT HOOD SURVIVOR SHOT IN HEAD VOWS TO WATCH TERRORIST FACE HISTORIC FIRING SQUAD
He opened fire inside a medical processing building where soldiers were preparing for deployment, shouting "Allahu akbar" before shooting at service members with a handgun. Hasan was shot by law enforcement during the attack and left paralyzed from the waist down.
U.S. Army soldiers salute their fallen comrades during the III Corps and Fort Hood Memorial Ceremony at Fort Hood, Texas, November 10, 2009. The memorial was held to honor the 13 victims of the shootings which took place on the Fort Hood Army post on November 5. (Reuters/Jessica Rinaldi)
During his 2013 military trial, Hasan acknowledged carrying out the shooting and represented himself after dismissing his attorneys. He was sentenced to death.
The execution would mark the first military execution in more than 65 years. The last U.S. military execution took place in April 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged.
However, Hasan could still seek to delay his execution through a habeas corpus petition in civilian court, a legal challenge that experts say could significantly postpone the proceedings.
Trump also used his Truth Social post to criticize the Obama administration's handling of intelligence involving Hasan, pointing to electronic communications between the former Army officer and radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki that were intercepted by the FBI before the attack.

articles.title_orig: The Tesla Roadster 2 Is Here—and It Flies
articles.title_zh: The Tesla Roadster 2 Is Here—and It Flies
articles.content_orig:
On Thursday night, Tesla and CEO Elon Musk unveiled what’s been billed as the company’s last human-driven car. Maybe human-piloted is a more accurate way to say it.
At a demonstration event in McGregor, Texas—at SpaceX’s rocket development and testing facility—the new car did what Musk has long promised. With a herky-jerky burst of steam, it flew into the air. At one point, the car appeared to flip over the automaker’s entire line-up, floating several feet over its electric semi-truck. Tesla executives said the vehicle could accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in one second.
“This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car,” Musk said. (It’s also likely to raise the eyebrows of federal regulators .)
Tesla says it will begin production on the Roadster 2 in 2028. Fans have waited a long time for the vehicle. The Roadster 2—the successor to Tesla’s first vehicle, the Roadster—was first announced in 2017, and at the time Tesla said the new sports car would be the fastest production vehicle in the world.
The “flying” technology is enabled by four thrusters, Tesla vehicle engineering head Lars Moravy said. He said the production version would “hopefully” travel up to 230 miles per hour, though Musk said he hoped to “crack halfway to the speed of sound”—around 385 mph. Modern Formula 1 vehicles usually top out around 220 mph. The company said the vehicle would travel more than 300 miles on one charge, middling for a mainstream EV and lower than most luxury vehicles. Tesla’s own Model 3 can travel up to 360 miles on a charge.
Tesla said the thrusters are powered by onboard compressed gas. Musk said that the same technology that allows the vehicle to fly will also create downward force that allows the vehicle to turn corners very quickly. “It’s going to crush every track record that has ever existed,” he said.
The company initially promised the Roadster 2 would ship in 2020. On Thursday, the Tesla team did mention the new timeline, but did not mention what the new car will cost. Musk has a long history of not following through on his loftiest product ambitions, and timelines for many Tesla releases have repeatedly missed targets.
The company posted on X that the Roadster 2 would come in three variants: a two-seater “Performance” road-ready version that lacks the thrusters Tesla showed off on Thursday; a “race ready” Thrust variant; and an “air ready” Rocket variant that has only one seat. The Tesla website lists the Rocket as “invite only” and the Thrust as “limited.” You can currently only place reservations for the Performance and Thrust versions.
When it was first announced, enthusiasts put down $50,000 deposits for what was advertised as a $200,000 car. (That deposit is worth more than $68,000 in 2026 dollars.) Some got sick of waiting . OpenAI CEO Sam Altman complained on X last year that he had trouble canceling his reservation. Musk posted that Altman received a refund in 24 hours.
A reservation page posted on Tesla’s site now charges a $5,000 reservation fee for the Performance variant, with an additional $45,000 due within 10 days. The Thrust is available for an initial $5,000 fee, with $245,000 due within 10 days.
Musk has said that Tesla should no longer be regarded as a carmaker and that the company is focused on building autonomous vehicle technology and robots.
The unveiling event comes at a weird time for electric vehicles . Sales of EVs have stalled in the US after the GOP-led Congress nixed federal support . Meanwhile, the global energy crisis has EV sales booming elsewhere . Electric luxury hypercars—the class to which the Roadster 2 belongs—are in an especially tricky spot. Several luxury automakers have said that wealthy buyers are now looking for the sound and power of a typical gas-powered vehicle. Lamborghini shelved its plans to make an EV earlier this year.

articles.title_orig: Trump names scapegoats as Republicans sweat in Texas
articles.title_zh: Trump names scapegoats as Republicans sweat in Texas
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Thursday said that if Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton loses, it will be the fault of incumbent Republican Sen. John Cornyn and conservative commentator Karl Rove .
Trump accused Cornyn and Rove of "doing everything possible to make it hard" for Paxton, the state's attorney general, to beat Democratic nominee James Talarico. Cornyn lost the Republican primary to Paxton, whom Trump controversially endorsed.
"If Ken Paxton loses, it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove, who have ineffectively opposed me for my entire political career," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Trump's preemptive blame-casting came as Texas has surprisingly become one of the most competitive battlegrounds of the 2026 midterm cycle. Most recent polls show state Rep. Talarico maintaining a lead in the low-to-mid single digits over Paxton.
The reliably red state has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1988. In 2024, Texans voted for Trump over Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris by nearly 14 percentage points.
Cornyn's office and Rove did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment on Trump's post.
Trump's decision to back Paxton in the GOP primary delivered a major blow to the four-term incumbent Cornyn, whom the president viewed as disloyal. The move was also seen as a major gamble, as Paxton's history of scandal and opposition within his own party has made him a polarizing figure.
Hoping to stave off Democrats' goal of winning majority control of the Senate, groups backing Republicans have poured hundreds of millions of dollars into the Texas contest, making it the most expensive race of the cycle.
GOP spending in the race has topped $370 million so far, eclipsing Democratic spending by nearly $235 million, according to AdImpact.
Trump has repeatedly lashed out at Rove, calling him a "loser" and urging Fox News to stop putting him on air.
Rove, who was a senior advisor to former President George W. Bush, "is so bad for the Republican Party, and completely wrong so often," Trump wrote in a Sept. 14 Truth Social post .
In a Wall Street Journal op-ed two days later, Rove said that he would back a Democratic candidate in a different race in Texas, voting blue for just the second time in his life.

articles.title_orig: The world’s most important airspace is a sliver of sky between two wars
articles.title_zh: The world’s most important airspace is a sliver of sky between two wars
articles.content_orig:
Expanding conflict zones force hundreds of daily transcontinental flights into a tiny corridor over Azerbaijan
Log-in here if you’re already a subscriber
Repeated Houthi missile strikes on Riyadh International Airport are exacerbating a key vulnerability for global aviation as growing instability across Europe and the Middle East forces hundreds of daily transcontinental flights into one acutely vulnerable sliver of airspace just 85 nautical miles wide.
Warnings to airlines and travelers to stay clear of Saudi Arabian airspace followed a ramp in attacks by Houthi militias on the kingdom’s airports. An Oct. 11 barrage killed at least 13 people at Riyadh’s King Khalid Airport days after destroying a Saudia Airbus A320 parked at a gate. The Federal Aviation Administration urged U.S. airlines to avoid the Jeddah Flight Information region that covers the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, warning of a “potentially hazardous situation” and citing “ongoing military activities” as well as Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) interference during overflight, arrival and departure.
That latest disruption follows more than a dozen years of progressively shrinking airspace essential for connecting Europe, Asia and Australia. Geopolitical instability raging across Northeast Africa, Eastern Europe and the Middle East continues to close off huge swaths of sky to commercial and cargo airliners, with no end in sight to the Ukraine-Russia conflict along with broader Russian airspace denial to North American, European, Australian and many Asian airlines.
Those expanding zones of conflict now force a large majority of traffic into a tiny corridor above the South Caucasus. Airspace over Azerbaijan has seen a five-fold increase in traffic in the last five years, with a sharp uptick since the U.S.-Israeli bombing campaign of Iran in February sparked a broader regional conflict, according to Rashad Hasano, Azerbaijan’s Deputy Minister of Digital Development and Transport.
The keyhole increasingly looks to be the most important airspace on the planet — and it sits over a disputed territory with its own history of armed conflict. A dispatcher from a long-haul U.S. cargo company described that narrow strip of airspace to The Air Current as “invaluable.”

articles.title_orig: Bird flu caused the death of Jackie, a California bald eagle who captured hearts
articles.title_zh: Bird flu caused the death of Jackie, a California bald eagle who captured hearts
articles.content_orig:
BIG BEAR LAKE, Calif. — Bird flu caused the death of a bald eagle named Jackie who had become an internet sensation and a symbol of the species' recovery in California, officials said.
A necropsy and additional testing found that the primary underlying cause of Jackie's death in August was highly pathogenic avian influenza, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife said Wednesday in a news release.
In the weeks before she died , Jackie was being treated at the Ojai Raptor Center for various ailments, including anemia. Chris Eksteen, the center's director, said in the news release that the necropsy results "have helped connect many of the findings" they saw during her hospitalization.
"In an uncommon presentation of the virus, the infection caused a severe ulcer in her stomach that led to persistent internal bleeding, anemia, and the development of bacterial sepsis," Steve Kubiski, the disease investigations director at the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, where the necropsy was conducted, said in the news release.
For more than a decade, nature lovers watched via an online video feed as Jackie and her partner, Shadow, tended to their nest each year atop trees near Big Bear Lake in the San Bernardino Mountains east of Los Angeles. There's no evidence Shadow is ill, according to the news release.
The nonprofit Friends of Big Bear Valley installed the nest camera in 2015 and documented the successes and failures of each breeding season.
Highly pathogenic avian influenza has been circulating in bird populations throughout the U.S. While waterfowl and shorebirds are natural hosts for bird flu viruses, eagles and other raptors can be exposed through contact with infected birds or by eating them, according to the news release.
Jackie's remains were cremated to prevent transmission of the virus, it said.
American bald eagles teetered on the brink of extinction until the pesticide DDT was banned in the 1970s and other protections were established, leading the species to rebound and be removed from the federal endangered list.

articles.title_orig: Katie Zacharia Admits Failing Bar, but Defends Calling Herself a Lawyer
articles.title_zh: Katie Zacharia Admits Failing Bar, but Defends Calling Herself a Lawyer
articles.content_orig:
Fox News host Sean Hannity absolutely grilled President Donald Trump's new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia , over her rocky debut at the briefing room podium, questioning, "What happened?"
Zacharia faced immediate backlash after her first briefing on Tuesday. The new press secretary fielded only three questions in 14 minutes, with much of that time spent on prepared remarks. One White House official even told MS NOW that she had gotten off on the "wrong foot" and needed to improve "fast."
While Hannity, a friend of the president's, initially defended Zacharia, calling her briefing "perfectly normal" and any attacks against her "nasty," he seemed to have at least somewhat changed his tune by Thursday, when she appeared on Hannity .
Noting that her debut was "widely panned," the Fox News host asked, "What happened? How did you feel it went personally?"
The new press secretary responded similarly to how she did earlier Thursday on Real America's Voice, noting that she accepted the job just days before delivering her first briefing and that her preparation materials weren't finalized until Tuesday morning.
"Am I hearing that you think the staff should have prepped you better?" Hannity wondered.
"I could have just given a brief intro," explained Zacharia. "Instead of taking questions, I probably should have stepped aside."
She emphasized, however, that she was proud to have announced Trump's decision to ask Kimberly Guilfoyle , the former U.S. ambassador to Greece, to step down amid damaging allegations about her conduct in office.
Next, Hannity moved on to a new line of questioning — new reporting that she never passed the bar exam despite repeatedly appearing on television and being identified as a lawyer.
HANNITY: You called it a "conspiracy theory" as it related to the issue of being a lawyer. Now, you did go to Pepperdine. Pepperdine is a good school — no doubt about it. You took the bar exam, but you didn't pass the bar exam. Correct?
HANNITY: Okay. Did you ever take it a second time?
ZACHARIA: So, for background, I graduated Pepperdine, got married in the same week, and we had all the intent to move out to China. I had already preregistered for the bar exam during — basically during the summer. I knew I would be living in China and the results of the bar were inconsequential, and I sat for it because I didn't want to have a withdrawal status. And then I moved over to China, where I did get a job in an international practice at a Chinese law firm. I was doing multi-cross-country border transactions and multi-million-dollar shareholder agreements and —
HANNITY: Okay, but I wanna ask you specifically — I know that part of the story, and you did do all of that — but did you ever take the bar exam a second time or a third time?
ZACHARIA: I did not, Sean.
HANNITY: You did not. Okay. So, you said you consulted with many people, and they advised you that it was okay to call yourself a lawyer but not an attorney. Correct?
HANNITY: Okay. There's a report out tonight that shows 15 social media posts where you identify yourself as an attorney.
ZACHARIA: I think they were retweets, and I corrected the record and said that that's not endorsing the title. They were retweets of a title that had been given.
HANNITY: Look, that is a very tough room, and I've known a lot of press secretaries over the years. Following on the heels of Karoline Leavitt is very tough. Speaking for Donald Trump makes everything tougher. Why not just say, "I went to Pepperdine Law School and then took a different career path, and I took the bar once and didn't pass it?" Why get into this long, drawn-out definition of the difference between a lawyer and an attorney? 'Cause I don't think most people see much of a distinction. Why didn't you just say, "I never practiced law?"
ZACHARIA: Sean, when I moved back to the United States, I didn't retake the bar. I had four kids in six years. It was never my intent to go into the practice of law. When I went to engage in media and give legal analysis, I consulted attorneys and legal professionals as to whether or not they agreed that I could be labeled a lawyer — both because I had a valid Juris Doctor from a good law school, a reputable law school, Pepperdine Law School, and in conjunction with the fact that I did have actual, substantive legal experience. I wasn't providing any legal analysis, Sean, or — excuse me — legal advice. I wasn't being paid for legal advice. I was giving a general review of the legal circumstances surrounding it.
HANNITY: Alright. Why only three questions in 14 minutes, and what might you do a little differently going forward? I can give you some unsolicited advice. That's never gonna be a friendly room to you.
ZACHARIA: Yeah. So, what I would say is I would absolutely be very well prepared on the briefing, Sean, and I would love — and I do love questions — and I would love to build a relationship with all of those members of the press corps, so there is a substantive component to us having an ability to interact, and I will be very prepared, Sean, and I will step up to the duty that President Trump has asked me to as press secretary.

Anna Faris is breaking her silence after Mom creator Chuck Lorre revealed that he initially didn’t want to cast her in the hit CBS sitcom, and the actress isn’t hiding the fact that his comments stung. However, her response also included a surprising personal revelation about her own journey with sobriety.
In his new book, Sitcom: A Memoir , Lorre admitted that he was hesitant to hire Faris for the role of Christy Plunkett, a single mother battling alcoholism and drug addiction. “I initially said no; I wasn’t sure Anna would be appropriate for this kind of material,” Lorre wrote. He ultimately reconsidered, citing lessons learned from his troubled working relationship with Charlie Sheen .
The revelation apparently caught Faris off guard. In a new Instagram post, the actress acknowledged reading Lorre’s comments and admitted that they were painful.
“Yikes. Yes, I read a few things. I really didn’t see that coming. Of course it hurts,” she wrote.
A post shared by Anna Faris (@annafaris)
Despite the surprise, Faris expressed gratitude for her seven seasons on the comedy, which ran from 2013 to 2021. “Chuck gave me a job I loved, and for seven years I never took a day of it for granted,” she continued. “I’m proud of what we made together, and nothing changes how grateful I am for those people and those years.”
Faris also shared a deeply personal update, revealing that she is now sober, drawing a connection between her own recovery and the character she portrayed for seven seasons.
“I’ve been sober for a year and a half. I was on a show about recovery, and then I lived it,” she wrote. “Now I’m healthy, I’m working, and I’m happier than I’ve been in a long time. If anyone reading this is where I was, I hope that’s useful. It gets better. I’m proof.”
Faris departed Mom ahead of its eighth and final season in 2020. Earlier this year, she opened up about her decision to leave, explaining that the intensity of the production had begun to affect her focus.

articles.title_orig: Justice Dept. sues California officials over 20K alleged noncitizen voters
articles.title_zh: Justice Dept. sues California officials over 20K alleged noncitizen voters
articles.content_orig:
DoJ had demanded that LA county confirm citizenship of people on list in thumb drive, but officials refused
US politics live – latest updates
Send us your questions about immigration and the midterms
The US Department of Justice sued California on Thursday, seeking a court order to prevent the state from tabulating certain ballots cast in the midterm elections .
The suit came two days after the department made a specious demand to the state. On Tuesday, the department sent election officials in Los Angeles county a thumb drive with a handwritten password purporting to contain the names of noncitizens registered to vote. The department asked officials to confirm the citizenship of anyone on the list and set aside ballots from those whose status could not be confirmed. It gave the state 48 hours – an extremely narrow window – to take action. It did not provide details on how it came up with the names on the list. In its lawsuit, filed in federal court in the central district of California , the justice department said it had provided the state with more than 20,000 names of likely noncitizens.
The Los Angeles county clerk and recorder, Dean Logan, said his office would not review the list, in part because it didn’t consider the USB drive secure.
“The Department of Justice has not provided the underlying evidence, source, or methodology supporting its assertions that individuals identified in its records are ineligible to vote,” Logan said in a statement. “We cannot withhold or refuse to count ballots based solely on unverified allegations, nor can we disregard the legal requirements governing our election – and we certainly have no authority to act on records that are outside of our jurisdiction.”
In a statement on Wednesday, the California secretary of state, Shirley Weber, a Democrat, said the justice department had not provided the list of voters to her office. “The [justice department’s] relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states’ protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections,” Weber said.
Justice department lawyers are asking the court to order the state not to count votes from those it had flagged.
“This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote-by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter’s citizenship status can be determined,” the lawsuit said. “This Court should order California (1) to set aside vote-by-mail ballots from persons identified by the Federal Government likely to be noncitizens and (2) to independently – or in collaboration with the Federal Government – verify their citizenship status (beyond relying on unverified statements of citizenship necessary to registering) before tabulating their vote-by-mail ballot.”
The request to block tabulation comes amid concerns that Donald Trump and his allies will interfere in the counting of votes in the midterm elections, in which Republicans are expected to lose seats in Congress.
The Trump administration’s methodology for identifying noncitizens has come under scrutiny. Earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said there could be as many as 278,000 noncitizens on the rolls in four states, including more than 190,000 in California and about 16,000 in Nevada.
after newsletter promotion
Officials at the DHS refused to share their methodology with Nevada election officials and later turned over just 185 names of people it had a strong belief were noncitizens. When Nevada officials investigated, they found every one of those people was a citizen.
Richard Hasen, an election law scholar at UCLA, described the justice department’s efforts in California as “a nice publicity stunt that gets attention for [the justice department] and reinforces the notion among the president’s most ardent supporters that California is not doing enough to combat voter fraud”.
“The Department of Justice has no standing to tell states and localities to go in and remove voters from voting rolls in the midst of an election. In fact, the National Voter Registration Act bars systematic purges of ineligible voters in the 90-day period before the election,” he wrote in a blogpost . “The purpose of this provision, unsurprisingly, is to stop false positives, that is the removal of eligible voters who are mistakenly flagged as noncitizens. A rushed process would almost certainly lead to disenfranchisement.”

articles.title_orig: Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills five, minister says
articles.title_zh: Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills five, minister says
articles.content_orig:
Five people have been killed and 16 injured in a Houthi missile attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city of Aden in southern Yemen, which is the seat of the internationally-recognised government, officials say.
Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told the BBC that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when five ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace.
The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said they struck "the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden".
A coalition led by Saudi Arabia backs the government and is providing air support for an offensive by pro-government forces against the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemeni health minister Qasim Buhaibeh said the casualties included "those working to guard the site and civilian employees".
The country's Prime Minister Shaya Zindani condemned the Houthis' attack on Aden, calling it "cowardly" and a "continuation of their criminal behaviour".
He said the government continued to carry out its duties and vowed that it would not weaken the resolve of its forces to continue operations against the Houthis on Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and other front lines.
Earlier, the Houthis denied that they had attacked Saudi Arabia on Thursday, after the coalition said its forces had intercepted a cruise missile in the Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest shrines.
The Houthis have been launching missiles and drones at airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the strikes on the territory that they control in western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.
On Saturday, a Houthi missile strike killed 13 people at Riyadh's international airport, which was the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
Saudi Arabia's deputy foreign minister accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis to escalate their conflict with the kingdom.
"Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN Security Council resolutions," Rayed Krimly told reporters, according to AFP news agency.
"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added.
There was no immediate response from Iran's government. However, it has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and said it only supports them politically.
Iran's foreign minister has also said it is ready to provide "any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of talks" between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes.
At least 1,282 people have been killed and 5,890 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry.
The UN says another 201,000 people have been displaced and that there has been an alarming surge in suspected cholera cases.

articles.title_orig: A brewing Pacific storm could become one of the planet’s strongest this year
articles.title_zh: A brewing Pacific storm could become one of the planet’s strongest this year
articles.content_orig:
A typhoon warning is in effect for Guam and Rota, with damaging winds, torrential rain and dangerous seas forecast across the Mariana Islands this weekend.
Tropical Storm Champi was forecast to strengthen into a typhoon and pass over or very near Guam on Sunday, potentially bringing Category 2 or Category 3 conditions, National Weather Service forecasters said in a 3 p.m. Friday briefing.
Tropical storm warnings covered Saipan and Tinian, where a typhoon watch also remained in effect.
The NWS forecast called for tropical storm force winds to begin Saturday night or early Sunday and peak Sunday.
Residents are urged to shelter from sunset Saturday through sunrise Monday. The typhoon warning means winds of at least 74 mph are expected within 24 hours, while a tropical storm warning means winds of 39 to 73 mph are expected within 24 hours.
“This thing's been making a beeline for the island of Guam, likely as a typhoon on Sunday,” said Landon Aydlett, the NWS warning coordination meteorologist.
He said typhoon-force winds were expected on Guam and Rota, with Rota’s risk increasing if the track shifted northward. Saipan and Tinian were not expected to experience typhoon conditions, but forecasters said those conditions remained possible.
As of the briefing, Champi was about 590 miles east-southeast of Guam, near 11.4 degrees north latitude and 153.3 degrees east longitude.
It was moving west at 24 mph, with maximum sustained winds of 50 mph. The forecast track had held near Guam, but the cone of uncertainty stretched from south of Guam to north of Rota. Forecasters said the storm track stays within the cone 66% of the time and cautioned that shifts were still possible over the next 30 to 40 hours.
The briefing also described the islands as roughly 48 hours from the storm’s passage.
A Category 3 typhoon would bring extremely dangerous winds and cause devastating damage to homes, trees and infrastructure.
"The current forecast track does bring a Category 2 developing to a Category 3 typhoon directly over Guam on Sunday. We're going to have to take this very seriously," Aydlett said.
Aydlett said Champi is moving faster than previous Super Typhoons Bavi and Sinlaku, which means it could spend less time over the Marianas if it keeps up its pace.
Residents are advised to start preparing now and stay up to date with the weather.
"If we take a direct hit from a CAT 3, this will be the worst typhoon to strike Guam since Typhoon Mawar. If we see those conditions across southern Guam, this will be the worst conditions southern Guam to see for a number of years because southern Guam did not see CAT 2 or CAT 3 conditions during Mawar," Aydlett said.
Aydlett said this is going to be a typhoon shutter event. While there is are still hours to shift, it is "not a very good outlook for Guam."
He said Guam could face its most significant typhoon strike since Super Typhoon Mawar in May 2023, with winds potentially worse than those from Tropical Storm Choi Wan two weeks earlier and Super Typhoons Sinlaku and Bavi earlier in the year.
Forecast wind impacts varied by island. Tinian could see severe tropical-storm-force winds of 58 to 73 mph, while Saipan was forecast to have lesser tropical-storm-force winds of 39 to 57 mph. Aydlett warned that FEMA-rated 55-mph tents would not provide adequate protection for people on Rota.
“Those FEMA tents will not provide you the protection you need if you're on Rota living in those tents,” Aydlett said.
Residents in tents or compromised housing were implored to seek secure shelter and contact local homeland security offices about available options.
On Guam, forecasters advised residents to secure tents, canopies, tarps, trash bins and other loose items, and to close shutters because of the risk of flying debris.
Heavy rain and flooding were also expected.
According to NWS meteorologist Taelor Mesa, torrential rain was expected from Saturday through Sunday, with totals of 12 to 20 inches on Guam, 15 to 18 inches on Rota, and 8 to 12 inches on Saipan and Tinian.
Residents in flood-prone and low-lying areas, especially near streams and creeks, were urged to prepare for flooding and consider moving to shelters.
The briefing forecast life-threatening marine conditions, with a coastal flood watch in effect for Guam, Rota, Tinian, and Saipan. Expected coastal inundation was up to 5 feet on Guam, 2 to 4 feet on Rota, and 1 to 3 feet on Saipan and Tinian.
“We have combined seas of 10 to 13 feet for Guam and Rota Saturday night, and then it's going to peak. We're expecting 20 to 30 feet on Sunday morning,” Mesa said.
For Saipan and Tinian, combined seas were forecast at 10 to 13 feet Saturday night, peaking near 15 feet Sunday.
High surf was forecast for most shores, with the largest waves on north- and east-facing coasts. On Sunday morning, north-facing surf could reach 10 to 20 feet on Guam and Rota, with east-facing surf near 25 feet.
Saipan and Tinian could see north-facing surf of 8 to 12 feet and east-facing surf near 15 feet. Seas and surf were forecast to subside through Monday gradually.
Forecasters said the storm’s expected forward motion of 12 to 15 mph could limit the extent of coastal surge compared with slower-moving storms such as Sinlaku and Bavi.
They still warned of splashover and localized inundation, with the worst conditions expected near the storm’s direct path. Winds were forecast to remain breezy through Monday, with trade winds returning around midweek.
The briefing said fair weather and sea conditions were expected through Saturday morning, giving residents time to prepare.
The NWS said it would issue further updates on Saturday and directed the public to weather.gov/gum and weather.gov/gum/cyclones for the latest updates.
Gov. Lou Leon Guerrero has placed Guam in Condition of Readiness 2 as of 1 p.m. Friday.
She urged residents to finish preparations and secure their homes and belongings before Tropical Storm Champi arrives, especially as the island remains on a typhoon watch.
The governor said to remain indoors and make sure there is enough food, water, medicine and supplies for at least 7 days until she issues an all-clear.
"I want everyone to understand what this means. We have a serious storm approaching, and now is the time to finish preparing. We cannot control the strength of this storm, but we can do everything possible to prepare for it," Leon Guerrero said.
Leon Guerrero said people should charge their devices and prepare for possible power outages. If households are operating generators, she said they should be kept outdoors and away from windows and vents to reduce the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning.
She also wanted to be "absolutely clear" about one thing: stay out of the ocean.
"The waters of our island are especially dangerous during storms. No swimming, no fishing trips and no photography is worth risking your life or the lives of the first responders who may have to rescue you," Leon Guerrero said.

articles.title_orig: Authorities investigate letters with 'suspicious substances' sent to congressional, election offices
articles.title_zh: Authorities investigate letters with 'suspicious substances' sent to congressional, election offices
articles.content_orig:
Federal authorities say they are investigating "potentially hazardous" letters containing "suspicious substances" that have been sent to congressional and state election offices around the US.
The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) said they were trying to trace the "suspicious mailings", some of which were intercepted before they were received.
Authorities declined to say how many offices had been targeted, but several secretaries of state and congressional offices reported receiving the letters.
Coming just weeks before the US midterm elections, it echoes previous security scares involving suspicious mail.
The suspicious letters were sent to at least five Democratic senators' offices, most of which were intercepted before delivery.
They include California's Alex Padilla, Connecticut's Chris Murphy and New York's Kirsten Gillibrand, the senators' offices confirmed to the BBC.
New York Senator Chuck Schumer and Delaware Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester were also sent the suspicious pieces of mail, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.
"This incident is a stark reminder of the very real danger facing those who serve the public and who help administer our elections in the face of increasingly hostile political rhetoric," Padilla said in a statement to the BBC.
Several state offices have also received the suspicious mailings.
Delaware's Department of Elections said its office received and opened a letter containing a white powdery substance on Thursday, adding that staff followed security protocols on handling suspicious mail.
The Oklahoma State Election Board and the Louisiana secretary of state both said this week that their offices had received letters containing a white powder.
The Louisiana office was evacuated after a staff member opened the package on Tuesday, but it has since reopened after law enforcement found no evidence of harmful substances.
Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was the intended recipient of a letter containing white powder, but the USPIS had intercepted it.
The New York State Capitol in Albany and the Wyoming State Capitol in Cheyenne also received suspicious packages, according to emergency responder scanner feed reviewed by the BBC.
"This FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens," the agencies said in a statement on Thursday.
The suspicious mailings come just weeks before election day, which will determine the balance of power in Congress.
Ahead of the 2024 election, vote officials in 17 states received suspicious packages .
A year earlier, suspicious envelopes, some laced with fentanyl, were sent to election offices in at least five states.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said Wednesday that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump are responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's military-grade Starlink network.
Writing on X, Musk said that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Ukraine had accused SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on the Starshield internet service without warning, leading to disruptions to Ukrainian military operations amid fresh Russian strikes on its energy infrastructure.
On Wednesday, Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, said SpaceX had implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion, without notifying the country's defense forces.
That had disrupted some missions, and the same restrictions also applied to Starshield, he said on Telegram . Starlink is used to operate Ukraine's interceptor drones, the "most effective solution" against Moscow's Shahed drones, Beskrestnov said.
Starshield is a military-grade satellite network, while Starlink is only meant for "civilian or defensive activities," Musk said.
Some restrictions appear to have been partially lifted, with former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov thanking Musk early Thursday morning that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers an hour had been restored. "Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," Fedorov added.
The developments come amid tensions between Kyiv and Washington over an "energy ceasefire," between Ukraine and Russia announced by Trump.
Ukraine has, however, welcomed a deal subject to Moscow honoring its commitment, while Russian authorities said talks were ongoing, without confirming whether they had reached an agreement. On Monday, Zelenskyy accused the Russians of breaching the ceasefire.
Trump had also taken aim at Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities, saying that Kyiv's attacks were responsible for the increase in diesel prices, instead of the U.S.' war with Iran.
Washington has threatened to cut intelligence sharing with Kyiv, Reuters reported Wednesday, while Ukrainian officials said a day earlier that they have not received warnings of Russian attacks on the country for two straight days.
— CNBC's Elsa Olhen contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Tesla Roadster Reveal Dents TSLA Stock 4% [2026]
articles.title_zh: Tesla Roadster Reveal Dents TSLA Stock 4% [2026]
articles.content_orig:
The next-gen Roadster has been in development for nearly a decade. But perhaps it was worth the wait.
The next-gen Roadster has been in development for nearly a decade. But perhaps it was worth the wait.
Elon Musk promised a flying car. And the Tesla Roadster did exactly that.
Tesla demonstrated its next-generation Roadster at an event in Waco, Texas, where the electric supercar drove upside down, briefly flew, and accelerated to 60mph in under a second. It was an impressive demonstration of a car that likely will come with some heavy caveats if it ever goes into production.
The event was less than 30 minutes and felt more like a stunt show than a product reveal. Indeed, there was no mention of price, trim levels, or other such mundane details. Who cares about that boring crap anyway? The people were here to see a car fly, and that’s what Tesla gave them.
The next-gen Roadster certainly took the scenic route in getting here. A prototype version was announced as a “one more thing” style surprise during the 2017 Tesla Semi event . The specs sounded ludicrous even back then: 0-60 mph in 1.9 seconds, a top speed over 250 mph, a 200 kWh battery delivering up to 620 miles of range, and a $200,000 starting price tag. Musk said deliveries would start in 2020, which sounded perfectly doable at the time.
Early adopters quickly threw down $50,000 deposits (or $250,000 for the limited Founders Series), effectively interest-free loans to help fund Tesla’s scaling ambitions. But then Tesla seemed to forget about the Roadster, as cementing its status as the ultimate vaporware . Production deadlines slipped as Tesla prioritized mass-market vehicles like the Model Y, while also wrestling with the overly complicated Cybertruck. Occasionally, when Musk would remember that the Roadster existed, he would up the ante about its capabilities. This culminated in the “SpaceX package” that would equip the supercar with cold-gas thrusters, bestowing hover powers and a 0-60 time under one second.
Musk has also sought to downplay the Roadster’s significance, calling it a “small potato situation” that will not “move the needle in a major way financially.” He’s framed the supercar more as a joint engineering collaboration between Tesla and SpaceX, even questioning whether it’s “even a car anymore” given its experimental nature. Some analysts theorize that the decision to re-release the Roadster is an attempt to set the stage for a rumored Tesla-SpaceX merger .
Tesla’s failure to bring the Roadster to market allowed other automakers to slip passed the company with their own hyper-powered EVs. Rimac has smashed performance records with the Nevera, Porsche has refined electric performance with the Taycan, and Chinese giants like BYD are producing track-ready supercars at a fraction of the cost. The Roadster is no longer shocking the world as an impossible prototype; it’s playing catch-up to an industry that spent nine years building what Tesla merely rendered.

articles.title_orig: Measles cases reach 42 in rural Minnesota amid outbreaks
articles.title_zh: Measles cases reach 42 in rural Minnesota amid outbreaks
articles.content_orig:
Create an account or log in to save stories.
Thanks for liking this story! We have added it to a list of your favorite stories.
Public health officials are urging anyone who has not been vaccinated against measles to get vaccinated as case numbers in the state climb.
Since mid-September, the Minnesota Department of Health said there have been 25 cases of measles confirmed in two unrelated clusters amid a resurgence of the preventable disease. Six cases are in Fillmore County in southeast Minnesota, and 19 cases are in Todd County in central Minnesota. All involve unvaccinated people.
“There are pockets of unvaccinated or under-vaccinated people across Minnesota, and anyone who isn't vaccinated against measles is at risk — especially right now,” the health department wrote in a press release Thursday.
The median age of Minnesota’s measles cases is about 7 years old. Todd County, which has the most cases, has the lowest vaccination rates in the state for kids born in 2023 , according to state data. No one has been hospitalized in Minnesota due to measles this year, but some people have had to seek emergency room care.
MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all.
Minnesota’s outbreaks are not connected to multiple outbreaks in Wisconsin. In the past month, the number of people infected in Wisconsin has skyrocketed from 166 to 267 measles cases .
The United States declared measles eliminated from the country in 2000, but the disease has had a resurgence due to plummeting vaccination rates, said Jayne Griffith, senior epidemiologist with the health department.
“Up until probably the past couple of years, most of the measles cases that we saw in the United States were sparked by an unvaccinated person who traveled internationally, got infected and then got sick when they returned home,” Griffith said. “That is no longer the case. What we are seeing now in the United States is people just getting infected in the United States.”
The CDC has reported 4,080 confirmed cases in the U.S. so far this year, already surpassing last year’s total count of 2,289. It’s the highest number of reported cases of measles since 1991.
In Pennsylvania, which has seen a particularly large outbreak, at least six people have died from measles in recent months. Two were infants who were too young to receive the MMR vaccine.
Griffith said vaccine skepticism has grown, partly fueled by false claims from top federal government officials. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr has repeatedly claimed, without evidence, that childhood vaccines cause autism. And the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted many families routine medical care, meaning many kids missed out on their scheduled vaccinations.
Griffith said that if people have questions or concerns about the vaccine, they should talk to their health provider.
“There really is a lot of measles in the United States, and the best way to not have to worry about getting it is to be vaccinated,” Griffith said.

articles.title_orig: New York City Comptroller Defends Decision Not to Invest in Israeli Bonds
articles.title_zh: New York City Comptroller Defends Decision Not to Invest in Israeli Bonds
articles.content_orig:
Get the best experience and stay connected to your community with our Spectrum News app. Learn More
New York City Comptroller Mark Levine is walking back his campaign pledge to invest city pension funds in Israel bonds, saying the decision came down to financial returns.
In an interview with The New York Times , Levine said the decision was not politically motivated, though he acknowledged struggling with it on a personal level.
“I always said this would be based on financial considerations only, not politics — that's still my position,” Levine told the Times. “But as of now, we feel that because of some technical challenges, and because of financial considerations, that this is not an investment that we can make right now.”
During his campaign, Levine vowed to purchase Israel bonds after his predecessor, Brad Lander, opted not to renew the investments in 2023.
The Times reported that Israel bonds have returned around 5% on two- and three-year investments, and their technical ratings remain below levels from early 2023.
Levine’s decision has disappointed some Jewish leaders across the city, including former Comptroller Scott Stringer, who invested millions of dollars in Israel bonds during his tenure.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he supports Levine’s decision during a separate news conference.
“I don't believe that our city should purchase Israel bonds, we don't purchase the bonds of any other sovereign nation, I don't think we should make an exception when it comes to Israel,” Mamdani said. “And also, this is the decision that the comptroller is making and it's one that I support.”
When asked by The New York Times why he made the campaign pledge, Levine said he did not have a full understanding of the financial picture.

articles.title_orig: Cracks are beginning to show in the stock market as doubts about AI investments grow
articles.title_zh: Cracks are beginning to show in the stock market as doubts about AI investments grow
articles.content_orig:
Just one week after hitting fresh all-time highs, U.S. stocks are showing signs of strain as investors begin to fret about returns on the trillions of dollars that have been put into AI.
For U.S. consumers, it could mean a shakier economy moving forward.
After trading closed Thursday, the S&P 500 was off 1% from its week-ago record, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq had fallen more than 3% below its peak last week.
Driving the declines: Quarterly revenue growth at Anthropic has slowed, the Financial Times reported Wednesday. The AI giant is expected to be worth more than $1 trillion when it goes public, and at nearly $17 billion, its revenue is still massive and the company said it is profitable.
There are also rising concerns about whether China-based memory technology companies could undermine, or even overtake, their Western rivals. And even though the AI data center buildout has created a global shortage of processing chips, there are fears that Chinese mass production of memory chips could flood the market with an oversupply.
Meanwhile, investors have begun selling off the bonds backing some data centers , primarily over fears that AI revenues won’t be sufficient to cover the massive sums that have been borrowed to finance the building of the centers.
On Thursday, economist Ed Yardeni, a widely respected market commentator, lowered his year-end target for the S&P 500 to 7,900, down from 8,400, over what he said was rising investor caution about the artificial intelligence trade and lingering doubts about inflation and higher interest rates. The S&P 500 currently sits at about 7,600.
Most Americans don’t directly own tech stocks, let alone work in AI, which a growing number of studies show may have begun to limit job opportunities. Still, the AI buildout has been a massive part of what’s bolstering the economy, at least on paper.
Nearly half of all U.S. economy growth this year is attributable to tech-related spending . Those investments have also lifted the stock market even as a growing swath of other companies have experienced sharp declines in their share prices.
The tech-driven gains have in turn created a wealth effect that has helped propel steady U.S. consumer spending and, by extension, the job market. The result has been sturdy economic growth, even as lower-income and even middle-income households have continued to struggle under stubborn inflation and declining earnings.
“While higher interest rates, higher oil prices and persistent inflation create risks to the economy, strong positive forces such as the investment in AI infrastructure, high employment levels and consistent wage growth continue to outweigh the risks,” Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf said this week.
But other economists say consumers are already contending with a host of stressors that stand to weaken their position. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Thursday that inflation among businesses reached its highest rate since December 2022 — price growth that could eventually trickle down to consumers.
If tech spending — and stocks — show any sign of sustained declines, broader U.S. economic growth would likely be at risk.
“Higher interest rates, elevated energy prices, slow job growth and the sell-off in equities (if it continues) are all downside risks to consumer spending,” analysts with Citi wrote in a note Thursday.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

Nearly 1 in 4 confirmed Ebola patients in North Kivu is a child under the age of 5, yet children continue to face major barriers to accessing innovative medical tools.
Daniella, 10, smiles at the camera after being discharged from the Munigi Ebola treatment center. | DR Congo 2026 © Miora Rabearisoa/MSF
Children are paying a devastating price in the Ebola outbreak unfolding in northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). They account for a significant share of confirmed Ebola disease cases and are also more likely to die from the disease than adults.
According to Epicentre, the Doctors Without Borders/Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) epidemiological research center, nearly 1 in 4 confirmed Ebola cases in North Kivu province is a child under 5. MSF is deeply concerned by the disproportionate impact on children and is calling for the medical and research response to ensure that they are no longer left behind in access to vaccines, treatments, and clinical research.
The impact on children is particularly stark In North Kivu, where 24 percent of confirmed cases are among children under 5 years old; more than half on them — 54 percent — are infants under 1. In Ituri, by comparison, children under 5 account for 13 percent of confirmed cases, of whom 46 percent are under 1 year old.
While Ebola remains a deadly disease for all age groups, the youngest children face the highest risk of death. At the Ebola treatment center in Butembo, North Kivu, MSF teams have recorded a particularly high fatality rate among children. Between June and September 2026, 24 out of 30 children admitted to the center died from Ebola disease — most of whom were under the age of 5. The rapid spread of the disease in communities and limited access to specialized care in health facilities are contributing to these alarmingly high fatality rates.
A child-centered approach must be at the heart of medical care, operational planning, and research efforts.
“Primary health facilities often lack the specialized expertise, equipment, and infection prevention and control measures needed to identify and safely manage suspected cases,” explains Stéphanie Hoffmann, project coordinator for MSF in Butembo. “Most of the [children] admitted to our Ebola treatment center in Butembo had already been hospitalized for other illnesses in several facilities during the days or weeks before their admission. Their family members did not have Ebola themselves, and it is highly likely that these children contracted the disease inside health care facilities.”
To maintain access to essential non-Ebola health services while reducing the risk of Ebola transmission in health care facilities, infection prevention and control measures must be urgently strengthened in health facilities. This includes ensuring the availability of personal protective equipment (PPE) and strengthening training for health care workers in non-Ebola health centers across at-risk areas.
Efforts have been made to reduce the emotional toll of isolation on children in Ebola treatment centers, including the creation of visibility areas where parents can see and communicate with their hospitalized children. But admission to an Ebola treatment center remains a deeply distressing experience for children, many of whom are too young to understand what is happening and why.
MSF has recruited and trained caregivers to provide daily support and comfort to children inside several MSF-supported Ebola treatment centers while wearing full PPE. These caregivers have a range of experience, including caring for Ebola survivors. Today, 13 caregivers are supporting children at Kitatumba Ebola treatment center in Butembo. While not a perfect solution, this initiative provides essential human contact and emotional support for children suffering from the disease.
Historically, children have often been excluded from clinical research or included only after significant delays, creating dangerous gaps in the evidence available to guide and improve their care and delaying access to potentially lifesaving interventions.
"On top of enormous challenges caring for young patients, medical [teams] are dealing with a lack of pediatric dosing guidance and limited availability of child-friendly formulations of investigational medicines," said Dr. Guyguy Manangama, epidemiologist and deputy director of operations at MSF. "A child-centered approach must be at the heart of medical care, operational planning, and research efforts."
In the ongoing Ebola outbreak in DR Congo, children with the disease are at a disproportionately higher risk of dying.
"Treatments, vaccines, and other preventive tools should be evaluated for use in children from the outset of research efforts and made available to them without delay," added Dr. Manangama. "Yet in the current outbreak, children are still being left behind, with very limited access to vaccination trials and campaigns, as well as the latest therapeutic innovations — despite bearing a significant burden of disease. Children cannot continue to wait for data generated from adults before benefiting from advances in Ebola care and prevention."
MSF urges national authorities, research institutions, pharmaceutical developers, and international funders to prioritize the inclusion of children in all ongoing and future Bundibugyo virus studies. Ensuring equitable access to research and new medical tools, including vaccines, is essential to reducing preventable deaths and improving outcomes for one of the most vulnerable groups.
The impact of the outbreak on children extends beyond Ebola infection itself. Disruptions to essential health services can rapidly increase the risks of vaccine-preventable diseases, malnutrition , and other common childhood illnesses. Preserving routine immunization, nutrition programs, and access to primary health care — while reducing the risk of Ebola transmission in health facilities — must be considered a core component of the outbreak response, not an afterthought.

articles.title_orig: ‘He’s a Cabinet Secretary!’ Reporter Snaps At RFK Jr. Aide Trying to Stop Question on Measles Deaths
articles.title_zh: ‘He’s a Cabinet Secretary!’ Reporter Snaps At RFK Jr. Aide Trying to Stop Question on Measles Deaths
articles.content_orig:
A member of the press snapped at an aide of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Thursday when she tried to stop him from asking a question about measles deaths.
After a healthcare roundtable in Virginia Beach, Virginia, Kennedy was joined by Rep. Jennifer Kiggans (R-VA) to field questions from the press. At one point, a reporter asked about recent measles deaths in Pennsylvania.
"Do you believe that five deaths, potentially six, from measles in the state of Pennsylvania–," the report began. Before he could finish his question, however, an aide standing beside Kennedy quickly cut him off.
"We're also not going to talk about measles," the aide responded.
Kennedy protested and said he was "happy" to answer the question. At the same time, the reporter fired back at the aide much more aggressively.
"He's the highest-ranking health official in the country!" the report began. "He can answer that question! He's a cabinet secretary!"
Kennedy was then able to answer the question, saying:
We've done better. We're having a global measles outbreak right now. It's all over the world, and the measles outbreak is occurring because so many people went unvaccinated during the COVID pandemic, and this is something that Anthony Fauci, in fact predicted. He said we're gonna kill more people from measles and we save from COVID as we're shutting down measles vaccination programs. So now, six years later, We're seeing that population, we have a global outbreak. We have done better and particularly my administration has done better at controlling the outbreak than any other country in the world. We've had 4,000 measles cases this year. Mexico, which is a third of our population, had 20,000. Canada has 7,000, has one-eighth of our population. In Europe, they've had 135,000 cases. We're doing better at controlling it than any country in the world.
Kennedy then blamed Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) for the state's outbreak, accusing him of refusing CDC Epi-Aid.

articles.title_orig: Rick Kaplan Will Depart NAB
articles.title_zh: Rick Kaplan Will Depart NAB
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › People News
Rick Kaplan, a key figure at the National Association of Broadcasters for the past 14 years, will leave NAB at the end of the year.
For the last five years he has been NAB’s chief legal officer and EVP for legal and regulatory affairs, putting him at the elbow of President/CEO Curtis LeGeyt through some of NAB’s biggest issues.
The association also announced that in January it will bring its government relations and legal teams together under Shawn Donilon, who will be chief advocacy officer. LeGeyt called Donilon “a trusted leader and a skilled strategist.”
NAB said this structure will strengthen coordination between its advocacy on Capitol Hill, its interactions with the administration and its work with the Federal Communications Commission.
NAB had high praise for Rick Kaplan. President/CEO Curtis LeGeyt cited his ability to build consensus and his “tireless” advocacy.
According to the announcement text, Kaplan “led NAB through a decade of critical court wins, including a unanimous victory at the Supreme Court removing outdated restrictions on broadcast ownership. He also oversaw a seminal victory for the radio industry before the Copyright Royalty Board, which dramatically lowered streaming rates for broadcasters. That win paved the way for a landmark settlement in the most recent webcasting proceeding.”
NAB said he also worked on regulatory and legal issues including ATSC 3.0, retransmission consent, the FCC’s broadcast spectrum incentive auction, music licensing, sponsor ID rules and reducing broadcasters’ regulatory fees.
Prior to NAB, Kaplan held several roles at the FCC, including chief of the Wireless Telecommunications Bureau and counsel roles with Chairman Julius Genachowski and Commissioner Mignon Clyburn.

articles.title_orig: Partnership with World Wide Technology Raceway Opens Doors to Motor Sports Industry for First-Year Students
articles.title_zh: Partnership with World Wide Technology Raceway Opens Doors to Motor Sports Industry for First-Year Students
articles.content_orig:
The last few weeks have been exciting for students in the Rawlings Sport Business Management Program at Maryville University. Nearly 100 first-year students assisted in set-up and operations for both the NASCAR O’Reilly Auto Parts Series and Enjoy Illinois 300 NASCAR Cup Series Chase races held at the World Wide Technology Raceway in Madison, Il.
By design, Rawlings Sport Business Management students don’t just study the business of sport — they live it, and as raceway crew, they logged about 600 hours on-site during two set-up days, plus another 300 hours during event days. For many, this was their first opportunity to work in the industry.
Their impact on the success of the motor sport events did not go unnoticed.
“Rawlings Sport Business Management students are excellent, and we appreciate having them assist us with these national events,” said Declan O’Neil, vice president of partnership marketing at World Wide Technology Raceway.
Through such important experiential learning opportunities, students develop a wide range of industry skills. They also see how knowledge gained in the classroom plays out in the real world, said Daniel Schmidt, 10′, MBA ’16, instructor in the program.
“Their work at World Wide Technology Raceway involves corporate sponsorship, activation, event management and operations as well as ticketing and customer communication,” he said. “They also get exposed to motor sports — a part of the sports industry they’ve probably never considered before.”
Students appreciate the opportunity to practice skills, expand their resumes, build professional networks and discover first-hand what it takes to host a successful major event.
First-year student Karli Dean learned that being adaptable and paying attention to details is important. Student, Parker Medina, agreed. “The little details really go a long way when setting up these events,” Medina said. “Putting so much time and effort on the small things really shows how much the hosts care about their events as well as how much it means to the consumers and sponsors.”
Charlie Phillips, discovered the ticketing department involves much more than just selling tickets. “Ticketing covers a lot more to make sure fans are happy and have a great experience — so they’ll come back again and again,” said Phillips, a Rawlings Sport Business Management student.
Andra Alexander helped lead her team of fellow students as they hung scrim along fences on the racetrack as well as near fan engagement areas. “This really made me realize how much work gets put into any kind of event and is going to make me appreciate my experiences even more, whether I’m behind the scenes or in the stands,” Alexander said.
Erick Gates, who will enter the job market when he graduates in spring, understands the value of such opportunities. “Diversifying my resume with experiential experiences has been key,” he said.
The partnership with World Wide Technology Raceway has continued to deepen over the past seven years, says Schmidt, including both onsite and project-based learning opportunities as well as in-classroom sessions with executives of the raceway.
“Because of this partnership, we’ve had numerous students serve as interns and others hired as employees,” he said. “Our World Wide Technology Raceway opportunities are unique learning experiences specifically tied to the Rawlings Sport Business Management program, and we’re grateful for the confidence and trust they have in our students.”
About Maryville University Founded in 1872, Maryville University is a comprehensive and nationally ranked private institution with an enrollment of well over 9,000 students. Maryville offers over 90 degrees at the undergraduate, master’s and doctoral levels, as well as several certificates that align with the undergraduate and graduate education levels. Maryville is recognized as the third fastest-growing private university in the United States by The Chronicle of Higher Education, serving students from 50 states and 56 countries. More than 50,000 Maryville alumni globally, many of whom work and live in the St. Louis region.

articles.title_orig: Cornell president faces contentious faculty senate meeting over Jane Doe allegations
articles.title_zh: Cornell president faces contentious faculty senate meeting over Jane Doe allegations
articles.content_orig:
Cornell University’s president was met with scrutiny and sharp questions from its faculty senate Wednesday, when the group convened to discuss a no-confidence vote over the university’s handling of an alleged 2024 sexual assault at a fraternity house, according to an audio recording obtained by NBC News.
Discussion of a no-confidence vote comes after serious concerns were raised by students and staff over how the university responded to the allegations.
University President Michael Kotlikoff defended himself and Cornell’s administration as he took a series of pointed questions from the school staff.
At the meeting, most speakers were heard identifying themselves before speaking. Risa Lieberwitz, a professor of labor and employment law, said the issue of sexual assault “is a systemic problem. It deserves systemic attention.”
She told Kotlikoff that thus far it appeared he had “simply reacted to pressure.”
“It feels that the administration is considering more about how do we respond to pressure rather than the kind of leadership, which should have been doing systemic work and prioritizing these issues all along,” she said.
Kotlikoff argued that replacing its leadership was not the solution.
“We need to be able to work together to be able to change the culture, educate our students and try and address this problem,” he said at the meeting. “I want Cornell to be a leader in this area, and we have plans to really invest in this area. But the idea that you can somehow, because an event has occurred, eliminate it immediately — it’s just unrealistic.”
Last month, a former student identified as Jane Doe sued the university and seven current and former students in connection with her allegation of sexual assault.
In 2024, Cornell shut down the Chi Phi fraternity chapter at the university and expelled two students after Doe reported the incident. Others were suspended or faced lesser disciplinary action. The university also said it launched the Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault shortly after the incident and implemented recommendations to address sexual assault on campus.
No criminal charges were brought at the time, and the investigation has been reopened following Jane Doe’s lawsuit. Four of the men, through their attorneys, have denied coercing Jane Doe with drugs or sexually assaulting her. NBC News was not able to reach the other three men named in the lawsuit.
While the faculty senate does not have the authority to remove the president, the move would greatly increase the pressure on Cornell and its administration.
Darlene Evans, a senior lecturer emerita, asked Kotlikoff why he was only taking steps now “towards serious systemic change” when he had been in leadership roles at the university for more than a decade.
Evans noted that more than 35% of female undergraduates surveyed at Cornell University reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact involving physical force, threats of force or incapacitation, according to a Cornell University poll conducted last year, a figure that was up from 23% in 2023.
“It wasn’t until a no-confidence vote was introduced that Cornell’s administration announced any real steps to prevent sexual assault on this campus, or to seriously support survivors,” she said. “So saying what we’re going to do now kind of rings hollow here. Why haven’t you taken these things more seriously until now, when there’s a firestorm of press looking at Cornell?”
Kotlikoff announced Tuesday that all parties at fraternity houses and events would be banned through the rest of the academic year.
“We don’t have full ability to be confident that what goes on in those houses is safe, and so for the time being we will stop that activity,” he said during the meeting Wednesday.
He also addressed calls from some over whether Greek life at the university should be banned altogether.
“If at the end of the day, fraternities cannot exist in a safe environment, and we can’t be convinced that they can be safe, then we should make that decision,” he said. “But we should make it based on data and study and expertise, not on emotion.”
After a question-and-answer session, the faculty senate began debating the no-confidence resolution, with another meeting scheduled for later this month. Many spoke in favor of the resolution, while others wanted to delay the vote until the results of an upcoming independent investigation.
Earlier this month, the university announced that Sally Yates, the former deputy U.S. attorney general and acting U.S. attorney general, would lead an independent review on how Cornell University responded to the allegations and, more broadly, how it responds to sexual harassment, assault and misconduct on campus.
New York Attorney General Letitia James is also investigating the allegation. A spokesperson said staff members from the attorney general’s office have “spoken with the Tompkins County District Attorney, Jane Doe’s attorney and several candidates for outside counsel to support the investigation.”
After the meeting, music professor Ariana Kim said she was “really inspired by everyone who spoke and was brave in favor of the resolution — it takes a lot to stand up in front of the president and ask direct questions of him.”
Kim said she has received some 200 emails from alumni saying they support the no-confidence resolution and want the administration to be held accountable.
The professor said some at the meeting held up signs that read, “I stand with Jane Doe,” “How many more?” and “We demand accountability.”
“Some people broke down and held each other after the meeting,” she said.
Political history professor Richard Bensel said that so far the central administration “has not responded in a way that is going to diminish faculty and students’ despair over the way that the university has treated the issue.”
Bensel said he was unsure if he wanted the president to resign, but said he thought university leadership “will not reform itself without passage of the no-confidence resolution.”
“I can imagine a way the trustees through the president can reconcile their relations with the Cornell community but that requires a real change in governance style, and I don’t think that is possible under this administration,” he said. “There are real problems in the way the university is run.”
Adam Reiss is a reporter and producer for NBC and MSNBC.
Daniella Silva is a national reporter for NBC News, focusing on immigration.
Abigail Brubaker is a Desk Editor/Associate Producer based in New York
