articles.title_orig: DOJ sues California, demands it purge voter rolls for alleged noncitizens
articles.title_zh: DOJ sues California, demands it purge voter rolls for alleged noncitizens
articles.content_orig:
Washington — The Justice Department sued California on Thursday, alleging that the federal government has identified more than 20,000 noncitizens who are unlawfully registered to vote.
The lawsuit , filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, came after Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter sent letters to counties earlier this week, including Los Angeles, ordering them to review a list of names of suspected noncitizens who he alleged received mail-in ballots for the upcoming midterm elections.
"State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement announcing the lawsuit.
"If found responsible in a court of law, the State of California will have seriously undermined confidence in our electoral system and violated laws that protect our nation's representative system of government."
In the letter that McCotter sent to the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk, he enclosed a password-protected thumb drive that he said contained names compiled by the Department of Homeland Security, and imposed a 48-hour deadline for the clerk's office to review the list.
Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder and clerk, said in a statement responding to McCotter's demands that the county would not be reviewing the materials on the thumb drive because doing so would conflict with "established data privacy and information security protocols." He said the device was not considered a "secure medium."
Secretary of State Shirley Weber, meanwhile, said the Justice Department had not provided the list of names and blasted the Trump administration for what it said were "unsubstantiated claims" that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls.
In Thursday's lawsuit, the Justice Department accused the state of failing to work with the federal government to correct the alleged problems with its voter rolls.
"The Federal Government asked California to work collaboratively to identify any noncitizens registered to vote in the State. California made no serious effort to do so," the lawsuit said.
"The United States thus seeks commonplace election relief when a ballot is called into question. This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote-by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined," it added.
In a statement provided to CBS News, the California Secretary of State's office said, "Due to the pending litigation, we have no further information we can share regarding the matter." It directed CBS News to its news release on the situation and Weber's letter to McCotter.
CBS News has also reached out to the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk for comment.
The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division has filed 31 lawsuits in an effort to force states to hand over unredacted copies of their voter rolls. The division has said it wants to ensure states are keeping clean voter lists, but it has since acknowledged that it also intends to share the data with the Department of Homeland Security so that the lists can be screened for noncitizens.
Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, sent letters to all 50 states in July threatening to take criminal action if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls.
So far, the Justice Department has lost 26 of those cases, and has not achieved one legal victory to date.
It has resorted to using publicly available voter lists and other investigative means to try to identify noncitizens who may be registered in those states.

articles.title_orig: Our model puts us within 'shooting distance' of China's AI models, says Reflection CEO
articles.title_zh: Our model puts us within 'shooting distance' of China's AI models, says Reflection CEO
articles.content_orig:
Tim Cook and Mark Zuckerberg have clashed for years, but with John Ternus taking the reins at Apple , the rivals are finding common ground in artificial intelligence.
Meta and Apple revealed a new collaboration Thursday that will enable developers to easily run Meta's new open-weight AI model on Apple's high-end desktop computers.
The collaboration centers on Muse Spark Open, the most capable open-weight model released under a license that allows for limited commercial use, according to Meta. It's an 816-billion-parameter model using a so-called mixture-of-experts architecture . As an open-weight model, developers can download the technology's parameters, or weights, from the internet and run the model on a wide range of hardware.
Customers will be able to pair between two and four Mac Studio PCs to use Muse Spark to code, analyze video or do other agentic work. The model runs locally, instead of in the cloud, adding a layer of security and saving users money, the companies said.
Thursday's announcement, following months of collaboration, is a sign that the AI boom has shifted historical alliances in Silicon Valley. For years, Apple and Meta regarded each other warily and avoided public partnerships, and the relationship hit rock bottom after Apple introduced privacy changes in 2021 that limited the targeting capabilities of digital ad companies. Meta estimated in early 2022 that the change would cut its revenue that year by $10 billion.
Representatives from Apple and Meta declined to say if the Muse Spark Open collaboration was the start of a deeper relationship.
Zuckerberg posted a picture on X showing the Meta agent working on a Mac computer. He wrote, "Muse Spark Open -- weights releasing today -- runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple."
Ternus responded , "Congrats to the team! Amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open's caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk. Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI!"
Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said in an interview that many powerful open-weight models are too big to be run on the majority of personal computers, but Apple's Mac Studios make enough memory available to users so that it's practical to run Muse Spark Open.
The move represents an important show of confidence in Meta's rebooted AI efforts and could pose a challenge to OpenAI and Anthropic. It could also signal Apple's growing strength in AI chips, a market that Nvidia has dominated so far due to their prevalence in large data centers.
" We worked with Apple to bring leading Agent capabilities to your desktop for the first time on the Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios, so you know we're really excited about this," Wang said. Developers can download a version of the AI model from websites like Hugging Face without extra configuration for Apple's silicon. Muse Spark Open has also been tuned to run faster on Apple's hardware, and the iPhone maker revealed new benchmarks for its chips and published technical documentation about its MLX AI framework's ability to split open-source models across multiple machines.
Mac Studios aren't cheap though, and this AI model requires the fastest Apple chips and as much memory as possible.
Currently, a Mac Studio with the required M5 Ultra chip and 256GB of memory costs at least $10,799. A more expensive version with 512GB of RAM will be released later this month.
Plus, users will need to buy multiple machines.
The two companies are collaborating on open-source AI, which has become a point of contention in Washington as politicians worry that free Chinese models could undercut American AI. Although Meta once centered its AI strategy on its older open-weight Llama family of models , it has since focused on creating proprietary models under the leadership of Wang , who joined Meta when the company invested more than $14 billion into his former startup Scale AI last year.
While Apple and Meta, then known as Facebook, partnered on iPhone extensions over a decade ago, they haven't struck any public partnerships since 2017 after Apple removed system-level Facebook integration from the iPhone.
"Most of the animosity predates my tenure at the company, but obviously there's been a long history between Meta and Apple," Wang said, pointing to one member of his team, AI researcher and former Apple director Daniel Gross, as a reason for the collaboration. Gross, along with former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman , was a major Zuckerberg hire last year as the Facebook founder was overhauling his company's AI strategy.
Their leaders have also traded harsh words.
Cook, who was Apple CEO until Ternus succeeded him last month, took a shot at Zuckerberg in 2018, during the Cambridge Analytica scandal, saying, "I wouldn't be in this situation." Cook often criticized Meta for compromising user privacy.
Zuckerberg has also insulted Apple in public, telling Joe Rogan last year that the company "hasn't invented anything great since the iPhone." Zuckerberg has long sought to find a platform that Meta can own so it's not beholden to Apple.
Ternus, a hardware engineer, has already started changing things at Apple, including when it releases products.
And Meta's developers haven't been able to resist Apple's products. The company bought hundreds of Mac computers so its Superintelligence team could experiment with local AI and agents earlier this year.
Meta is just the latest AI model developer to team up with Apple.
In 2024, Apple announced a partnership with OpenAI to integrate ChatGPT into Siri, although the integration " dramatically underperformed " and didn't lead to OpenAI user growth, OpenAI said in a filing that's part of a legal dispute with Elon Musk 's xAI. Apple sued OpenAI in July, alleging trade secret theft, a claim OpenAI denied.
Earlier this year, Apple announced a deal with Google , to use its Gemini models in Apple Intelligence as well as Google Cloud infrastructure.
Still, Apple's AI strategy has drawn criticism from investors and customers in part because its new version of Siri, released last month, isn't as advanced as chatbots and agents from leading labs.
Meanwhile, Meta has bet big on becoming a leading lab but has struggled to keep up with the competition and its business remains almost entirely reliant on ads. Recent developments, such as Meta's Muse personal agent app and its latest proprietary foundation model, Muse Wonder, released earlier this week, have begun to excite investors who are optimistic about new AI business opportunities.
Open source remains part of Zuckerberg's AI strategy. In August, Meta debuted a small open-weight AI model dubbed Muse Glimmer , with Zuckerberg pledging to eventually release something bigger and more powerful.
Muse Spark Open isn't as advanced as Muse Wonder, a proprietary offering, but Wang said it's good enough to potentially entice more coders to upgrade.
"These aren't the most capable models that we've developed or released," Wang said. "But we think that there will be a lot of companies and developers who sort of use this model and tinker with it at small scale and then seek to ramp up and scale up their usage."

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: S&P 500 rises as tech stocks pare losses; Nasdaq turns higher, Dow advances as Treasury yields drop
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: S&P 500 rises as tech stocks pare losses; Nasdaq turns higher, Dow advances as Treasury yields drop
articles.content_orig:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose on Thursday as concerns around tech companies overspending on artificial intelligence led investors to rotate out of the trade and seek value elsewhere. Traders also digested U.S. data that pointed to persistent inflation.
The blue-chip index added 556.21 points, or 1.08%, to end at 52,177.69. The S&P 500 gained 0.33% to close at 7,744.06. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite closed up 0.08% at 26,713.03, rebounding from session lows. At one point, the index was down 1.4% on the day.
Seagate Technology and Western Digital added to their declines this week, along with shares of SK Hynix , which drove a rout in South Korea's Kospi index overnight. Traders were becoming concerned about a potential memory chip glut as South Korea faces increasing competition from China. Tesla CEO Elon Musk discussed the matter in a post on X , saying that "China will be making a LOT of RAM in 2028."
Compounding worries in the AI space, sources told CNBC that Anthropic's revenue grew to $16.8 billion in the third quarter, with some traders concerned the AI giant's top line might not be growing fast enough to justify the lofty gains in chipmakers.
However, other stocks in the AI trade recovered. CoreWeave shares gained almost 6%, reversing course from the prior day's losses. The stock tumbled more than 15% in the previous session as investors grew fearful that the company was borrowing too much for its AI build-out. CoreWeave corporate bond yields also surged . Additionally, Micron Technology rebounded from earlier losses to gain nearly 2%.
"When Treasurys are yielding 5% and that's the highest since the early 2000s, investors are going to start weighing that versus taking a huge bet on on AI," said Alex Shahidi, co-CIO of MAI Capital Management's Evoke. "It's not are you in or out of AI; it's how concentrated you want to be."
The market was supported by gains in areas outside of tech. Shares of retailer Walmart climbed 1.5%, while Nike shares jumped more than 5%.
Investors also reacted to more insights on the inflation front. The September reading on producer prices recorded an increase of 1.3% on the month and 6.3% year over year — the biggest monthly and yearly gains since 2022.
Concerns that the Federal Reserve could tighten monetary policy more aggressively before year-end weighed on equities Wednesday after new data showed consumer prices in September rose faster than expected on a year-over-year basis.
"Today's PPI report, after Wednesday's CPI, confirms inflation is getting worse as energy prices stay high," said David Russell, global head of market strategy at TradeStation. "Election or no election, prices are rising and the Fed might be forced to act."
The three major averages finished Thursday's session with gains.
The S&P 500 rose 0.33% to end at 7,744.06, while the Nasdaq Composite gained just 0.08% to 26,713.03. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 556.21 points, or 1.08%, to 52,177.69.
Analysts at Barclays say they're seeing signs that a SpaceX - Tesla merger is something that executives are thinking about, analysts with Barclays said Wednesday.
"We believe recent management comments indicate they see key benefits of a combination," analyst Dan Levy wrote to clients in a Wednesday note, though he didn't get into the details.
Vertical integration of production pipelines for two the companies, in addition to the elimination of overhead redundancies, would boost value added, Levy said. He put the Texas-based Terafab data center, which is already structured as a joint venture, at the center of his estimation.
"We see Terafab as a key driver of the potential combination as CEO Elon Musk strongly believes that Terafab will be required to support TSLA/SPCX compute needs," he wrote.
Performance is broadening out within the S&P 500.
More than half of S&P 500 stocks are trading above their 200-day moving averages, an improvement from  less than 40% at the end of September when gains were more concentrated, likely within tech stocks.
Some of the names moving above their 200-day moving averages for the first time in more than a month were Walmart ( WMT ), Kroger ( KR ), HCA Healthcare ( HCA ) and United Health Services ( UHS ).
— Nick Wells and Tobias Burns
CoreWeave stock broke into black in Thursday afternoon, trading up 3.5% just as of 2:53 p.m., after being down as much as 9.5% in morning trading.
The uptick proved a Wednesday Deutsche Bank note to be prescient. Analyst Brad Zelnick said that Wednesday's dislocation was "presenting buying opportunity."
"If this is purely about broader AI financing concerns, we'd argue CoreWeave continues to scale rather responsibly," he wrote to clients. "Near-term liquidity is in decent shape."
The stock got hit with a combination blow on Wednesday, with higher-than-expected inflation data initially pushing up bond yields, industrial titans fretting about the stock online, and some warnings from analysts about its sector.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) is lower for an eighth straight trading day, its first eight-day slide since September 2015; it fell for nine sessions in May 2006. The ETF has fallen more than 15% over that stretch. The fund was last down around 2%.
The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) is also down an eighth straight day, making it the longest slide since May 2006 when it fell for nine straight sessions.
— Sarah Min and Nick Wells
More than half of S&P 500 constituents are trading above their 200-day moving averages, a notable improvement from late September when that figure was around 40%.
The shift suggests that participation in the market's advance is broadening beyond recent high flyers of the AI trade. The 200-day moving average is a widely watched indicator of a stocks' long-term trend and a shift above that level can show improving momentum.
Among the names moving above their 200-day moving averages for the first time in a month are Walmart , Kroger , HCA Healthcare and Universal Health Services .
Wall Street firm Baird upgraded Bank of America to outperform from neutral Thursday, while maintaining its $62 price target, implying a 21% upside from its Wednesday close of $51.
The higher rerating on the bank comes despite it reporting a soft quarter before the open Thursday.
Bank of America delivered an earnings per share miss and weak noninterest income along with higher expenses on Wednesday, sending shares lower.
Baird called the sell-off "overdone" and sees the stock's weakness as a buying opportunity. That stems from the firm's view that the bank's 2027 net interest income outlook is an "incremental positive" coupled with the stock's attractive valuation.
Gil Luria, analyst at DA Davidson, said Anthropic's revenue for the third quarter was "not what anyone wanted to see."
Sources told CNBC that the AI giant's revenue grew to $16.8 billion in the third quarter , up from its second-quarter revenue of $11.6 billion. But, that growth in the third quarter was slower than its rise in the previous one, as first-quarter revenue for the company was just $4.7 billion.
Luria said, though, that there was good news as the Financial Times reported that Antrhopic had positive cash flow in the third quarter, pushing back on the narrative that the AI labs can't get to profitability. But he added that investors shouldn't be looking at a single company to judge the performance of the sector, and rather focus on corporate and consumer spending on the technology.
"We expect the overall market for AI spend to continue on a steep path as it diversifies away from Anthropic and OpenAI," he wrote in a Thursday note. "These two will see their market get cut from providing all-encompassing AI services to only providing frontier tokens for mission critical cost-insensitive applications… This overall demand should support more AI compute demand and more data center construction, even if it doesn't meet the most outlandish extrapolations."

articles.title_orig: Ilhan Omar's husband snaps over rumors she fled US after federal immigration fraud raid
articles.title_zh: Ilhan Omar's husband snaps over rumors she fled US after federal immigration fraud raid
articles.content_orig:
Rep. Ilhan Omar's, D-Minn., husband, Tim Mynett, responds to rumors that the congresswoman fled the country after HSI raided their Washington, D.C., home as part of a federal criminal investigation. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)
While Ilhan Omar , D-Minn., has not been seen publicly since federal agents raided her Washington, D.C., residence on Monday, her political consultant husband was once again spotted emerging from their shared rental home this week.
Tim Mynett was seen Wednesday stepping out in the neighborhood to walk their Golden Labrador Retriever dog Teddy, a second time later that same day to take out the trash and a third time to walk out his wife's staffer.
"There are rumors that the congresswoman left the country, is that true?" Mynett was asked while on an evening walk with Teddy.
"You guys are annoying the hell out of all the neighbors around here, man," he told Fox News Digital when approached about the developments this week, including President Donald Trump weighing in on the saga.
One of Omar's congressional staffers was captured the same day bringing into the couple's home two large bags from fast food chain Burger King. Security escorted her to the door and staked out in front of the house after she entered with the meal.
ILHAN OMAR’S EMBATTLED HUSBAND APPEARS AT SCENE OF HSI RAID IN MIDST OF CRIMINAL FRAUD INVESTIGATION
An image of Ilhan Omar overlaid over her neighborhood in DC. (Getty Images)
Rumors swirled that Omar fled from the country following the raid carried out by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) as part of a criminal fraud investigation looking into the Somali-born congresswoman’s immigration paperwork, as first reported by Fox News Digital.
Omar’s cellphone and passport were reportedly seized by federal authorities during the search.
The congresswoman's staff helped to get her birth year adjusted from 1981 to 1982 in the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library, according to reporters. Omar gained citizenship automatically through her father’s naturalization since she was reportedly 17 years old at the time. If Omar was born in 1981, she would have been 18 years old, meaning the validity of her citizenship could be threatened because she was no longer a minor.
The altered birthdate was published during her entire time serving in Minnesota’s House and for months into her time serving in Congress.
When asked about the federal investigation earlier this week, Mynett told Fox News Digital he has "no concerns" about what federal authorities will find on his wife while investigating her immigration pathway.
"My wife came here when she was 12 years old as a child war refugee," Mynett said. "No concerns."
His comments to Fox News Digital come after Omar’s relatives were reportedly issued subpoenas as part of HSI’s investigation into the congresswoman's immigration paperwork. At least two of Omar's relatives were subpoenaed, one of which is reportedly Omar’s sister, Sahra Noor.
ILHAN OMAR’S HUSBAND INSISTS HE HAS ‘NO CONCERNS’ AMID FEDERAL IMMIGRATION INVESTIGATION
Fox News Digital asked Mynett about President Donald Trump publicly questioning Omar’s net worth by alleging on Truth Social that her accountant may have reported fraudulent money when her previous financial disclosure listed the couple's shared net worth as high as $30 million.
"Why did Ilhan Omar report a Net Worth of up to 30 Million Dollars just a short time ago, and then immediately say, "Oh, I made a mistake! It’s really $100,000." Could it be that her highly paid accountant actually reported the money that was stolen from her fraudulent activities in Minnesota? Would something like that be possible? Do you think the accountant actually gave the right number the first time, 30 Million Dollars, and then she was forced to disavow because she never would have been able to report where that much money came from? She must have freaked out when she saw that money!" Trump posted to Truth Social on Tuesday.
"Where did her house come from, where did her cars come from, and what about her lovely place in Washington, D.C.? I didn’t know that Congressmen and women made that kind of money, but I do know her husband, according to information and belief, makes almost nothing, so it couldn’t have come from him. How many people did she illegally bring into our Country from Somalia? America wants answers, and we want them, NOW!"
Mynett is at the center of yet another investigation into Omar — this time looking into her finances.
Following Monday’s HSI raid, U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said Tuesday that her office is also investigating Omar's financial disclosures about reporting of her and Mynett’s shared net worth.
OMAR FACES MOUNTING SCRUTINY AFTER FRAUD RINGLEADER SENTENCED TO 41 YEARS
Rep. Ilhan Omar sits with husband Tim Mynett during the first day of the Democratic National Convention at the United Center on August 19, 2024, in Chicago, Illinois. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
Scrutiny of Omar's finances intensified after her 2024 congressional financial disclosure listed business interests associated with Mynett valued between $6 million and $30 million. Omar's office subsequently said the figures were incorrect and amended the filing.
The largest change in the documents was from Mynett’s assets . His reported ownership interests in both his winery and venture capital advisory firm, which were previously valued in the millions of dollars, are listed with no value now.
In Omar’s 2024 financial disclosure records, Mynett’s share in his winery was valued between $1 million and $5 million, and his share at the venture capital advisory firm was valued between $5 million and $25 million. Now, his equity interests are both listed at $0.
Omar's office previously told Fox News Digital that Mynett has partners in both businesses and said the earlier disclosure mistakenly reflected the businesses' total equity rather than his ownership interest. The office also said the original filing listed assets without accounting for liabilities.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Officials noted that the investigation into Omar's financial disclosures is unrelated to the raid on her home.
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Scientists Uncover D. Rex: Gigantic New 'King' Fungus From China Traces Its Roots to 65 Million Years
articles.title_zh: Scientists Uncover D. Rex: Gigantic New 'King' Fungus From China Traces Its Roots to 65 Million Years
articles.content_orig:
Yunnan Province in China is famous for its mushrooms and fungi, but somehow, scientists have only just come across a new species that has rightly earned the name 'king'.
Named Dianjunus rex (or D. rex for short), its gigantic, club-like fruiting bodies can grow up to 50 centimeters tall, which is about one and a half feet, or the height of a traffic cone.
But its impressive size is not the only exciting thing about this fungus. Its genes also contain clues about a major moment in the history of life on Earth.
Mycologist Indunil Senanayake of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and her colleagues describe the new species in a paper published in Frontiers in Fungal Biology .
D. rex is the only known member of its family, Dianjunaceae .
"This remarkable species… provides a rare window into the evolution of extreme fungal body forms," says Senanayake.
"The discovery illustrates how much fungus biodiversity remains to be discovered in East Asian forests."
D. rex's fruiting bodies were discovered in the forests of Yunnan Province. (Song et al., Frontiers in Fungal Biology , 2026)
The researchers found the Dianjunaceae family split off from its closest known relatives about 65 million years ago, by comparing its DNA to hundreds of other fungi whose evolutionary history is well-known.
"This timing raises an intriguing possibility," says Senanayake.
The family emerged just 1 million years after the Chicxulub asteroid impact, which triggered a mass extinction event.
The dramatic changes to Earth's climate that resulted from the asteroid wiped out three-quarters of plant and animal species on Earth, including, famously, all non-avian dinosaurs .
"After the mass extinction, forests experienced dramatic changes, including the sudden availability of large amounts of dead plant material," Senanayake says .
"For wood-associated decomposing fungi, such environmental disruption may have created new ecological opportunities."
This isn't the first time scientists have proposed that the dinosaur-killing asteroid led to a worldwide fungal 'boom' . Fossils found in North Dakota, Colorado, and New Zealand show that massive spikes in fungal activity followed in the wake of this mass extinction.
Fungi typically prefer cooler temperatures and acidic environments. The cooler and darker conditions that arise when geological calamities shade our skies – as Chicxulub did – could have easily set the scene for an era dominated by fungi.
Close examination of D. rex under a microscope reveals its identifying features, including its asci and spore-producing structures (h-p). (Song et al., Frontiers in Fungal Biology , 2026)
D. rex is related to fungi like morels, truffles, and cordyceps , in the phylum Ascomycota . Like all fungi, Ascomycetes live as mycelium, below the ground or inside the substrates (wood, poop, your toenails, etc.) upon which they feed.
D. rex is often found at the base of oak trees, including the Chinese cork oak ( Quercus variabilis ) in the forests of the Yunnan Province in south-western China. The specimens on record so far were growing on the decaying roots or stumps of these trees.
When it comes time to reproduce, D. rex sends out its gigantic white fruiting bodies, which are called stromata. These serve the same purpose as mushrooms do for other fungi, broadcasting spores into the air so more D. rex may flourish on the forest floor.
But it's unclear why D. rex 's stromata are quite so gargantuan – the largest of any Ascomycete on record. Some specimens the researchers collected weighed a whopping 2.2 kilograms.
"A fruiting body which towers above surrounding vegetation and debris could have better dispersal of spores by wind in dense forests," Senanayake proposes .
"However, such a large structure requires substantial energy investment, suggesting that this strategy likely evolved only where the ecological benefits outweighed the costs."
The research has been published in Frontiers in Fungal Biology .

articles.title_orig: CoreWeave's slump spotlights growing burden of debt behind AI boom
articles.title_zh: CoreWeave's slump spotlights growing burden of debt behind AI boom
articles.content_orig:
CoreWeave 's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.
CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure buildout. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.
Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.
Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive .
Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.
Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.
While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.
Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.
Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.
The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.
A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.
No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.
"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.
CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.
"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."
The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft , Meta , IBM and Caterpillar , Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.
"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.
Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle 's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.
"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

articles.title_orig: Google updates Android earthquake alerts with more info, expands to 200+ regions
articles.title_zh: Google updates Android earthquake alerts with more info, expands to 200+ regions
articles.content_orig:
Google is delivering an update to Android’s earthquake alerts system that will show more information while also expanding support to over 200 regions across the globe.
Launched in 2021, Android’s earthquake alerts system uses the sensors in Android smartphones to detect the earliest signs of an earthquake and provide a precious few seconds of warning prior to destructive impacts. While the system has had a couple of mishaps , it has also saved lives and Google says it has sent over a billion alerts.
Effective today, the Android earthquake alerts system is now live in more than 200 regions across the globe, up from 98 previously. Google specifically calls out Panama and Guatemala as new additions.
Beyond the regional expansion, Google is also updating the design of earthquake alerts. Specifically, the “Be Ready” step is going to offer more information on the location of the earthquake’s epicenter and the estimated magnitude.
We’ve built-out our Be Ready alert with new helpful guidance. In the coming months, you’ll see a map with a radius of where we’ve detected shaking, estimated earthquake magnitude, action you can take, and a button to learn more about the earthquake as information comes in.

articles.title_orig: Eric Deters files defamation lawsuit against Kimberly Guilfoyle
articles.title_zh: Eric Deters files defamation lawsuit against Kimberly Guilfoyle
articles.content_orig:
Eric Deters, the Republican donor who accused Kimberly Guilfoyle of asking him to wire her $100,000 to pay her American Express bill in exchange for her help with the Trump administration ahead of her Senate confirmation hearing, has filed a defamation lawsuit against Guilfoyle and her legal team.
Guilfoyle was pushed out of her ambassadorship to Greece earlier this week, announcing her resignation Tuesday. Guilfoyle's team publicly disputed the authenticity of text messages Deters shared with multiple news outlets, including CBS News.
Deters filed the lawsuit in Kentucky state court on Thursday.
Deters said Guilfoyle's legal team issued a statement to the Wall Street Journal claiming Deters owed Guilfoyle money and did not fulfill his obligations. The Journal published part of her attorney's statement, that Guilfoyle "was owed a balance for traveling to and supporting these patriotic events," which Deters denies.
"Kim Guilfoyle and her lawyers claimed my allegations were false and they would defend the allegations vigorously," Deters wrote in a statement accompanying his lawsuit. "Now they can in Kentucky."
CBS News has reached out to the attorneys named in the lawsuit — Jesse Binnall and David M. Schwartz — for comment.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine hits Russian refinery as Starlink satellite services are restored
articles.title_zh: Ukraine hits Russian refinery as Starlink satellite services are restored
articles.content_orig:
Russia has accused Ukraine of attacking an oil refinery on Thursday after President Volodymyr Zelensky said such strikes, halted at the request of the US, would resume.
Zelensky said he had restricted attacks for three days while Russia continued striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure. "We're done," he told the Financial Times .
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Kyiv had also tried to hit refineries on Wednesday - which Ukraine denied - but there had been no "significant damage".
Zelensky also accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing to pressure Kyiv into ending attacks but Ukrainian defence sources later told the BBC some functionality on Starlink satellite services had resumed.
They said "operation while on the move", part of Starlink's military service Starshield, had been restored, although it remains unclear whether restrictions on the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining Starlink internet connection have been fully lifted.
Officials were still working to clarify "the reasons and circumstances" behind the move, the sources added.
In a separate development, seven people are missing after a drone attack set a chemical tanker on fire off Romania , according to naval officials. Moscow said it had hit two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port, without naming them.
The Kremlin said Kyiv had "attempted a large-scale attack" on a refinery south of Moscow early on Thursday.
According to Russia's defence ministry, four missiles and dozens of drones were intercepted and the falling debris caused a fire at the site in Ryazan.
Zelensky said dozens of Ukrainian cities had come under Russian attack in the past day.
He previously said he would agree to the "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it.
But he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it had agreed to the deal.
Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support.
European leaders have rallied around the Ukrainian president. Italy's Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told the BBC that the US restricting its intelligence-sharing with Kyiv would be a "complete mistake".
"Because it is a fundamental form of support. This means denying a country any chance of defending itself."
He added: "Peace will be achieved when Putin will be convinced that there is a stalemate... that he cannot advance anymore. But if he sees a weakness on the Ukrainian front, if the United States takes its resources away, then Putin will think he can win, and so he will continue the war."
Zelensky met Nato chief Mark Rutte as a two-day summit of European leaders began in Brussels on Thursday. The head of the military alliance said they had discussed "the importance of implementing an energy ceasefire as well as Nato allies' continuous support for Ukraine".
Zelensky told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence".
Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet links are used throughout its war effort to guide drones and protect its skies.
There were suggestions a technical glitch was to blame for the sudden Starlink restrictions on Tuesday evening, but owner Elon Musk appeared to deny this and suggested it was the Trump administration's doing .
"It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT.
Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing. Starlink's sister service Starshield is provided to Ukraine under a US defence department contract. The BBC has approached the US authorities for comment.
Zelensky spoke to the FT during a visit to London on Wednesday which also included a meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street - who announced the UK would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Kyiv .
The Ukrainian president told the newspaper he would now only halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to cutting off revenue streams to its war machine - if the US supplied more Patriot air defence missiles.
Ukraine has suffered a shortage of the US-made defences since the outbreak of the Iran war consumed stockpiles.
Striking a more defiant tone than recently, the Ukrainian president told the newspaper his American counterpart had an affinity for autocratic leaders like Putin.
He said it was not up to him to mend US-Ukrainian relations given the events of the past week: "We didn't destroy any relationship."
Tensions have previously frayed between the two leaders. After returning to the White House last year, the pair shared a fiery Oval Office meeting in which Trump implied Zelensky was the main block to a peace deal.
Zelensky has since walked a careful diplomatic line, showing willingness towards US-brokered deals while stressing that the terms of any peace deal must be just.
But he criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace , struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort.
That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which has sent fuel costs skyrocketing.
Zelensky told the FT: "The question will be: when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas."
With Russia continuing to strike Ukraine, Zelensky suggested the disruptions to US support was no coincidence.
Local officials report at least 13 people were killed across Ukraine on Wednesday in what Zelensky called a "constant", large-scale Russian attack. He said more than 850 drones had been launched at dozens of cities and communities.
At least three people were killed in the central region of Kirovohrad as it suffered its largest attack since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022, officials there said, with nearly 360 drones launched during a 10-hour barrage. Deaths were also reported in Donetsk, Kherson and Volyn.
"It is clear that Russia deliberately escalated these attacks, taking advantage of the easing of sanctions and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelensky wrote on social media.

Crude makes up a quarter of Brazilian shipments to Chinese buyers, but growth has slowed since Gulf tankers started sailing again
Trade between Brazil and China reached a record US$143 billion in the first nine months of the year, driven by Brazilian oil sales that surged after the war on Iran disrupted Gulf supply, according to a report by the Brazil-China Business Council.
Crude oil accounted for most of the gain, with sales to China jumping 49 per cent to a record US$21.8 billion as shipments rose 27 per cent by volume and prices climbed 16.8 per cent. China took half of all the crude Brazil exported, nearly seven times the share of India, the next-largest buyer.

Eric Deters, the Republican donor who accused Kimberly Guilfoyle of asking him to wire her $100,000 to pay her American Express bill in exchange for her help with the Trump administration ahead of her Senate confirmation hearing, has filed a defamation lawsuit against Guilfoyle and her legal team.
Guilfoyle was pushed out of her ambassadorship to Greece earlier this week, announcing her resignation Tuesday. Guilfoyle's team publicly disputed the authenticity of text messages Deters shared with multiple news outlets, including CBS News.
Deters filed the lawsuit in Kentucky state court on Thursday.
Deters said Guilfoyle's legal team issued a statement to the Wall Street Journal claiming Deters owed Guilfoyle money and did not fulfill his obligations. The Journal published part of her attorney's statement, that Guilfoyle "was owed a balance for traveling to and supporting these patriotic events," which Deters denies.
"Kim Guilfoyle and her lawyers claimed my allegations were false and they would defend the allegations vigorously," Deters wrote in a statement accompanying his lawsuit. "Now they can in Kentucky."
CBS News has reached out to the attorneys named in the lawsuit — Jesse Binnall and David M. Schwartz — for comment.

articles.title_orig: The world is waging a ‘war on nature’ as progress on biodiversity targets lags
articles.title_zh: The world is waging a ‘war on nature’ as progress on biodiversity targets lags
articles.content_orig:
Facebook Twitter Print Email
Fewer than half of the national targets set to protect the world’s plants, animals and ecosystems are on track, the UN warns in a new report, days before countries gather in Yerevan, Armenia, for the COP17 biodiversity conference.
The landmark deal struck in Montreal in 2022 – the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework – set out a vision of “living in harmony with nature” by 2050, with urgent action needed by 2030.
The new report suggests the world is falling behind.
“ Biodiversity underpins life on Earth ,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres wrote in the report. “Safeguarding biological diversity is essential to the health of our planet, the resilience of our economies and the wellbeing of all people .”
One of the deal’s flagship goals was to protect at least 30 per cent of the world’s land, inland waters, coasts and oceans by 2030.
Yet even if current commitments are met, only 26 per cent of land and 12 per cent of the ocean would be protected by that deadline , the report finds.
Progress is also lagging on money, skills, cooperation and data, as well as on economic incentives that reward protecting nature rather than destroying it.
“ This bad news means that the war on nature has not yet ended ,” Mr. Guterres said at the report’s launch in Yerevan.
He warned that the world is still caught in three interlinked crises: climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution.
There has been some progress since 2022, however.
Nearly 90 per cent of countries that are parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity have set national targets, and more than half have drawn up their own plans to deliver them.
More than 70 per cent have measured and reported on their results.
Indigenous Peoples, local communities, regional and city authorities, charities and businesses have also made some 5,000 commitments – though the report warns of a serious gap between ambition and action.
Closing that gap will require money and expertise for developing countries on a far bigger scale, the report says.
Governments need to scrap subsidies that harm nature, strengthen social protection, redirect spending towards protecting nature and work with businesses on strong disclosure rules.
Better coordination is also needed between governments, business, civil society, young people, women and Indigenous Peoples to strengthen accountability, enforcement and cooperation.
“Biodiversity must be part of every decision being made – across policies, regulations and budgets,” Mr. Guterres said.
“Nature won’t thrive on good intentions.”

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul wasted no time in bringing up President Donald Trump as she attacked her Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman in their only debate.
But it took more than 40 minutes for Blakeman to mention the bogeyman who helped him cruise to re-election last year as Nassau County executive: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
Chapin Fay, a spokesperson for Strong and Safe New York, a super PAC backing Blakeman, said it comes down to popularity.
“Mayor Mamdani is one of the most popular politicians on planet Earth. Kathy Hochul, who is notably not, is trying to tie herself to the mayor,” Fay said. “Why would Blakeman do the job for her?”
A Siena University poll released last month found 46% of likely voters around the state viewed Mamdani favorably, compared to 48% for Hochul, 35% for Blakeman and 34% for Trump.
During an hourlong debate hosted by Spectrum News and broadcast around the state, Hochul and Blakeman clashed over data centers, immigration policy and state spending.
The democratic socialist mayor’s name came up fewer than 10 times. Trump, by contrast, was mentioned more than 50 times.
“I did not wrap myself in the shroud of Donald Trump the way you did,” Hochul charged Blakeman at one point.
“No, you wrapped it in Zohran Mamdani,” Blakeman replied.
“Who Donald Trump actually thinks is a great mayor,” Hochul retorted, a reference to multiple positive joint appearances between the president and the mayor.
Blakeman said he didn’t bring up Mamdani earlier because he wasn’t asked about him.
The county executive went on to call Mamdani an antisemite, but complimented him for keeping Jessica Tisch in place as NYPD commissioner. Mamdani, who has been fiercely critical of Israel’s conduct in Gaza, said Blakeman’s attacks were racist. The mayor has appeared with Jewish leaders and repeatedly denounced antisemitic vandalism and other crimes.
Hochul, a moderate, rejected Blakeman’s characterization and called Mamdani “a partner.” She said the two are planning to campaign together.
“I invited him to watch a Buffalo Bills game with me like we did last year,” said Hochul, an Erie County native. “Given that the Bills are looking so good these days, I think he'd enjoy the experience.”

articles.title_orig: HIMA China Innovation Center debuts at German Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai
articles.title_zh: HIMA China Innovation Center debuts at German Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai
articles.content_orig:
The opening of the HIMA China Innovation Center is celebrated by (left to right) Zena Zhou, GM of HIMA China), Daisy Zhu, deputy executive director of the German Chamber of Commerce in China—East China, and Jörg de la Motte, CEO of HIMA Group.
While cohosting Operational Excellence (OpEx) Day with the German Chamber of Commerce in China (GCC) , HIMA Group introduced Sept. 15 its new HIMA China Innovation Center (CIC). The event highlighted HIMA’s localization journey in China and provided deeper insights into functional safety and OT security, while showcasing how its solutions protect people, assets and the environment.
HIMA Group reports it brought its functional safety expertise to the Chinese market in 2002, laying the foundation for partnership with local players. It established its wholly owned subsidiary HIMA (Shanghai) Industrial Automation Co. in 2016, marking a landmark shift from market representation to fully localized operation, technical service and project delivery. This year marks the 10-year anniversary of HIMA China’s operations, reflecting a decade of deep market trust and sustained growth.
To continue HIMA’s commitment to excellence, the new CIC will focus on developing safety applications and digital solutions tailored to the evolving needs of China’s industries, fulfill local requirements, and contribute to HIMA’s global innovation roadmap. The center will operate under a dedicated HIMA China Innovation Board, ensuring strong governance and alignment with the group’s strategic objectives. A streamlined, group-wide innovation process will leverage best practices across the organization, enabling rapid ideation, validation and implementation of projects.
In addition, CIC will serve as a collaborative platform, engaging customers, institutes, technology partners and industry experts to co-create future technological solutions. Key focus areas include digitalization, industrial cybersecurity and intelligent systems that support China’s push toward high-quality manufacturing and operational excellence. Ultimately, it serves to foster a win-win ecosystem through stronger connections and shared industry intelligence.
“Launching the HIMA China Innovation Center is an important next step in HIMA China’s development,” says Jörg de la Motte, CEO of HIMA Group. “We’re combining HIMA's unique expertise with the local innovation capabilities of our team in China to develop solutions that create value for customers in China and beyond.”
HIMA reports the CIC has a structured roadmap for safety applications and digital solutions, paving the way for continued expansion of its safety business in China. Since its inception, this initiative achieved several important milestones. For example, a key achievement was the official launch of HIMA’s HMI local version software, which not only delivers traditional HMI functionalities, but also integrates digital features to support smarter, more efficient operations.
“The China Innovation Center launch is a major milestone for our 24 years journey in China,” adds Zhou Yao (Zena), GM of HIMA China. “This is an open platform that brings together HIMA’s global safety expertise with local customers, institutes, EPCs, OEMs and partners. Our vision is clear—innovation without borders. To deliver it, our core aims are: build a strong local system, solve real safety challenges, develop local talent, and export Chinese innovations globally. In practice, we’re prioritizing digitalization, cybersecurity and intelligent systems, by working closely with local partners, we create solutions that meet China’s needs while also delivering value to industries worldwide.”

articles.title_orig: All Four Artemis II Astronauts Have Now Retired From Spaceflight, Here's What They're Doing Next
articles.title_zh: All Four Artemis II Astronauts Have Now Retired From Spaceflight, Here's What They're Doing Next
articles.content_orig:
Once upon a time — April, in fact — they went to the Moon . Now, they'll never leave home again. As of Tuesday, all four Artemis II astronauts have announced new life plans, and returning to the void of space isn't in any of them. It's a shame that NASA (and its Canadian cousin the CSA) will be losing this level of talent and experience from its active duty astronaut program. At the same time, these four brave humans accomplished an extraordinary achievement in the flight around the Moon, and that's as good a time as any to move on to new things.
Remember that the Orion space capsule, which they lived in for 10 days, is essentially just two small rooms stacked on top of each other . That's a long time to share space with other people, in a place without showers, high-end meals, family, trees, or daylight. Plus, if anything were to go wrong, you'd die in the vacuum of space. No pressure, then (certainly not in the vacuum of space). Would you want to do that twice? Probably not. With that experience behind them, it can't be too surprising that they're ready to hang up the gloves. So, what is an astronaut to do if not floating around in microgravity?
Mission specialist Christina Koch will have the highest profile post-astronaut job, at least currently. Staying at NASA, she is being promoted all the way up to acting deputy chief engineer of the entire agency. She will replace the current holder of that position, Katherine Van Hooser, who is retiring after 35 years at NASA. This is a pretty major role, in which Koch will oversee engineering teams and missions across the agency. Aside from orbiting the Moon and spending 328 consecutive days on the International Space Station, she's also served in the leadership of NASA's Astronaut Office and Johnson Space Center in Houston. She will formally retain "management astronaut status," but this means she is not on the roster for spaceflights.
Mission specialist Jeremy Hansen, the lone Canadian on the Artemis II crew, has retired from the CSA and is no longer an active duty astronaut. Simultaneously with his work with the Canadian Space Agency, he had been a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force; he's now transitioned to reservist status there. His focus remains on pushing forward Canada's space sector, developing his nation's ability to reach and access space without the aid of a partner (say, America). As a reservist, he won't be working full time; this sounds like he might be searching for the right opportunity to become his new day job.
Pilot Victor Glover has gone back to school , but he won't be taking any tests. A graduate of the California Polytechnic State University, he is now an executive advisor to its president. What does that mean exactly? "We're still figuring it out," he said. "It's not going to be nine to five... It'll be where the school needs me the most." That sounds like he might be a bit of a fundraiser and advertiser for the university, which would be a lot more chill than flying around the Moon. In the meantime, NASA has granted him astronaut emeritus status, which means he will still advise and mentor the agency and its astronauts, but will not fly again.
Mission commander Reid Wiseman has also received astronaut emeritus status ... and hasn't announced anything else. Functionally, it sounds like he helps out where he can, but is otherwise semi-retired from NASA. The agency itself says that that gives him "the flexibility to pursue other opportunities." So like Hansen, he is likely biding his time and searching for the right next step, whatever that may be.
In all four cases, it appears that once they got around the dark side of the Moon, each astronaut saw the Earth and decided to never leave it again. They all received the Congressional Space Medal of Honor together , they've all toured the country to applause and acclaim. Now, they're all adjusting to life after the Moon. Enjoy the rest and new roles, astronauts. You deserve them.

articles.title_orig: Yemen's Houthis hit palace in Aden, coalition details attacks on Saudi infrastructure
articles.title_zh: Yemen's Houthis hit palace in Aden, coalition details attacks on Saudi infrastructure
articles.content_orig:
Yemen’s Houthis have hit the vicinity of the al-Maashiq presidential palace in the port city of Aden with multiple missiles.
The Yemeni Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said in a social media post on Thursday that Houthis had targeted the al-Maashiq presidential palace with five missiles.
The government says the prime minister and other officials are safe, but two of his bodyguards were killed in the attack.
Plumes of smoke could be seen rising from the vicinity of the palace.
Al Jazeera correspondents reported earlier on Thursday that there were explosions near the palace.
The palace is considered the headquarters and the seat of power for the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa, said the attacks on the headquarters of the internationally recognised government are the “first of their kind” by the Houthis.
“This is an indication that the escalation is going to intensify between both sides,” Mawry said, adding that fears are now growing inside the country of “an all-out civil war” that could potentially drag in other regional powers besides Saudi Arabia.
The attack in Aden came as fighting between the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), and Saudi-backed forces intensified in Taiz, which is effectively under siege by the Houthis.
Controlling Taiz, Yemen’s third city and the broader Taiz governorate, in the southwest of the country would ensure control over the critical Bab al-Mandeb strait for either side.
Forces allied with the Yemeni government said they are repelling a Houthi attack on Dhubab airport.
The pro-government Homeland Shield Force said in a statement that they are, along with the Southern Giants Brigades, securing the airport in the coastal city of Dhubab in Taiz governorate.
Aid agencies say the escalating violence in Taiz is pushing the healthcare system towards breaking point.
On Sunday, the Ministry of Public Health warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” there.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition says Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport has come under at least 20 Houthi attacks over the past 11 days with dozens of other airports, oil facilities and ports also targeted.
Major-General Turki al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the alliance, released footage showing strikes on the main airport with passengers seen fleeing for safety, during a news conference in the Saudi capital,
The coalition says the Houthi attacks have killed 17 people and injured more than 300.
Al-Maliki also accused the Houthis of obtaining ballistic missiles from other countries in the region.
Mohamad Elmasry, a professor at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, said the Saudi-led coalition’s news conference was intended as a response “to some of the, perhaps, military and security failures”.
“There’s kind of an image problem there because this is maybe affecting the perception of Saudi deterrence, the fact that missiles are getting through,” he told Al Jazeera.
Elmasry said the Houthis also have an image crisis, with the global community viewing their actions as “reprehensible, in particular these targeting civilian infrastructure”.

articles.title_orig: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour
articles.title_zh: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour
articles.content_orig:
International delegates agree leap second no longer tenable, but first leap hour not likely to happen for thousands of years
A fter decades of discussion, quibbling and worrying about clocks in computer systems, the world’s official timekeepers have voted to replace what many viewed as a tiresome correction: the leap second. It’s time, they say, for the leap hour.
Delegates from 69 countries cast their votes on Thursday at a conference in France of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, which ensures the world sticks to the same standards of time, weight, distance and more.
The decision to adopt the leap hour from next year aims to reduce the risk of computers and other technical systems tripping over as their software grapples with minutes lasting 61 seconds – and, worse, 59 seconds – instead of a round 60.
“After 30 years of debate, the leap second is making way for the leap hour,” said Dr Setnam Shemar, principal scientist in the time and frequency department at the UK’s National Physical Laboratory (NPL). “This will reduce the risks to the systems and national infrastructure that depend on accurate time while still preserving the fundamental link between our global time system and the rotation of the Earth.”
The vote at Versailles means that coordinated universal time (UTC) can drift up to an hour from astronomical time before a leap hour is needed, but that is unlikely to happen for thousands of years.
“We already have daylight saving where we change by an hour and no one gets bothered about that, apart from losing sleep or getting an extra hour’s sleep,” said Shemar, who sat on the international timekeeping expert committee that proposed the leap hour.
The more familiar leap year was introduced more than 2,000 years ago to ensure that the calendar year did not fall out of step with the time that the Earth takes to circle the sun. Adding a day to the end of February every four or so years does the job, because Earth orbits the sun every 365 and a quarter days.
Leap seconds are a much more modern invention. In 1955, Louis Essen and Jack Parry at the NPL built the world’s first practical, high-precision caesium atomic clock. The device revolutionised timekeeping, and in 1967 the astronomical definition of a second, based on the rotation of the Earth, was abandoned. Ever since, the formal definition of one second has been 9,192,631,770 vibrations of the caesium atom.
Atomic clocks are exceptionally stable and precise. Their timekeeping has become critical for modern computer systems, communications, satellites, trading systems and electricity grids. But the Earth’s rotation is far less reliable. Its spin is affected by the planet’s molten core, the shift of the oceans, global jet streams and other natural forces.
Broadly, Earth’s rotation is slowing down: when an asteroid doomed the dinosaurs, a day lasted about 23 and a half hours. Because of this, officials have added 27 leap seconds since 1972 to ensure UTC is aligned with astronomical time.
The strategy endured for more than 50 years until scientists spotted a fresh reason to fear technological mayhem. In the past decade, Earth’s rotation has sped up, meaning officials might have needed to add the first negative leap second, equivalent to lopping a second off UTC. The 30% probability of a negative leap second in the next decade brought the Versailles vote forward.
“Leap seconds can be tricky enough to deal with,” said Shemar. Telecommunications, electricity grids and navigation systems used high-accuracy timing, he explained, but software updates could apply leap seconds at the wrong time, knocking networks out of sync.
after newsletter promotion
“After the leap second applied in 2012, there were some computer systems whose operating systems couldn’t cope with 61 seconds in a minute. The servers froze, they seized up. Systems went offline. And those are the sorts of failures that can happen with positive leap seconds,” Shemar said.
Among the crashed websites were Reddit and LinkedIn. Separately, Qantas flights were hit with delays. Negative leap seconds come with even greater risks. “There could be software out there that hasn’t been tested on negative leap seconds because we’ve never had to apply one before,” Shemar said.
To test all the computer systems that talk to one another around the world would cost companies a fortune. It was this concern that swung the vote.
Historically, the UK has grumbled about canning leap seconds because of the link with Greenwich mean time. Russia has also opposed the move, citing concerns of the impact on its Glonass satellite navigation system.
The IERS Earth Orientation Centre, in Paris, tracks changes in the Earth’s rotation and other movements that feed into UTC. The centre also issues notices when leap seconds must be added.
Dr Christian Bizouard, the director of the centre, approved of the vote, but said it passed the decision to people far in the future. “It’s kind of a philosophical discussion, because if a leap hour happens, it won’t be for a very, very long time,” he said. “What we are doing is pushing back the decision.”

articles.title_orig: The world's coral reefs are running out of time
articles.title_zh: The world's coral reefs are running out of time
articles.content_orig:
This summer’s record-breaking wildfires have made the consequences of climate change impossible to ignore. As forests burn, the damage is visible. Smoke, blackened trees and an advancing fireline. But the real test often comes afterwards: can the forest recover, re-establish and provide the services that communities rely upon before the next fire arrives?
The world's coral reefs have faced a similar problem for decades, only largely out of sight.
For years, the fate of coral reefs has been presented as a countdown. Warm the planet enough, the argument goes, and reefs will disappear by 2050. That makes for a compelling warning, but it obscures a more complicated, and more consequential, truth. Coral reefs are not simply dying. They have shown the capacity to recover between disturbances, rebuilding coral cover when conditions allow. The concern is that time for this recovery is being diminished.
That is the central message of the Status of Coral Reefs of the World: 2025 , published on August 31st 2026, by the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN). Over the past four decades coral cover has declined from 30.2% (1980-2009) to 27.3% (2020-2024), a relative decline of around 9.5%, primarily driven by climate change-induced heat stress.
Since 1998, four major global bleaching events have resulted in global losses of coral cover. Bleaching is not a new phenomenon, but climate change has turned episodic shocks into more frequent, severe and recurring pressure. The interval between global bleaching events has fallen from roughly a decade to four to six years, and recovery is therefore becoming a race against time. Yet reefs can still recover. Between 2017 and 2019, after the third global bleaching event, global hard-coral cover increased by 6%, demonstrating the capacity for partial recovery when disturbance pressure is reduced.
Source: González-Rivero, M., Dallison, T., Wicquart, J., Brigdale, A., Logan, M., Fobert, E. K., Staub, F., and Planes, S. (eds.), 2026. Status of Coral Reefs of the World: 2025. Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network and International Coral Reef Initiative. https://doi.org/10.59387/LFPR6347 .
Text in the chart: hard-coral cover (three times)
With wildfires, not every disturbance is the same. Its intensity matters, as does the condition of the ecosystem beforehand. A forest weakened by drought, pests or poor management may fare worse; a reef burdened by pollution, overfishing or coastal development may be less able to withstand a marine heatwave.But this resilience can be strengthened through effective management and the reduction of local pressures to give corals a greater chance of survival and recovery. Effective management cannot stop the ocean from warming, but it can influence how reefs respond.
Regionally, coral-reef trajectories diverge, shaped by distinct pressures and environmental conditions. Four of the ten GCRMN regions exhibited long-term declines, four showed no evidence of net change and two demonstrated increases. This highlights both the urgency of the crisis and the opportunity for policymakers to influence outcomes for coral reefs and the communities that depend upon them.
Source: Status of Coral Reefs of the World: 2025.₹
González-Rivero, M., Dallison, T., Wicquart, J., Brigdale, A., Logan, M., Fobert, E. K., Staub, F., and Planes, S. (eds.), 2026. Status of Coral Reefs of the World: 2025. Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network and International Coral Reef Initiative. https://doi.org/10. 59387/LFPR6347
Policy treats coral reef pressures separately: warming through the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), biodiversity through the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), and fishing and pollution through national governments. But the reef experiences them all simultaneously. The ecological consequences become economic ones: weaker fisheries, declining tourism and less protection for coastal communities.
Reefs safeguard an estimated 5.3m people and $10 9 bn in GDP from storm impacts each decade and between 2000 and 2020 the population within 5km of a reef rose by 46%, underscoring the dependency of communities on the services they provide to humanity. Cutting emissions is essential but insufficient without local management that reduces pressures, and neither works without sustained funding and long-term monitoring.
The next few months will test whether international policy can provide alignment on the necessary actions to safeguard reefs. At the CBD’s COP17 in October, parties will review progress towards the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. The draft Global Report on Collective Progress , highlights significant gaps in baselines against which progress can be assessed including coral cover. The GCRMN helps address persistent gaps in marine-biodiversity monitoring by providing the world's most extensive long-term trends on hard-coral cover and reef condition.
The climate process provides a parallel opportunity. The second Global Stocktake under the Paris Agreement begins in 2026, assessing collective progress towards the agreement's goals and informing the next generation of national climate commitments. With the breaching of the 1.5°C threshold now considered increasingly likely, as stated in UNEP’s Limiting Overshoot Report , the message is straightforward: limiting warming remains essential, but it must be accompanied by action that strengthens resilience to the warming already occurring.
The UNFCCC's Ocean and Climate Change Dialogue is the most direct bridge between these agendas. Long-term reef monitoring can support that effort by providing a common evidence base: showing how reefs are changing, where resilience is improving and where further action is needed.
Source: Status of Coral Reefs of the World: 2025.
González-Rivero, M., Dallison, T., Wicquart, J., Brigdale, A., Logan, M., Fobert, E. K., Staub, F., and Planes, S. (eds.), 2026. Status of Coral Reefs of the World: 2025. Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network and International Coral Reef Initiative. https://doi.org/10. 59387/LFPR6347
The question is no longer whether coral reefs are changing, but whether our policies, investments and conservation efforts can keep pace with the scale and speed of that change. The report provides the knowledge needed to act. Accelerating implementation, scaling finance, strengthening protection and embedding the latest science into decision-making have never been more urgent.
The full report, regional chapters and summary for policymakers are now available on GCRMN .

articles.title_orig: U.S. sues California in fight over checking citizenship of mail voters
articles.title_zh: U.S. sues California in fight over checking citizenship of mail voters
articles.content_orig:
The federal government sued the state of California on Thursday in an escalating battle over how to prevent non-U.S. citizens from voting by mail in federal elections.
The lawsuit is the latest action by the Department of Justice targeting state administration of elections, which President Donald Trump has often criticized as susceptible to fraud and voting by noncitizens.
The civil complaint, which the DOJ had threatened to file, asks a judge to prevent California officials from tabulating mail-in ballots "from likely non-citizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined."
The Department of Justice asks that a judge order the state to set aside mail ballots from voters "identified by the Federal Government likely to be noncitizens," and to verify their citizenship status before their ballot is counted.
Non-citizens are barred from voting in federal elections.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom, in a post on X on Wednesday, said, in anticipation of the suit, "More dangerous nonsense from a President losing his grip on reality."
"Trump is now demanding that California election officials VIOLATE federal law," Newsom wrote. "Apparently, the rule of law only matters when it's convenient for MAGA's dear leader. California's elections are NOT Donald Trump's to control. We will ensure EVERY California voter can participate in a free and fair election.
The suit in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles came two days after acting U.S. Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, in a letter to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, gave the state 48 hours to determine whether any U.S. citizens were on a list of people the DOJ believes are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots for the Nov. 3 election.
The DOJ previously gave officials in Los Angeles County a thumb drive containing the questioned names to officials in Los Angeles County.
McCotter told Weber the state needed to tell local election officials to segregate mail ballots until the citizenship status of their voters could be determined, and not send a ballot to anyone who had not yet received one.
"If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," McCotter said in his letter.
Weber's office, in a statement on Thursday, said, "In July of this year, President Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullen made (still) unsubstantiated claims that California had 190,000 non-citizens on its voter rolls."
"Given the many high-profile examples of states purging US citizens from their voter rolls based on DHS/SAVE data, SOS immediately requested written information about their methodology and data sources to back up their claims," Weber's office said. "They refused and provided California with nothing."
"Now the USDOJ, under threat of 'emergency' litigation, demands that California blindly trust this administration without any evidence or legal authority to justify its request."
Weber, in a statement Thursday, said the DOJ's "relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections."
She also said that California "has robust state law requirements that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that any non-eligible registrants are removed from the State's voter rolls."
"My office and California election officials remain committed – as always – to ensuring a fair and smooth 2026 General Election," Weber said.
Weber's office declined to comment on the lawsuit Thursday, but pointed to a letter she had sent McCotter in response to his letter.
Weber, in her letter, said, "California's election administration will continue to be governed by applicable federal and state law, not by unsubstantiated claims and outrageous demands."
She said that "despite failing to send the list of alleged non-citizens to my office, you demand that we request transmittal of the list, review and confirm the citizenship status of each of the approximately 20,000 individuals on the list on the eve of an election and within a mere 48 hours."
"This is an emergency of the DOJ's creation," Weber said.
