articles.title_orig: Experts have voted to stop adding extra seconds to clock time – the outcome favours big tech
articles.title_zh: Experts have voted to stop adding extra seconds to clock time – the outcome favours big tech
articles.content_orig:
On June 30 2015 at 23:59:59 UTC (19:59:59 EDT), artist Sara Morawetz was standing in the middle of New York’s Times Square with a pair of cymbals. As the clock ticked to the next second, she struck the cymbals together.
This simple performance, titled 61/60, sought to highlight the strange blip of time where the clock read 23:59:60 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), instead of 00:00:00 UTC.
Since 1972, extra seconds, known as leap seconds, have been added to clock time whenever our slightly wobbly Earth falls out of sync with atomic clocks (which run more consistently). A total of 27 leap seconds have been added in those five decades.
They are therefore important in fields like astronomy because they keep the link between clock time and solar time – which is based on our planet’s movement.
But on Thursday 15 October, delegates at the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) in Versailles, France, voted to abolish them , starting from 2027.
Their loss might seem trivial to some people. But in the field of precision timekeeping, leap seconds are highly controversial. They have the potential to affect everything from financial trading, telecommunications and the energy sector to data centres and the legal system.
In fact, they have threatened to interrupt any sector that requires accurate timing. For example, data centres use time synchronisation to ensure distributed servers work together effectively. In finance, time stamps ensure orders are carried out accurately and provide an audit trail for complying with regulations.
When a leap second was added in 2012, it caused websites such as Reddit and Linkedin to crash and Qantas airline flights to be delayed.
In the reporting on today’s decision, these risks to computing systems are often described as the main reason for the end of leap seconds, but in fact the risk was to the single globally accepted standard of time.
In 2008, when a leap second was due to be added to the clock on December 31, Google was unwilling to risk adding it in a single step . Instead, the tech giant’s time servers deviated from UTC for a period of 20 hours, “smearing” the extra second across this time period in increments that were so small their systems did not notice them.
Effectively, Google determined that UTC was not suitable for its needs and invented its own form of clock time in response. Increasingly, other corporations adopted their own workarounds, raising concerns about the ability of UTC to retain its position as the pre-eminent determination of time.
As a result, conversations within the international bodies responsible for standardisation have, in recent years, focused on the ways that the current model of clock time no longer works as a standard for all.
As Mario Maniewicz, director of the International Telecommunications Union (ITU-R), has argued, clock time needs to be updated so that it can meet the needs of 21st century users .
At the 2022 CGPM, it had already been agreed by delegates that, by 2035, UTC would effectively be free of leap seconds . However, recent predictions of future changes in Earth’s rotation raised the possibility of the first negative leap second, where a second is subtracted rather than added to the clock.
Alarm over the unprecedented impact this situation could have led to it being likened to a new Y2K event. The increased risk of losing users of UTC to forms of timekeeping that do not require leap second adjustments led to the proposal agreed at Versailles, namely to bring forward the end of leap seconds to May 20 2027.
UTC has thus been redefined so that it can be reasserted as a shared standard, free of the controversy it once held for many economic activities .
As I’ve argued previously , the leap second debate has shown that our usual ideas of clocks as abstract, mathematical and objective are incorrect. These ideas do not take into account the way that clocks are designed tools that are reformulated when needs shift.
Global computing and tech companies now have the time they need for their systems to work more smoothly. But astronomers will no longer be able to use UTC as a broad proxy for the Earth’s rotation as they did before. The proposal brought before the CGPM mentions this, but more or less says they will need to look elsewhere for their requirements.
The implication of the decision seems to be that computing needs have been placed above the requirements of other sectors. But the larger question raised by today’s decision at the CGPM is one the broader public has rarely asked, namely what other “user needs” are going unmet by the assumption that all human activities can be coordinated by a single standardised clock time? Astronomy provides one example of this, but our own experiences of pressure and anxiety around time suggest there are others.
There is a strange kind of audacity in even considering the idea of changing clock time to suit our own needs. Google was able to do it in part because it is big enough to do so .
But think about the common habit of running our clocks slightly fast to help with getting to meetings on time. This is done so often that Apple had to introduce an official feature to its smart watch allowing people to set it to the wrong time on purpose.
Public clocks do this occasionally too, such as the turret clock on the Balmoral Hotel in Edinburgh. Since 1902, the clock has run three minutes fast to help travellers arrive on time at the nearby Waverley train station. There are also clocks that let you track time outside of the UTC standard that was redefined today.
Designer Scott Thrift has built a clock called The Present which features a single hand that moves with the changing seasons across a full year. Thrift described The Present as “no hours, no minutes, no numbers. Only the bigger picture”. US scientists working on Mars missions created their own watches to track Martian days (called sols) which run longer than Earth days.
Many people may think of clock time as immovable and inevitable. As the latest vote shows, the “shape” of the clock remains up for debate. Currently, if you are big enough it will bend to your needs. We need to decide if we are happy to just leave the big players to it.

articles.title_orig: In an AI World, Cybersecurity Requires Human Judgment
articles.title_zh: In an AI World, Cybersecurity Requires Human Judgment
articles.content_orig:
When a cyberattack disrupts a hospital, compromises a small business, or exposes a family’s financial information, the damage extends well beyond technology. It interrupts care, threatens livelihoods, and undermines trust. For Miami, a community whose economy depends on connections across industries and borders, preparing people to protect our digital systems is an essential investment in our future.
Artificial intelligence adds urgency to that responsibility. It can help cybersecurity professionals analyze information and identify threats. It can also help criminals craft convincing deceptions and exploit vulnerabilities.
As these capabilities advance, we must think carefully about what it means to prepare someone to defend an organization. Familiarity with the latest tools is only the beginning. Professionals need the knowledge to understand what those tools reveal, the skills to investigate what they miss, and the judgment to decide what happens next.
That should shape how we educate the cybersecurity workforce.
An AI system may flag unusual activity, but someone must determine whether it signals an attack. An automated response may contain a threat, but someone must consider whether shutting down a system will interrupt an essential service. A convincing result may still be wrong. Professionals must know how to question it, verify the evidence, and take responsibility for a decision.
The more capable our technology becomes, the more consequential those human responsibilities become.
At Miami Dade College, our national leadership in cybersecurity education rests on connecting academic knowledge with applied skills. The National Security Agency has designated MDC a National Center of Academic Excellence in Cyber Defense. Validated by the National Security Agency (NSA), MDC became the first college in Florida with both associate and bachelor’s degree programs in cybersecurity.
That recognition establishes a rigorous foundation. Our responsibility is to build on it as technology changes, preparing graduates who can understand complex systems, evaluate risk, and respond effectively under pressure.
Students need to know how networks operate, how information moves, and how vulnerabilities arise. Without that foundation, they may learn to operate a tool without understanding its findings. Strong academic preparation gives them the ability to investigate an unfamiliar problem and adapt when the tools change.
They also need opportunities to put their knowledge to work. At MDC’s Cybersecurity Center of the Americas, students use our Cyber Range to detect, investigate, and respond to realistic attacks in a simulated environment. They practice interpreting evidence, weighing options, and coordinating a response.
These experiences bring another essential set of capabilities into focus: communication, teamwork, critical thinking and ethical judgment. Cybersecurity professionals must explain risks to people with different responsibilities and levels of technical understanding. They must help leaders make informed decisions and work across an organization when time matters.
AI fluency belongs within this broader preparation. Students should understand how to use AI, assess its limitations, and protect sensitive information. They should be able to explain why they trust a finding and recognize when further investigation is necessary. MDC’s leadership in applied AI education strengthens our capacity to connect these capabilities with cybersecurity instruction.
This approach has implications beyond any one college.
Educators must assess whether students can apply knowledge in unfamiliar situations, justify their decisions, and communicate the consequences. Employers must help create those learning opportunities through internships, realistic training scenarios, and sustained engagement with faculty. Hiring practices should give candidates meaningful opportunities to demonstrate what they know and can do.
We must also make these pathways accessible. Working adults, veterans, and first-generation college students bring experience and perspectives that our cybersecurity workforce needs. Certificates, associate degrees, and bachelor’s degrees provide multiple entry points, allowing learners to develop skills and continue their education as their careers advance.
For Miami, developing that local talent connects economic opportunity with community resilience. It prepares residents for careers that help protect the businesses, institutions, and essential services around them.
Cybersecurity Awareness Month should prompt us to consider the people behind our digital defenses. Investing in their education requires a lasting commitment to knowledge, practical skills, and sound judgment.
As a National Center of Academic Excellence in Cyber Defense, Miami Dade College is helping lead that work. Our obligation is to prepare professionals who can use increasingly powerful technology with the understanding and responsibility that protecting a community demands.

articles.title_orig: Wholesale inflation jumped last month by most in four years as gas prices soared - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Wholesale inflation jumped last month by most in four years as gas prices soared - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Wholesale inflation rose more quickly than expected last month on a big jump in fuel costs, a sign that stubbornly rising prices remain an economic challenge for consumers and a political problem for Republicans in the midterm elections
WASHINGTON -- Wholesale inflation rose more than expected last month on a big jump in fuel costs as rising prices become a bigger economic challenge for millions of Americans, and a growing political problem for Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections.
The Labor Department’s producer price index — which captures inflation before it reaches consumers — soared 6.3% in September from a year ago, up from 5.6% in August and the biggest increase since December 2022, the government said Thursday.
On a monthly basis, wholesale prices rose 1.3% from August to September, marking the largest increase since March 2022, after a 0.5% gain the previous month.
Thursday’s data amplify the better-known consumer price index, released Wednesday, which also accelerated in September as gas prices jumped. A broad range of goods and services also got more expensive. Both inflation reports raise pressure on the inflation-fighters at the Federal Reserve to hike their key interest rate. Inflation has now topped the central bank’s 2% target for five and a half years.
Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 0.7% from August to September, up sharply from 0.2% in the previous month. Compared with a year ago, core prices rose 5%, up from 4.6% in August.
More expensive energy drove most of the increase as wholesale gas prices soared more than 20% from August to September. But the report also showed other costs rising, including those for electricity, vegetables, shipping, and air fares.
Ongoing inflation has eroded Americans' incomes and soured most consumers on the economy. The Labor Department said Wednesday that average weekly paychecks, when adjusted for inflation, shrank last month compared with a year ago for the first time since May.
Higher prices have also taken a toll on Trump’s standing with U.S. voters. A poll released this month by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of U.S. adults approve of Trump's handling of the cost of living. And only 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, a new low.
The Federal Reserve, meanwhile, will hold a policy meeting in two weeks and are expected to keep its key short-term interest rate unchanged. But officials had already penciled in another rate hike later this year, which economists mostly expect to occur in December.
The Fed raises borrowing costs in an attempt to slow borrowing and spending and bring down inflation.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft says Windows 11 is now ‘more responsive’ and runs better on 8GB of RAM
articles.title_zh: Microsoft says Windows 11 is now ‘more responsive’ and runs better on 8GB of RAM
articles.content_orig:
A lot of the speed improvements are thanks to smarter ways to manage memory and PC resources.
A lot of the speed improvements are thanks to smarter ways to manage memory and PC resources.
Earlier this year Microsoft laid out a plan to fix Windows 11 , with a focus on performance, reliability, and the overall OS experience. After months of fixes, Microsoft now says the “result is a Windows experience that’s up to 20 percent more responsive.”
Microsoft has made improvements to Start, File Explorer, Search, Edge, and other parts of Windows 11 to make it feel faster and more responsive. “A big part of that work is making smarter use of memory and system resources,” says Navjot Virk , corporate vice president of Windows experiences at Microsoft. “We’ve improved memory management and efficiency across Windows to help keep more of your PC’s resources focused on what you’re actively doing.”
The improvements to memory management now make a “meaningful difference” on PCs with just 8GB of RAM. “Windows can now keep up to 2GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage,” says Virk. “For example, on PCs with 8GB of memory or less, Widgets load only when you open them, making more than 200 MB of memory available for your apps and other work.”
Microsoft has also made Windows Update less disruptive , cleaned up the Widgets section, and finally allowed the taskbar to be repositioned to the sides or top of a display. Windows Hello sign-in has also been sped up, and Bluetooth pairing is more reliable, “including an AirPods pairing experience that’s up to 15 seconds faster.”
The next big step is a new Windows Search experience that’s a lot faster and more capable. I got to try it out last week and I think it’s one of the best new additions to Windows 11 this year . It’s currently available for Windows Insiders, and Microsoft says it will “roll out more broadly later this year.”

articles.title_orig: Commentary: John Gunther’s ‘Giant World of Texas’
articles.title_zh: Commentary: John Gunther’s ‘Giant World of Texas’
articles.content_orig:
Texas got a great deal of attention in his “Inside U.S.A,” even though his famous quote about the Lone Star State came from someone else.
By W.F. Strong October 15, 2026 8:00 am Arts & Culture , History , Stories From Texas , Texas Standard Original
Bill Dickinson / Flickr (CC BY-NC 2.0)
John Gunther is probably world famous for being quoted as saying, “If a man’s from Texas, he’ll tell you. If he’s not, no use embarrassing him by asking.”
Gunther is often depicted as a grizzled oil man, smoking a cigar as he doles out timeless advice to his son. But Gunther was neither a Texan nor the one who said this.
He was a journalist and author who heard the anecdote “near San Antonio” around 1947. He published it in his bestselling book, “Inside U.S.A . ” Gunther wrote it this way: “A child asks a stranger where he is from, whereupon the father rebukes him gently, ‘Never do that, son. If a man’s from Texas …'”  you know the rest.
Gunther published a whole series of “Inside” books over many years as a journalist and travel writer: “Inside Europe,” “Inside Asia,” “Inside Africa,” “Inside Australia.” But his bestselling of the series was “Inside USA,” and within that book, Texas got a great deal of attention. Harper’s Magazine even published his Texas insights and observations as a stand-alone article titled “The Giant World of Texas.”
» MORE: Three tales of Texas pride
It has been about 80 years since Gunther wrote that book. Texas had a population of 7 million then, less than 1/4 of what our population is today. Nonetheless, the cultural themes he observed then have not lost their resilience in modern Texas.
Here are few things Gunther observed:
Texas is the only state that, without consent of Congress, may split itself into five different states anytime. An old joke says that it would have performed this fission long ago, except that nobody could decide which of the new Texas states would get the Alamo … [But] nobody … would ever dream of it. Because then Texas would no longer be Texas.  …  Its most preciously guarded attribute is its bigness.
Gunther made the point that Texas is not Southern or Southwestern, nor does it belong to the West. He wrote: “It is an Empire, an entity totally its own. Also, it is beginning to seep over the edges;  Oklahoma, Arizona, New Mexico, even California, feel its mighty impact.”
Gunther says that given this influence,  it’s tempting to talk about Texas as an imperialist power.
When World War II came along, Texas was far from isolationist.
So many Texans went to Canada to enlist before Pearl Harbor that Montreal talked of “the Royal Canadian Texas Air Force.” Sam Rayburn told me (It’s just a joke, don’t mind), “Of course, the real reason Congress passed selective service was to get someone in the service [who was] not a Texan.”
In fact, so many Texans were in the Pacific Theater during World War II that Texas military men joked that they would accept Japan’s U.S. surrender. They would not require a separate one for Texas.
Gunther writes that Texas in the 1940s struggled to make the cultural compromises it needed to achieve the progress it aimed for. One such aim was to create one of the finest, top-ranked universities in the world.
Texas wanted, and wants, the greatest and richest university in the world.  Yet it did not quite grasp the point that no university can be worthy of the name without being anchored on something that many conservative Texans feared, academic freedom.
There’s plenty of Texas humor in Gunther’s expose. He told of a daughter of a “great Texas rancher [who] arrived at an eastern finishing school and was asked where she was from.”
“Nueces County, Texas” she replied.
“And where might that be?”
“It’s the northwest corner of my grandpappy’s cow pasture.”
Texans are exceptionally proud to be Texans. They are so proud of Texas, Gunther concluded, that “they cannot sleep at night.”
There were plenty of tall tales to be collected in Texas. A West Texan was asked if they ever had cyclones or tornadoes out there. The Texan said, “We did have one once, but it ran into a sandstorm about three miles out of town and got ripped to pieces.”
As Gunther traveled the state and told Texans that he was writing a book on the United States, many suggested that there should be two books, “one on Texas, the other on the other forty-seven.”

articles.title_orig: Scientists vote to end leap seconds, redefining how the world keeps time
articles.title_zh: Scientists vote to end leap seconds, redefining how the world keeps time
articles.content_orig:
Scientists just voted to redefine how the world keeps time
A new system, called the “leap hour,” will allow Earth’s rotation and official time to fall out of alignment by a full hour
By Emma Gometz edited by Clara Moskowitz
blckpichstudio/Shutterstock
Join Our Community of Science Lovers!
Today an international group of scientists, diplomats and timekeepers voted to end the leap second, which has been keeping Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) aligned with the time according to Earth’s rotation (UT1) within one second of difference. The length of a day according to UTC is close to that of UT1 but not exactly the same because our planet’s rotation is irregular. We add a leap second every few years to keep them from drifting too far apart.
But soon the leap second will be replaced with a leap hour, added much more infrequently, which will extend the allowed difference between UT1 and UTC to an hour, or 3,600 seconds.
“After 30 years of debates, we are ready,” said Noël Dimarcq, a senior scientist at the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS) and president of International Bureau of Weights and Measures’ (BIPM’s) Consultative Committee for Time and Frequency, just before the vote, which took place at the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) in Versailles, France.
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
UTC is the world’s standard timescale. It’s the reference for how computers, phones, boats, planes, satellites and everything else tell time and for how navigation systems such as GPS function . It’s calculated via a weighted average of the time according to atomic clocks around the world and disseminated by the BIPM.
Shortly after UTC was first established in 1960, scientists noticed Earth’s rotation was ever so slightly slowing down, so it was not keeping pace with the count of the seconds according to atomic clocks. At the behest of astronomers and other experts, the first leap second was added to UTC in 1972 to realign the time standard with Earth’s rotation. Since 1972, 27 leap seconds have been added.
In the mid-2010s, however, Earth’s spin began speeding up. Scientists predicted that a negative leap second would be necessary soon, perhaps as early as 2029 . Engineers say a negative leap second would be like a “mini Y2K” event because it would suddenly send the entire world one second backward in time, which could cause chaos in our digital infrastructure.
“Avoiding negative leap seconds is a very big driver to open the window” between UTC and UT1, says Nick Stamatakos, head of the Earth Orientation Department at the U.S. Naval Observatory, which manages the country’s GPS grid.
Since 2022 scientists, government officials, telecommunications professionals and others have been urgently trying to find a practical way to solve the leap second problem.
The BIPM, which is the official source of UTC, hosts CGPM every four years to discuss issues with member states. This morning officials at this year’s conference held the vote to end the leap second and make UTC continuous, with the change taking effect on May 20 (World Metrology Day), 2027. The resolution won by a majority vote.
Instead of using leap seconds, everyone has agreed that they will tolerate more drift between UTC and UT1 than they had in the past. And when things get really bad, we’ll add a leap hour instead. Although leap seconds have historically been added every few years, scientists predict that a leap hour won’t be needed for more than 1,000 years—effectively ending the BIPM’s procedure to link UTC with Earth’s position in the sky.
The change won’t be noticed by most of us, and switching to continuous time will be easier for our digital infrastructure—there will be much less risk of bugs or service outages arising from a leap second discontinuity. But the shift means that human civilization will even further diverge from our oldest way of telling time: by looking to the sky.
Great science journalism requires human expertise, time, effort and creativity. And it costs money. That’s why I and the journalists here at Scientific American hope you’ll join our community.

Our editors and reporters are often experts in their fields, which means they understand the nuances of big discoveries and can untangle the breakthroughs from the hype. With a subscription, you are also supporting rigorous fact-checking to ensure the words we publish are precise and accurate. And you’re supporting original illustrations, graphics and photos that bring you closer to an advanced laboratory, an ice sheet in Antarctica or a space mission in orbit. You’re helping us craft other types of high-quality journalism as well: Our newsletters are carefully written, edited and curated by staffers you have or will come to know and love. Our Science Quickly podcast is based on original reporting, collaboration with editors and scientists and exacting production.

articles.title_orig: Amazon’s Bee launches two new personal AI devices, starting at $75
articles.title_zh: Amazon’s Bee launches two new personal AI devices, starting at $75
articles.content_orig:
Last day at Disrupt IS 75% off. Don’t miss any more moments. REGISTER NOW
Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.
Amazon’s personal AI wearable maker, Bee , is announcing its first new products since being acquired by the retail giant last year . The tech company on Thursday introduced the Bee Frontier, the next generation of its device that can be worn on the wrist or pinned to clothes, along with Bee Eclipse, a credit-card-sized device that magnetically attaches to the back of your smartphone.
The latter puts Bee into more direct competition with AI devices like the Plaud Note or Pocket, but at a lower price point — the Bee Frontier is $74.99, compared with $159 for the Plaud Note (or $189 for the Note Pro), or $129 for the Pocket AI device .
The Bee Frontier will come in Onyx, Lavender, and Sage, while the $99.99 Bee Eclipse will be offered in Silver, Midnight, Honey, and Blush.
Like the original Bee, the idea with the new devices is to leverage AI to take notes from your everyday conversations, allowing you to remember the important things that were said, and then turn those into actionable to-dos, summaries, and insights.
For instance, if you discussed making plans with friends, the Bee would remember the date and time you agreed on, then create a calendar invite. You could also use the Bee to take lecture notes in class, or to jot down the care plan you discussed with a doctor, among other things.
All Bee devices can create conversation summaries and recaps for free, and offer 14 days of memory. With an $11.99 per month Bee Pro subscription, users receive unlimited conversation summaries and integrations with Amazon.com, Alexa+, and third-party applications. Pro users also get suggested to-dos, daily memories, a personal chat assistant, and conversation templates.
To make all this possible, Bee devices use a private computing security architecture, which doesn’t store the raw audio from your conversations. Instead, audio is processed in real time and then deleted. Transcripts of the conversation are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls, which means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you manually and intentionally share them.
In addition, you can opt to connect the Bee to Alexa, allowing your Echo device to use its ability to identify your voice, a feature called Voice ID, to recognize when you’re speaking. It can then record your conversations to provide Bee’s insights. (This aspect of Bee is optional, and Amazon notes you can delete transcripts and summaries at any time.)
With its new connections to Amazon.com and Alexa, Bee users can make purchases from Amazon or ask Alexa for their Bee insights, summaries, or to-dos hands-free.
Bee also works with your existing productivity software, like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Microsoft Outlook, so it can draft emails, set up meetings, surface action items, and more.
Plus, you can upload photos to Bee or connect it with Apple’s HealthKit to add a picture of your overall wellness to be integrated into your provided insights.
The Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse both have just one button that turns the device off and on, and include an indicator light when it’s summarizing a conversation. The Frontier also offers IP67 water resistance, up to seven days of battery life, USB-C charging, and dual microphones with advanced noise filtering.
All Bee devices come with a companion mobile app, which has also been newly redesigned, plus a new desktop app.
The Bee Frontier is available now on Amazon, and the Eclipse will be available soon thereafter.

From the latest big breakthrough to the most influential and inspiring figures on campus to Pitt in the community, Pittwire is your official source for what’s happening now.
The University of Pittsburgh placed among the world’s top 50 in 17 academic fields in the 2025-2026 University Ranking by Academic Performance World University Rankings by Field .
Surgery stood near the top at No. 4 globally and No. 3 in the U.S. Geriatrics and gerontology followed at No. 7 globally and No. 3 nationally. Pitt also placed No. 3 nationally in human movement and sports science, which saw a No. 19 global rank.
Pitt saw high rankings in several other health and clinical fields: infectious diseases (No. 14), pediatrics (No. 15), ophthalmology (No. 16), immunology (No. 22), medical and health sciences (No. 22), psychology and cognitive sciences (No. 23), neuroscience (No. 24), clinical neurology (No. 26), nursing (No. 28), oncology (No. 30) and dentistry (No. 44). Also cracking the top 50 were psychology (No. 25), philosophy (No. 43) and women’s studies (No. 46).
Pitt was ranked in 54 of 78 fields, placing among the top 100 in 26 categories. In URAP’s ranking of about 3,000 global institutions, Pitt placed No. 70 overall, No. 18 nationally and No. 8 among U.S. public universities.
The rankings come from the Informatics Institute at Middle East Technical University in Ankara, Turkey, which has published field-level results since 2012. The methodology relies entirely on bibliometric data, weighing article output, total documents, citations, article and citation impact, and international collaboration. The ranking does not survey reputation or assess teaching.

articles.title_orig: A fungus is threatening the world’s food supply. Scientists just found a new defense
articles.title_zh: A fungus is threatening the world’s food supply. Scientists just found a new defense
articles.content_orig:
Scientists have uncovered a promising new way to protect some of the world's most important food crops from a destructive fungus that threatens global food security. By engineering the natural immune defenses of plants, researchers have developed an experimental approach that could eventually help wheat, rice, and barley resist fungal infections more effectively.
The international research team, led by scientists at the John Innes Centre in the United Kingdom, investigated a recently discovered group of plant immune receptors. They identified how these proteins recognize invading pathogens and demonstrated that they can be modified to detect multiple fungal threats. The findings could open the door to crops with stronger, more durable disease resistance.
"We've discovered something that could lead to a potential intervention on what is the worst fungal disease of cereals," said Professor Mark Banfield, a research group leader at the John Innes Centre and an author of the study, which involved collaborators at Kobe University in Japan.
A Devastating Fungus Threatens the Global Food Supply
The target of the research is Magnaporthe oryzae , the fungus responsible for blast disease. It causes the most serious fungal disease affecting cultivated rice and has also become a major threat to wheat and barley in parts of Asia and Africa.
The damage is enormous. Each year, rice blast destroys enough rice to feed approximately 60 million people. As the fungus spreads into additional agricultural regions, developing effective ways to protect crops has become increasingly important for global food security.
The fungus infects plants through a sophisticated biological strategy. It delivers specialized molecules known as effectors into cells in the leaves and stems. These molecules interfere with normal plant functions, allowing the pathogen to establish an infection and promote disease.
Plants, however, have evolved their own defense systems. Specialized immune receptors can recognize these foreign molecules and trigger a protective response. One important mechanism involves causing infected cells to die in a controlled, localized area, helping prevent the pathogen from spreading farther through the plant.
Scientists Discover a Hidden Plant Immune Defense
For more than three decades, much of the research into plant immunity has centered on proteins called Nucleotide-binding and leucine-rich receptors (NLRs). These receptors have played a central role in understanding how crops recognize and defend themselves against blast disease and other infections.
More recently, scientists have begun investigating another group of immune proteins found in cereal crops, known as tandem kinase proteins (TKPs). Although researchers are still learning how these receptors operate, they appear to offer additional opportunities for strengthening plant defenses.
Earlier studies revealed that some TKPs contain a specialized region called a Heavy Metal Associated (HMA) domain. Similar regions are also found in certain NLR receptors, where they help recognize pathogen effectors and initiate immune responses.
This shared feature attracted the attention of Banfield and his colleagues because it suggested that scientists might be able to redesign the receptors to recognize additional fungal threats.
"This piqued our interest," said Professor Banfield. "If we can engineer these integrated HMA domains for new properties by making amino acid protein changes where effectors bind, we can gain what we call novel recognition specificities - and potentially a new frontline for defense of plants against disease."
Turning Fungal Attack Molecules Into Targets
In the study, published in Science Advances , researchers examined precisely how HMA domains interact with the molecules released by the blast fungus.
Using biophysical techniques and crystallography, a method that allows scientists to determine the detailed three-dimensional structure of molecules, the team obtained a high-resolution view of how these plant receptors bind to fungal effectors.
The results revealed that HMA domains can function as biological bait. By binding to molecules the fungus uses during infection, these regions help plants recognize the presence of an invading pathogen and activate their defenses.
Armed with this structural information, the researchers modified TKP immune receptors so they could recognize two different fungal effectors associated with infections in wheat and barley.
This ability to detect multiple targets, known as dual specificity, is unusual in naturally occurring immune receptors. Demonstrating that it can be introduced through protein engineering suggests a promising way to expand the range of threats that crop immune systems can recognize.
The findings also provide a foundation for investigating other recently identified TKPs in different cereal crops. Scientists may eventually be able to design customized immune receptors that detect several fungal effectors simultaneously, potentially making plants more difficult for pathogens to infect.
Engineering Crops With Stronger Disease Resistance
Although the findings are encouraging, the technology remains at an early experimental stage.
The researchers conducted their initial tests using protoplasts, individual wheat cells that serve as a simplified model for studying how plant tissues respond. The next step is to determine whether the engineered receptors can provide effective protection in whole plants grown under controlled greenhouse conditions.
"Our study indicates that this new class of resistance proteins is amenable for engineering purposes. We now know that the previous tools we used in engineering NLR receptors may also work with this new class," said Dr. Daniel Yu, the first author of the study.
Understanding exactly how fungal effectors attach to plant immune receptors could also help researchers take advantage of other technologies. Precision breeding and artificial intelligence may provide additional ways to redesign HMA domains, allowing them to recognize pathogen molecules that previously escaped detection.
One particularly promising possibility involves combining different types of immune receptors within the same crop.
Because NLRs and TKPs appear to activate plant defenses through different mechanisms, using them together could create several layers of protection. This might make it harder for fungi to evolve ways around a plant's immune system.
"We think these two classes of immune receptors, NLRs and TKPs, are probably activated in different ways," said Professor Banfield. "That gives the potential for more robust immunity in the field because you are not putting all your eggs in one basket. Further down the road, we may be able to use techniques to stack genes encoding TKPs and NLRs together against the same disease, making a super-resistant crop. They will have different ways of activating immunity, so it is likely to be more difficult for a pathogen to evolve away from," he added.
A Growing Threat to Wheat, Rice, and Barley
The need for better protection is becoming more urgent as blast disease continues to threaten major food crops.
Wheat blast was first identified in Brazil during the 1980s and has since spread to parts of Asia and Africa. Although the disease has not been detected in the United Kingdom, climate change could eventually create conditions that allow it to threaten cereal production in northern Europe.
For farmers, the emergence of blast disease in new regions presents a serious challenge, particularly because the fungus can threaten crops that are essential to feeding large populations.
By revealing how a previously underexplored class of plant immune receptors can be engineered to recognize multiple fungal threats, the researchers have identified a possible new strategy for protecting future harvests.

articles.title_orig: AI giant Anthropic woos potential investors ahead of stock market debut
articles.title_zh: AI giant Anthropic woos potential investors ahead of stock market debut
articles.content_orig:
Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic has been drumming up support for its expected stock market listing as it seeks to reassure investors of its profit-making potential.
Anthropic revenue surged by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.7bn) in the three months to the end of September, the BBC understands.
In common with other AI firms, it is seeking to position itself as being able to generate huge profits despite spending billions on tech.
It also emphasised safety at its event after warnings by current and former researchers of serious and even existential risks to humanity posed by AI.
Anthropic's revenue has risen in successive quarters this year, from $4.7bn in the first three months to $11.6bn the following period.
The company also told investors during the event at its headquarters in San Francisco that it had made a third quarter profit on an adjusted basis, an accounting method which ignores non-recurring costs.
Investors reportedly left the Anthropic investor event optimistic about the company's rapid revenue growth and path to profitability.
Alongside concerns about profit generation, there have also been fears about the safety of AI models.
Anthropic has been vocal about AI's risks, with its chief executive Dario Amodei calling on the pace of development to slow down .
In September one of its researchers warned of a greater than 10% chance that AI could "kill all humans" within the next decade , and a former researcher said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity .
The firm itself said in September it had identified and disrupted attempts to use its AI model for "malicious activity" which could support the development of biological weapons .
However, US President Donald Trump has said researchers have been " bringing up things that won't happen " and that in a race between the US and China to develop the technology, "whoever wins AI, wins".
Rival tech firm OpenAI has also warned about safety, with its chief executive Sam Altman saying in September that his company will not go public this year as it addresses concerns.
The ChatGPT-developer is also eyeing a bumper stock market listing, which is expected to value the firm at more than $1tn.
Anthropic's revenue figures, along with those of rival OpenAI, are an important gauge of the AI industry's growth and ability to finance the infrastructure needed to develop the technology.
Stocks in some US technology companies dropped on Wednesday over concerns around investments in AI.
Shares in chip makers - including AMD, Nvidia and Intel - fell sharply.
In Asia, shares in Japanese tech investment firm Softbank were down by more than 9% on Thursday. South Korean semiconductor giants also dropped, with Samsung falling by 9.5% and SK Hynix 11% lower.
Shares have been falling this week after remarks by Hock Tan, the chief executive of US tech manufacturer Broadcom, over AI spending.
Tan said at a conference in Singapore on Monday that many investors have "no clue" and have set "extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino".
The falls deepened after US inflation data released on Wednesday showed price rises accelerated by more than expected in September.
Investors are concerned that higher inflation will mean the US Federal Reserve is more likely to put up the cost of borrowing.

articles.title_orig: DOJ gave California a voter list, a 48-hour deadline — and a threat of court action
articles.title_zh: DOJ gave California a voter list, a 48-hour deadline — and a threat of court action
articles.content_orig:
Washington — The Justice Department sued California on Thursday, alleging that the federal government has identified more than 20,000 noncitizens who are unlawfully registered to vote.
The lawsuit , filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, came after Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter sent letters to counties earlier this week, including Los Angeles, ordering them to review a list of names of suspected noncitizens who he alleged received mail-in ballots for the upcoming midterm elections.
"State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement announcing the lawsuit.
"If found responsible in a court of law, the State of California will have seriously undermined confidence in our electoral system and violated laws that protect our nation's representative system of government."
In the letter that McCotter sent to the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk, he enclosed a password-protected thumb drive that he said contained names compiled by the Department of Homeland Security, and imposed a 48-hour deadline for the clerk's office to review the list.
Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder and clerk, said in a statement responding to McCotter's demands that the county would not be reviewing the materials on the thumb drive because doing so would conflict with "established data privacy and information security protocols." He said the device was not considered a "secure medium."
Secretary of State Shirley Weber, meanwhile, said the Justice Department had not provided the list of names and blasted the Trump administration for what it said were "unsubstantiated claims" that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls.
In Thursday's lawsuit, the Justice Department accused the state of failing to work with the federal government to correct the alleged problems with its voter rolls.
"The Federal Government asked California to work collaboratively to identify any noncitizens registered to vote in the State. California made no serious effort to do so," the lawsuit said.
"The United States thus seeks commonplace election relief when a ballot is called into question. This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote-by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined," it added.
CBS News has reached out to the secretary of state and the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk for comment.
The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division has filed 31 lawsuits in an effort to force states to hand over unredacted copies of their voter rolls. The division has said it wants to ensure states are keeping clean voter lists, but it has since acknowledged that it also intends to share the data with the Department of Homeland Security so that the lists can be screened for noncitizens.
Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, sent letters to all 50 states in July threatening to take criminal action if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls.
So far, the Justice Department has lost 26 of those cases, and has not achieved one legal victory to date.
It has resorted to using publicly available voter lists and other investigative means to try to identify noncitizens who may be registered in those states.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Senate GOP see Starlink become latest flash point over Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Trump, Senate GOP see Starlink become latest flash point over Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said Wednesday that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump are responsible for any curbs on Ukraine's military-grade Starlink network.
Writing on X, Musk said that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Ukraine had accused SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on the Starshield internet service without warning, leading to disruptions to Ukrainian military operations amid fresh Russian strikes on its energy infrastructure.
On Wednesday, Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technology, said SpaceX had implemented a speed limit on Starlink terminals in motion, without notifying the country's defense forces.
That had disrupted some missions, and the same restrictions also applied to Starshield, he said on Telegram . Starlink is used to operate Ukraine's interceptor drones, the "most effective solution" against Moscow's Shahed drones, Beskrestnov said.
Starshield is a military-grade satellite network, while Starlink is only meant for "civilian or defensive activities," Musk said.
Some restrictions appear to have been partially lifted, with former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov thanking Musk early Thursday morning that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers an hour had been restored. "Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," Fedorov added.
The developments come amid tensions between Kyiv and Washington over an "energy ceasefire," between Ukraine and Russia announced by Trump.
Ukraine has, however, welcomed a deal subject to Moscow honoring its commitment, while Russian authorities said talks were ongoing, without confirming whether they had reached an agreement. On Monday, Zelenskyy accused the Russians of breaching the ceasefire.
Trump had also taken aim at Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities, saying that Kyiv's attacks were responsible for the increase in diesel prices, instead of the U.S.' war with Iran.
Washington has threatened to cut intelligence sharing with Kyiv, Reuters reported Wednesday, while Ukrainian officials said a day earlier that they have not received warnings of Russian attacks on the country for two straight days.
— CNBC's Elsa Olhen contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Scientists knew the Doomsday Glacier was melting. They didn’t realize how ‘aggressively’
articles.title_zh: Scientists knew the Doomsday Glacier was melting. They didn’t realize how ‘aggressively’
articles.content_orig:
The planet’s widest glacier is melting “more aggressively” than previously projected, meaning its impacts on global sea level rise could be double current estimates, according to new research by a team of glaciologists.
Thwaites Glacier in West Antarctica — nicknamed the Doomsday Glacier because of the catastrophe its collapse would trigger — is a huge wildcard when it comes to forecasting global sea level rise.
Real-time coverage, so you're never caught off guard.
The Florida-sized glacier, which lies in one of the least accessible places on Earth, has been retreating for decades and its melting ice currently contributes around 4% to global sea level rise.
But the mechanisms behind its retreat are exceptionally complex, making it tricky to precisely map out its future.
It’s a vital task, however, as Thwaites holds enough water to raise sea levels by more than 2 feet if it were to collapse. Because it also acts as a cork holding back the vast Antarctic ice sheet, it could ultimately lead to around 10 feet of sea level rise, devastating coastal communities from Miami to Manila.
Glaciologists from the University of California, Irvine and NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory have developed a new ice sheet model they say better reflects what’s happening underneath this ice giant.
Thwaites’ rapid retreat is driven by processes at its “grounding line” — the point at which the ice rises up from the seabed and starts to float on the ocean as an ice shelf.
But while typical ice sheet models have tended to view the grounding line as something fixed and mostly stable, “we have come to acknowledge a different arrangement beneath Earth’s major ocean-terminating glaciers,” said the report’s lead author Mattia Poinelli, a project scientist at UCLA who was an Earth system science researcher at UC Irvine at the time of the study.
Satellite data reveals the grounding line is actually a “grounding zone,” sometimes miles wide, where seawater constantly flushes in and out with the tides, lifting and lowering the thick ice in a process known as “tidal pumping.” This allows relatively warm ocean water to penetrate “deep underneath the ice sheets and causing vigorous melting,” Poinelli said.
When the scientists adjusted models to include the concept of a grounding zone, they found Thwaites could contribute up to 1.2 inches of sea level rise by 2100 — twice previous estimates — even without further global warming, according to the findings published Monday in the journal Nature Communications.
Scientists looked deep beneath the Doomsday Glacier. What they found spells potential disaster for the planet
The land on which Thwaites sits slopes downward, meaning as the glacier melts, more ice is exposed to warm ocean water. The topography is complicated, however, by two key underwater ridges, which “pin” the ice, holding it back from flowing into the ocean more rapidly.
The melting processes at Thwaites’ grounding zone are accelerating the “unpinning” of ice from a large ridge called the Mouginot Ridge, the study found. There is a 60% chance that it will be unpinned by the end of the century, the study found, after which the glacier is likely to retreat quickly down the sloping bedrock toward the next major ridge.
The findings suggest the impacts of losing Thwaites might have been underestimated. A sea level rise of 1.2 inches may not sound much but it’s enough to greatly magnify dangers to coastal populations.
The results “predict greater risk of and exposure for coastal flooding than anticipated in the coming decades,” said Eric Rignot, a report author and professor of Earth system science at UC Irvine.
Ted Scambos, a senior research scientist for the Earth Science and Observation Center at the University of Colorado Boulder, who was not involved in the research, said the findings could be “a real gamechanger for sea level forecasting from Thwaites.”
But he and other experts caution that more research is needed to understand the impacts of different grounding zone melting processes, not least by getting direct data from underneath the glacier.
Journey to the disappearing edge of the Arctic
“The reality is that there is a lot we still need to find out about grounding zone processes to be able to make confident predictions about how fast ice will be lost,” said Robert Larter, a marine geophysicist at British Antarctic Survey, who was also not involved in the study. The environment beneath Thwaites, which is very difficult to access, is even more complex than the paper describes, he added.
Getting observational data from Thwaites’ grounding line is the next step, Rignot said. The scientists are planning to travel there in 2028 to deploy instruments able to document the flushing in and out of seawater.
“We have been aware of the impacts of climate change on our planet’s sensitive ice sheets for decades,” Rignot said, “but a mounting realization gained in recent years of what is really happening on the undersides of glaciers like Thwaites is leading to an even greater sense of alarm.”
He said the world must cut planet-heating pollution now to limit the impacts but warned, “even if we do, we can expect higher sea levels in the future resulting from the damage that has already been done.”

articles.title_orig: Red Magic 12 Pro+ gaming phone launches with Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, liquid-cooling system, 8,400mAh battery, and more
articles.title_zh: Red Magic 12 Pro+ gaming phone launches with Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, liquid-cooling system, 8,400mAh battery, and more
articles.content_orig:
Add GIZMOCHINA as Preferred Source on Google
As an Amazon Associate, Gizmochina earns from qualifying purchases. Links on this page may earn us a commission at no extra cost to you.
Red Magic 12 Pro+ has officially launched in China with a range of hardware upgrades aimed at mobile gamers. The new flagship combines high-refresh-rate visuals with advanced cooling technology and a large battery. It also retains several gaming-focused features, including a 3.5mm headphone jack and dedicated shoulder triggers. Here’s everything you need to know about Red Magic’s newest gaming phone.
Starting from the front, the Red Magic 12 Pro+ features a 6.85-inch BOE X11 OLED display with a 2,688 × 1,216-pixel resolution, a 185Hz refresh rate and ultra-narrow 0.96mm bezels. Since it does not have a camera punch-hole, it offers a truly full-screen viewing experience.
The panel supports a 500Hz touch sampling rate and up to 5,000Hz instantaneous touch sampling, alongside 10-bit colors, 1,900 nits of global brightness and 5,000 nits of local peak brightness. It also offers 2,592Hz PWM dimming at low brightness and DC-like dimming at higher brightness.
Performance comes from Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset, paired with RedCore R5 gaming and G1 display control chips. The phone supports LPDDR5T memory running at up to 10,667Mbps and UFS 4.1 Pro storage. Red Magic also supports simultaneous super-resolution and frame interpolation at up to 2K resolution and 185Hz in compatible games.
The device packs an 8,400mAh battery with 120W wired charging, 80W wireless charging, and bypass charging for powering the phone directly during gaming. Its ICE cooling system combines an active cooling fan with a liquid-cooling setup, alongside additional thermal materials. The built-in fan reaches 25,500rpm and carries an IPX8 water-resistance rating, while the phone itself is rated IP68 and IP69 for dust and water resistance.
The rear camera setup comprises a 50-megapixel primary camera with optical image stabilization and a 50-megapixel ultra-wide camera. A 16-megapixel OmniVision sensor sits beneath the display for selfies and video calls.
The phone runs Android 17-based RedMagic OS 12 and features an ultrasonic in-screen fingerprint sensor. Other features include 700Hz shoulder triggers, dual 1115E linear speakers, three microphones, an X-axis linear motor, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.3, NFC, an IR blaster, USB 3.2 Gen 2 and a 3.5mm headphone jack.
In China, the Red Magic 12 Pro+ is available in Dark Night Transparent, Silver Wing Transparent and Ice Blue Transparent finishes. The 12GB+256GB model is priced at 6,999 Yuan (~$1,050), while the 16GB+512GB and 16GB+1TB variants cost 7,999 Yuan (~$1,200) and 8,999 Yuan (~$1,350), respectively.
Red Magic also previewed a limited-edition Golden Saga model with 24GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, featuring a forged-carbon cooling design. Its price and exact release date have yet to be announced. There is no confirmed international availability yet.
What’s your opinion about the Red Magic 12 Pro+ gaming phone’s specs and price? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: China indicates rare earths will keep flowing to EU, regardless of U.S. trade deal expiration
articles.title_zh: China indicates rare earths will keep flowing to EU, regardless of U.S. trade deal expiration
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — China intends to keep exporting rare earths to Europe regardless of whether a U.S. trade deal with Beijing gets extended past January.
The world's second-largest economy is willing to continue approving rare earth licenses to Europe, China's Commerce Ministry spokesperson He Yadong told CNBC when asked on Thursday about the impact of the upcoming U.S. deadline.
Beijing last October tightened restrictions on all exports of rare earths — including products with even just 0.1% of China-sourced rare earths . The move followed a new U.S. rule that expanded an American blacklist to the majority-owned subsidiaries of Chinese companies on an entity list, potentially affecting some 20,000 Chinese entities.
However, both the U.S. and China agreed to suspend those measures for one year at a meeting in late October 2025 between Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump. Ahead of the leaders' latest summit last month, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the truce was extended by two months to January.
Trade tensions between the EU and Beijing cooled last week after European trade commissioner Maroš Sefčovič met with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao in Beijing . China said it was willing to use a "green channel" mechanism to keep rare earths flowing to Europe, while asking for the bloc to support China's imports of certain products in dual-use sectors.
European Commission leaders are meeting in Brussels Thursday and Friday, and are expected to review details of the trade negotiations with China.

Dutch semiconductor equipment giant ASML expects China to account for about 20 per cent of its total sales this year, after seeing shipments to the market more than double during the previous quarter despite mounting US pressure for tighter export restrictions on less advanced chipmaking machinery.
The company’s sales to China surged 109 per cent in the third quarter compared with the previous three months, according to financial results released on Wednesday. That took China’s share of ASML’s machine sales to 23 per cent, up from 14 per cent in the second quarter.
The revenue jump comes as Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten faces pressure from Washington to tighten restrictions on sales of chipmaking machines to China.

articles.title_orig: The world’s most dangerous tree lives in Florida. Here’s how it can kill you
articles.title_zh: The world’s most dangerous tree lives in Florida. Here’s how it can kill you
articles.content_orig:
Anthony Talcott , Digital Journalist
ORLANDO, Fla. – Florida is no stranger to danger, whether it’s massive sinkholes , powerful hurricanes , or invasive threats .
But what many residents might not know is that there’s a tree native to the Sunshine State that’s considered the most dangerous in the world.
That’s according to the Guinness World Records , which has granted the moniker to the Manchineel tree.
At first glance, there doesn’t appear to be anything all that dangerous about the Manchineel.
The tree is native to South Florida, and it gets its name from the Spanish word for “little apple,” which references the fruit that can be seen growing on the Manchineel.
However, researchers with the UF/IFAS warn that the tree has also been dubbed the “Tree of Death” due to the plant’s and its fruit’s deadly nature.
According to the UF/IFAS, all parts of the Manchineel tree are extremely poisonous, as the tree oozes a sap from its leaves, twigs, bark and fruit that can cause burn-like blisters when it comes into contact with skin.
“People have reported heavy inflammation of the eyes and even temporary blindness from irritants carried in the smoke of this tree’s burning wood,” researchers wrote. “While some claim that they are immune to the noxious sap when it interacts with their skin, ingesting any part of this tree can be lethal and is not recommended.”
[BELOW: Invasive chameleons infest Central Florida neighborhood]
Over two decades ago , a doctor who inadvertently tasted the Manchineel’s fruit described it as “pleasantly sweet,” though she later noticed a “strange peppery feeling” in her mouth.
Soon, that feeling coalesced into a burning sensation and tightness in her throat. The symptoms reportedly became excruciating and took around eight hours to subside.
“Even standing under this tree in the rain can be harmful,” another study states . “Reports of students who took shelter during a storm under this tree gave rise to concurrent dermatitis and ophthalmitis .”
The sap’s poison is so potent, researchers claim, that Native Americans historically used the substance to coat their arrows when hunting.
Nowadays, warning signs and red rings are often posted near Manchineels to warn unwary visitors to stay away.
That being said, most residents in the state aren’t likely to come across a Manchineel during their day-to-day routine.
This is because the Manchineel tree is an endangered species, meaning it’s in danger of becoming extinct.
[BELOW: Here’s the story behind the ‘Devil’s Tree’ in Florida]
In the Sunshine State, the tree can be primarily found in the Everglades, with reports documented in Monroe and Miami-Dade counties.
Regardless, though, it’s a good idea to give a wide berth to any of these trees if you come across one. After all, coming into contact with its sap in any way could put you in an incredibly painful situation — or worse.

articles.title_orig: Still smiling at 117, Albanian may be world's oldest woman
articles.title_zh: Still smiling at 117, Albanian may be world's oldest woman
articles.content_orig:
At 117, Qamile Marra is not particularly concerned with proving she may be the world's oldest woman -- or even persuading Albanian pension officials that she is not dead.
For a woman born under Ottoman rule, who turned 36 a fortnight before the end of World War II and outlived Albania's communist dictatorship, her focus remains firmly on enjoying life.
"Life is beautiful, like Mount Tomorr in bloom," she told AFP with a smile, referring to one of Albania's loftiest peaks as she sat outside her home in Ferras, about 100 kilometres (60 miles) south of the capital.
Surrounded by fruit trees, Marra has spent almost her entire life in the village, growing her own food and tending livestock.
"You live as long as God has decreed," she said, her deeply wrinkled face framed by a traditional white headscarf.
According to her birthdate as listed on several official documents -- August 19, 1909 -- Marra would be two days older than Britain's Ethel Caterham, recognised by Guinness World Records as the world's oldest living woman.
Definitively proving the age of "supercentenarians" can be difficult.
Many of the people famous for living the longest are from places where shoddy recordkeeping and suspected pension fraud are rampant, according to a study that won the 2024 Ig Nobel prize, which awards offbeat scientific research.
But Marra has extensive records that appear to confirm her age.
Her relatives have contacted Guinness and hold a birth certificate issued in 1945, a passport issued in 1978 and a recent identity card, all showing the same date of birth.
Her age even surprised local authorities, who stopped her pension when she turned 100, according to her 80-year-old son Hysen.
"They didn't believe my mother was still alive," he said, recalling how he had to show proof, including witness statements, to resume the meagre payments.
Earlier this month, the government issued her a special state pension to mark her age.
Perhaps the answer lies in Marra's habits and lifestyle.
She rises early to sweep the yard, water her flowers and feed the chickens before settling down with her favourite coffee.
She still enjoys regular walks through her carefully tended orchard with her son, who lives with her, stopping to pick ripe pomegranates along the way.
She also slips basil leaves in her pockets to "enjoy the aroma".
Whatever the secret, her son says she has never even visited a doctor.
"She is in good health and has never taken any medication."
Marra's husband died 36 years ago, but she still smiles when talking about their decades together -- an arranged marriage, but a loving one.
"Otherwise, how could I have had seven children with him?" she said.
She has now seen five generations of her family grow up around her.
Tears welled up as she remembered the family and friends she had lost. But her face brightened when a niece called to chat.
"I've watched them get engaged, marry and build their own homes and lives," she said.
"When I see people coming and going in the house, I am so happy."
From her own youth, she has kept a single photograph: a near-century-old picture of a young woman wearing a white scarf just like the one she had on.

articles.title_orig: UNESCO hosted regional capacity-building workshop for natural World Heritage in Central Asia and Mongolia in Almaty - International Union for Conservation of Nature
articles.title_zh: UNESCO hosted regional capacity-building workshop for natural World Heritage in Central Asia and Mongolia in Almaty - International Union for Conservation of Nature
articles.source: International Union for Conservation of Nature
articles.content_orig:
UNESCO and IUCN brought together State Party representatives and site managers from the heart of Eurasia, with support of the UNESCO/Republic of Korea Funds-in-Trust project aiming to enhance transnational cooperation.
13 October 2026 -  The capacity-building workshop for natural World Heritage properties in Central Asia (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan) and Mongolia was held in Almaty on 7 and 8 October 2026. The two-day event aimed to further strengthen the technical capacity of site managers and national authorities to protect natural World Heritage properties, with a particular focus on transboundary cooperation.
The workshop was coordinated by the UNESCO World Heritage Centre , the UNESCO Regional Offices in Almaty and Beijing and IUCN . It was built on the 2025 capacity-building workshop held under the same project, which aims to enhance transboundary cooperation among natural and mixed World Heritage properties in Asia by strengthening existing site management, mapping knowledge and capacity gaps, and identifying further opportunities for transboundary cooperation.
The workshop was financed by the Republic of Korea through the UNESCO/Republic of Korea Funds-in-Trust project “Enhancing Transnational Cooperation and Fostering Peace: Natural and Mixed World Heritage in Asia”. The project’s donor is the Korea Heritage Service (KHS). Russian–English interpretation was provided throughout.
Participants reviewed the concept of Outstanding Universal Value and World Heritage activities in Central Asia and Mongolia, including state of conservation, Periodic Reporting, the Upstream Process, Preliminary Assessments and nominations. They discussed how to ensure management effectiveness using tools such as Enhancing our Heritage Toolkit (EoH) 2.0 and the new 2026 Managing World Heritage Manual, and how conservation principles and governance help sustain the values and integrity of properties. State Party representatives and site managers shared experiences from Tajik National Park (Mountains of the Pamirs) , the Tugay forests of the Tigrovaya Balka Nature Reserve (Tajikistan), Western Tien-Shan (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan), Cold Winter Deserts of Turan (Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan), Uvs Nuur Basin (Mongolia/Russian Federation) and Landscapes of Dauria (Mongolia/Russian Federation), followed by lively exchanges among the participants. Scientific research and monitoring were also on the agenda, including species as indicators of ecosystem health, monitoring needs, techniques and tools, and common challenges, alongside the IKI project “One Health in Nature Conservation in Central Asia” and its support for World Heritage properties.
Natural heritage knows no borders; its conservation requires our shared responsibility and collective commitment. Central Asia and Mongolia are home to invaluable Outstanding Universal Value and unique ecosystems. - Ms Yunjung Lee, Director, World Heritage Division, Korea Heritage Service
The main tools for tackling issues are coordination, capacity building and awareness raising. These require a change in attitudes and in management approaches in our daily work.  And for this we need to establish cooperation and improve existing coordination. - Mr Amir Piric, Director, UNESCO Regional Office in Almaty
A significant part of the discussion focused on transboundary conservation and management. Participants examined conservation principles and governance through case studies of the serial transnational World Heritage properties represented at the workshop, as well as other examples from Asia such as Phong Nha-Ke Bang and Hin Nam No National Parks (Lao PDR/Viet Nam). Lessons learned from the East Asian–Australasian Flyway Partnership (EAAFP) highlighted the importance of connecting people, including site managers, and building relationship and trust as the foundation of regional cooperation and conservation across borders.
Experts from ICCROM and IUCN addressed how to assess impacts on Outstanding Universal Value, including Environmental Impact Assessments (EIAs), assessing cumulative impacts through Strategic Environmental Assessments (SEAs) and the transboundary dimensions of regional impact assessments. The new GEF8 EcoLand joint IUCN-UNDP project on “Integrated Conservation Management and Restoration of High-Value Landscapes in Uzbekistan” was presented, together with opportunities through UNESCO’s Natural Sciences programmes and the outcomes of UNCCD COP17 in Mongolia. An interactive exercise mapped networks and potential synergies, and the workshop concluded with reflections, feedback and a discussion of strategic next steps.
Representatives of each State Party shared their reflections on the workshop and highlighted potential follow-up activities, including strengthening operational capacities (e.g. harmonization of Tentative Lists, SEAs and resource mobilization) and further exploring thematic areas such as sustainable tourism, invasive species and climate change, through knowledge-sharing and exchange, as well as the development of a common communication platform. Building on the rich discussions during the workshop and with the support of the UNESCO/Republic of Korea Funds-in-Trust project, UNESCO and IUCN will continue to engage with national authorities and site managers across the region to support their ongoing efforts to safeguard the natural heritage located in the heart of Eurasia and further strengthen transnational cooperation.
Conservation funding rarely reaches the people who know the lands and territories best. Podong sets…
Government and scientific and technical experts from across sectors started jointly identifying how…
IUCN, through the Oceania Regional Office, is pleased to welcome Te Tira Whakamātaki from Aotearoa…
